reports.headline: Jamaica Bay fluke slide out to the inlet as bay water tops 78
reports.subhead: New moon springs build through the weekend, and the flush through Rockaway Inlet is setting up the best bite of July so far.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the bay got warm — warmer than I like to see it in early July, honestly. We were sitting in the high 70s in the back channels off Broad Channel and up toward Grassy Bay, and that kind of heat pushes fluke off the flats fast. When the shallow water gets soupy like that, doormats don't stick around to get lazy in it. They slide toward moving water — the inlet, the channel edges, anywhere the tide keeps things flushed and oxygenated. That's exactly what happened, and it's why the bite this week has a different address than it did in June.

This week the moon is sliding toward new — full new moon lands the 13th — which means we're building into spring tides right now, bigger swings each day through the weekend. Bigger tide means more water moving through Rockaway Inlet on the exchange, which means bait gets pushed and pulled harder, which means gamefish know exactly where to sit and wait. It also means Marine Parkway Bridge, my favorite piece of moving water in this whole system, is about to get a lot more interesting on the outgoing. When the current really rips through there this weekend, that's when the bass stack up on the down-current side of the pilings and let the tide do their hunting for them.

So here's what's actually happening on the water, not just what should be happening. Fluke: the pattern has flipped from bay flats to hard structure and moving water. Guys drifting Gulp Swimming Mullets in white and chartreuse — 4 and 5 inch, on 3/4 to 1 ounce bucktails — through the Rockaway Inlet channel and the deeper cuts by the Ruffle Bar and Ambrose Channel edges are doing better than the flats guys right now. Depths in the 15 to 25 foot range on the last two hours of the outgoing has been the sweet spot. I fished it myself Sunday and had three keepers to 4 pounds in about ninety minutes of drifting, lost two more to short strikes I never connected on — that tells me there's fish there but they're not exactly falling over themselves for it. You've got to keep the bucktail ticking bottom, not just drifting through the water column, or you'll miss the bite entirely in that current.

Stripers at Marine Parkway are doing what they always do this time of year — staging on the outgoing, working the rip lines off the bridge structure. Live eels fished on the bottom, or bunker chunks if you can get fresh bait, have been the better call over the past week compared to plugs, though I did hear of a few fish taken on white bucktails worked slow along the bridge shadow line right at dusk. Nothing giant — mostly schoolies and a few fish pushing the mid-20s — but consistent enough that it's worth the trip if you're fishing the two hours around the outgoing. Bring a heavier leader than you think you need; those bridge pilings have teeth.

Bluefish have started showing in decent numbers off Rockaway Beach, chasing bunker pods that are working the surf line from about Beach 90th down toward Jacob Riis. Nothing like a fall blitz yet — don't get that confused — but if you see the bunker balling up and the birds start diving, that's your window. Diamond jigs or metal-lip swimmers thrown into the melee will get bit fast, but it doesn't last long, maybe twenty, thirty minutes before the blues push the bait somewhere else. Worth keeping a rod rigged in the truck if you're beach walking this week.

Porgies are steady but unspectacular around the rocks by Breezy Point and along the Cross Bay Bridge pilings — small stuff mostly, bloodworms or clam on a hi-lo rig fished right on bottom, good action if you've got kids along or just want a bend in the rod, but nothing that's going to fill a cooler with dinner-plate porgies yet. Blackfish season's closed this time of year in our waters, so that's off the table until fall.

On weakfish — I want to be straight with you, because I know the water temp reports have some people excited. The bay's been warm enough for a while now, but I haven't heard of a single weakfish caught in this system in weeks. Warm water gets them here, but warm water alone doesn't make them bite. Until somebody actually puts one in the boat, I'm not sending anybody chasing a ghost.

Looking ahead: the new moon springs peak around the 11th through the 13th, and that's when I'd expect the Marine Parkway outgoing to really turn on, especially right at sunset when the tide and the light change over together — that's a dependable combination in this bay. If the bigger tidal push also flushes more bait out through the inlet, the fluke bite on the channel edges should hold, maybe improve, through the weekend. I'd fish the outgoing at the bridge Friday evening if the wind stays reasonable, and I'd have a backup plan to drift the inlet channel for fluke if the bass don't show — that's how I'm planning my own week. Canarsie Pier is still a solid bet for bottom fishing if you want an easy access point without a boat, and Breezy Point surf is worth a look early mornings for anyone chasing that first real bluefish run of the summer. Keep an eye on the bait — where the bunker go, everything else follows.

reports.headline: New moon springs load up the Race as fluke push out of the bays and into the rip
reports.subhead: Building current through Plum Gut and Orient Point is stacking bass in the eddies while bonito make their last-call push into the Sound's eastern mouth.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the Race was still riding out the slack cycle off the June full moon — current strong but not violent, topping maybe 3.5 knots on the big pushes, and that gave the bass room to spread out instead of stack. Surface water's been sitting warm, upper 60s pushing 70 in the harbors, and a run of southwest wind kept the afternoons choppy and green through Plum Gut. Fishable, but sloppy enough that I was picking my windows — dawn and the last two hours of daylight, when the wind laid down and the rip cleaned up.

That's changing fast. We're building toward a new moon around the 13th, and that means spring tides loading in hard through the weekend. Watch what that does to the Race and Plum Gut — current speed ramps back up toward that classic 5-knot scream, and when it does, the bass quit roaming and get pinned into the eddies behind the rock piles and drop-offs where they don't have to fight the full flow to eat. The window I'm circling hardest is Friday through Monday, July 10–13. High stand at Orient is lining up close to sunset those evenings, which means the top of the tide — when the current eases just enough to let fish feed instead of just hold — hits right as the light goes gold. That's the first real PM flood window we've had since before the full moon, and it's worth building your evening around.

Fluke have been the story of the last two weeks, and it's not really about the Sound itself — it's about the bay water pushing them out. Peconic and the back harbors have gotten warm enough that the fluke are abandoning the flats and sliding toward anything with moving water and a temperature break. That means the mouths near Orient, the deeper edges of Plum Gut, and the rip lines off Fishers Island are holding better fish than the bays right now. I've been dragging 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails through 25 to 40 feet on the last of the outgoing at the Gut, letting the bait bounce bottom on the drift instead of ripping it — the fluke here are eating slow presentations, not aggressive hops. Best fish this week went about 5 pounds off the Orient rip on a chartreuse bucktail tipped with squid strip, but it's not a slam-dunk bite — you're covering water and culling through short fish to find the keepers.

Stripers are still very much a night-and-gray-light game right now. The bigger fish — and there have been some genuine 30-plus-pound reports scattered between here, Block Island, and out toward the Cape — are holding deep in the eddies at the Race in 60 to 90 feet, and they're coming up to feed hard right at the tide change. I've been running big soft plastics and 2-ounce bucktails down into the current seam, letting them swing and stall in the slack pocket behind the boulder fields rather than fishing them straight through the flow. Surface plugs — bone Danny-style swimmers and pencil poppers — have drawn a handful of violent strikes at first light off Orient Point when bait's been pushed up shallow, but that bite has been more feast-or-famine than steady; some mornings it's on for twenty minutes and dead the rest of the tide.

Bluefish are the more dependable player right now. Solid choppers, 4 to 8 pounds, are showing consistently in the rip current itself, especially where the Race dumps into deeper water on the ebb. Metal — Kastmasters and Hopkins, half-ounce to two-ounce depending on how hard the current's running — worked with a fast retrieve through the moving water has been drawing consistent hookups, and topwater has worked when there's bird activity marking bait on the surface. If you want a guaranteed bend in the rod this week, this is closer to it than the bass.

Porgies are stacked deep and reliable on the humps and rock piles inside Plum Gut and around Fishers Island — 25 to 45 feet, sandworms or clam on a high-low rig, bounced right on bottom during the slower current stages when the current's too strong for anything else to hold station. It's not glamorous but it's a near-guaranteed box of fish if the bigger stuff isn't cooperating.

Worth watching: this is the tail end of the pelagic window for the eastern end. First bonito and Spanish mackerel sign has started showing on the ocean side toward Moriches and Shinnecock, and with the bonito corridor widening east past Block Island, there's a real chance the first ones push into the mouth of the Sound around Orient and Fishers on clean incoming water before this window shuts down after the weekend. I wouldn't build a whole trip around it, but if you're already out there working the rip, keep a light spinning rod rigged with a small metal ready to fire.

Weakfish, for the record — still nothing. Water's plenty warm enough, but that species has ghosted this stretch of Sound for weeks now and I'm not counting on it changing. If I've got one day to fish this weekend, it's the Friday or Saturday evening flood at Plum Gut, working the eddy seams as the tide tops out into sunset. Plan B if the bass don't show is simple — drop down on the fluke drift at the Gut mouth and let the bucktails do the talking.

reports.headline: New Moon Springs Load the Narrows — Stratford Shoal Wakes Up at Dusk
reports.subhead: Bigger tides are pushing bait through the Central Sound pinch points, and the bass and blues are starting to answer the dinner bell right on schedule.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week was a mixed bag out here, and if you were watching the same water I was, you know why. We came off a stretch of blustery afternoon wind — nothing dramatic, but enough sustained chop out of the southwest to roil the bait pods and push the surface temp around. The bays warmed up fast on the back of it. Port Jeff Harbor and the coves off the Norwalk Islands got soupy and warm in the shallows, while the mid-Sound current lanes through Stratford Shoal and the Middle Ground stayed cooler and cleaner because that water's always moving. That split — warm skinny water versus cold moving water — is the whole story of this week's bite. Bait doesn't like getting cooked in the shallows any more than we do, so it's sliding toward the channels and the rips where the tide keeps things fresh.

This week the moon is doing the heavy lifting. We're building toward a new moon, and that means bigger swings on the tide boards — the kind of springs tide that really cranks the current through the pinch points that make Central Sound what it is. Stratford Shoal, the Middle Ground rip, the cuts between the Norwalk Islands — all of that structure works because the Sound narrows here and squeezes bait through like a funnel. Bigger tide, harder squeeze, more bait getting disoriented in the rip lines. The best of it lines up Friday through Monday, when the PM flood is converging with sunset — high stand right around last light. That's the window I'm circling. We haven't had a good evening flood bite like this since before the June full moon, and the timing on this one is about as clean as it gets.

Striper fishing has been honest, not spectacular. I've had a few solid evenings working the downcurrent side of Stratford Shoal on the last two hours of the outgoing, drifting bunker chunks on fish-finder rigs in 25 to 35 feet, and connecting with schoolies mixed with a few fish pushing 30 inches. Nothing that's going to make the wall at the tackle shop, but steady enough that I'd call it a real bite, not a fluke session. The better fish have been coming on live bunker fished on wire near the Middle Ground Light bar — there's been enough peanut bunker stacking up on that bar to draw bass up shallow at dawn and dusk, and a few guys trolling small umbrella rigs through there have found better-grade fish, low 30s, in that top 15 feet of water. Once the new moon tide starts really moving this weekend, I expect that bar to get more interesting. Bigger current means more bait getting pinned against the structure, and that's when the bigger bass show up to work it.

Bluefish have been the more reliable player the last ten days, and they've been mixed right in with the stripers wherever the peanut bunker shows. Charles Island and the reef structure off it have had chopper blues in the 3-to-6-pound class blowing up on top in the last hour of daylight — poppers and stick baits worked fast get bit, and if you slow down you just get cut off. The Norwalk Islands — Cockenoe, Sheffield, Copps — have had similar action on the down-current edges as the tide drops, bluefish and schoolie bass mixed together, nothing picky about presentation as long as it's moving.

Fluke have shifted, and if you're still working the shallow flats inside the harbors you're behind the fish. The warm water in Port Jeff Harbor and the back coves has pushed the better fluke out toward the channel edges and the deeper structure — I've had my best luck in 28 to 35 feet off the Stratford Shoal drop, dragging four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on three-quarter-ounce bucktails, slow and right on bottom. Nothing huge, mostly fish in the 16-to-19-inch range with the occasional keeper mixed in, but the bite has been consistent on the last of the outgoing when the current is still moving enough to keep the bait working but not so hard you can't hold bottom.

Porgies are about the most dependable thing going right now. The reef structure around Charles Island and the rockier stretches off the Norwalk chain have porgies stacked up in 15 to 25 feet, and high-low rigs with sandworms or clam strips are getting hit about as fast as you can drop. If you want a guaranteed bend in the rod with the kids aboard, that's still your play. Blackfish are closed this time of year in both states, so leave the tog jigs in the box until fall.

Weakfish remain a ghost. I haven't heard a credible report out of Central Sound in weeks, and given how quiet they've been everywhere else with warm water sitting on them for a while now, I'm not holding my breath. If they show, it'll be incidental — a surprise on a bass rig, not a target worth planning a trip around.

As for bonito — it's still early. I know the itch starts this time of year, but the real push through our stretch is usually an August story, once the water's had more time to build and hold. I'll be watching the bait schools at the mouth of the harbors for signs, but I wouldn't burn a tank of gas chasing them yet.

If I had one shot this week, I'd take it Saturday evening at Stratford Shoal, working the last two hours of the flood into the sunset high stand with bunker chunks and a couple of topwater casts thrown in as light fades. The tide's building, the bait's getting squeezed through the right places, and that convergence of high water and last light is the kind of setup that's produced for me before. Plan B if the current doesn't cooperate — work the Middle Ground bar at first light instead, before the boat traffic stirs things up.

reports.headline: New moon springs reopen the sunset flood bite at Execution Rocks and Stepping Stones
reports.subhead: Bass are stacking on the PM tide as bunker pour past Matinecock and fluke abandon the warm harbors for deeper water.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the Sound did what it does every July — it got soft and sleepy in the middle of the day and came alive at the edges. Water in the harbors, Manhasset Bay and Hempstead Harbor especially, pushed well up into the mid-70s under a string of sunny, light-wind days, and that heat pushed the fluke right out of the shallow stuff and into the channels where they belong this time of year. Tide-wise we were riding out the back side of the June full moon cycle, so the current was still carrying some push through the week, but nothing dramatic — clean water, no real blow to speak of, and that let bait settle into its usual summer stations. Bunker schools have been thick off Matinecock Point on the last two hours of the incoming, and where you find bunker in July, you find blues and you find bass working underneath them.

This week the story is the new moon. We're building into new-moon springs through the weekend, with the tightest alignment falling July 11-13 — and that matters more than the moon phase itself. What it means practically is that Kings Point high stand is now lining up with sunset, which reopens the PM flood-sunset window for stripers for the first time since the June full moon cycle faded out. That's a real thing on this stretch of Sound — when the flood peaks right as the light goes down, bass move up onto the rockpiles and current breaks to feed in that low-light stretch before full dark, and Execution Rocks and Stepping Stones are ground zero for it. Bigger tide swings from the new moon also mean stronger current through the Throgs Neck rips and around Hart Island, which should reshuffle bait and put fish back on the reaction bite rather than the sluggish daytime pattern we've had.

On the striper side, it's been a mixed week honestly — not bad, but you had to work the tide stage right or you got nothing. The fish that are around Execution Rocks have been sitting tight to the rockpile on the last two hours of the outgoing, and the guys drifting bucktails — bone or white, 1 to 1.5 ounce, tipped with a strip of fresh bunker — have done the most damage in the 20 to 35 foot depths off the light. Live-lining bunker under a slip float around Stepping Stones on the early incoming has also produced, with a few fish pushing 30 inches, but you had to grind for them. The predictable window everyone should circle is the sunset flood I mentioned — Friday through Monday, July 10-13 — when that high stand at Kings Point lines up with dusk. That's when I'd be positioned on the up-current side of Execution Rocks with a swimming plug or a bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig, because that's the two-hour stretch where the bigger fish have been showing.

Bluefish have been the more consistent player. The bunker pods off Matinecock Point have blues underneath them most mornings on the tail of the incoming, and it's about as simple as fishing gets right now — heavy bunker spoons trolled through the edges of the school, or if you want to make it interesting, snag a bunker on a treble and freeline it back into the chaos. Choppers in the 3 to 6 pound range, occasional bigger fish mixed in. This bite tends to shut off hard once the sun gets up over the trees, so first light through about 8:30 is your window.

Fluke have shifted, same as I said above. Manhasset Bay and the mouth of Hempstead Harbor got too warm and too thin on bait, and the better fish have slid out to the channel edges and the deeper water toward Execution Rocks and the Throgs Neck approaches. Four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the outgoing in 25 to 40 feet, have been the ticket — nothing gaudy, just a slow drag along bottom with occasional bumps to keep it in the strike zone. Sizes have been fair, mostly 16 to 19 inches with the occasional keeper mixed in, so it's not a bent-rod bonanza but it's a legitimate meal if you put in the drift time.

Porgies have been steady and honestly the most reliable thing going right now. The rockpiles at Execution Rocks and around Stepping Stones are holding good numbers, and a simple high-low rig with bloodworm or clam strips on size 6 or 4 hooks, fished tight to structure on a slowing tide, will fill a cooler without much drama. This is a good one to have in your back pocket on days when the bass and blues are being stubborn.

Weakfish, I'll be straight with you — quiet. Water's warm enough on paper, but I'm not hearing of real reports coming out of this end of the Sound, and I wouldn't plan a trip around them right now.

Looking ahead, the new-moon spring tides building into the weekend are the whole story for this zone. If that PM flood keeps lining up with sunset at Kings Point like the tide tables suggest, I'd be at Execution Rocks or Stepping Stones Friday through Monday evening, working the last two hours of the incoming into dark. If the bass don't cooperate on that stage, my backup is the Matinecock bunker school at first light — that bite has been the one sure thing all week, and with the tighter spring current pushing bait harder through the funnel points, I don't see any reason it slows down soon.

reports.headline: Fluke bail out of the bays as summer heat pushes them to the inlets
reports.subhead: Manasquan and Barnegat are stacking doormats on the outgoing while stripers thin out and the new moon springs load up for the weekend.
reports.body_markdown:
Let me tell you what happened this week — the back bays cooked. Barnegat Bay and the shallow flats up in Raritan pushed into the upper 70s, some spots probably kissing 80, and that's too warm for a fluke to sit comfortable in three feet of skinny water with the sun beating down on it all day. So they did what they always do when the bay gets like bathwater — they packed up and ran for the inlets and the ocean front where there's moving current and cooler water underneath. We got a shot of upwelled ocean water this week too, dropped the front-beach temp down into the low 70s, and that's a gift. Cooler, cleaner water meeting warm bay water at the inlet mouths is exactly the kind of seam that turns a slow week into a good one.

Now look ahead — we're building into new moon springs, peaking Saturday through Monday, July 11th through the 13th. Bigger tide swings, more water moving, more current speed through the inlets, which means more bait getting flushed and more fish stacking up to eat it. The moon's going dark right as those tides peak, so the flood tide in the evening lines up close to sunset this weekend — that's the window I want. When the flood stacks up against last light, bass and blues both get more comfortable coming shallow to feed, and you get that hour where everything just seems to switch on at once. If I only had one evening this week, I'd burn it Saturday on that sunset flood.

Fluke is the story right now and it's a decent one, not a great one — you've gotta work for it. Manasquan Inlet has been giving up keepers on the outgoing, working the seam along the rock jetty in 15 to 25 feet, bucktails tipped with a strip of squid or a 4-inch pink Gulp Swimming Mullet dragged slow along bottom. Guys are finding fish to 24 inches doing exactly that, though for every keeper you're picking through a pile of shorts, so don't expect a five-fish box on autopilot. Barnegat Inlet's fishing similar — channel edges near the Coast Guard station, same deal, outgoing water, bounce the bucktail don't rip it. Sandy Hook's channel and the flats off Horseshoe Cove have some fluke mixed in too, but that bite's spottier — more of a search-and-drift game than a sure thing.

Bluefish have been the bright spot for anybody willing to run bunker chunks. Jumbo blues, real tackle-busters, showing up off the Shrewsbury Rocks and out past Sandy Hook in that 10 to 20 foot depth, hammering chunks fished on wire or heavy mono leader. Topwater's working too early and late — pencil poppers and big soft plastics if you can find them busting bait on the surface, which they have been doing sporadic mornings off the Hook.

Striper fishing, I'll be straight with you, is tough right now and that's normal for July on this stretch. Most of the migratory fish have pushed north into cooler water, and what's left in Raritan Bay and off Sandy Hook is holdover fish — schoolies mostly, some better ones mixed in — and they're playing the night shift. Best bet is fishing the rips off Sandy Hook and around the Chapel Hill and Flynn's Knoll structure after dark, live eels or bunker chunks fished slow on the bottom during that new moon flood. Don't expect a blitz. Expect a few quality bites if you put your time in on the right stage of tide.

Down in Cape May and the Delaware Bay side, black drum are winding down — the run's basically over for the season, a few stragglers left around the reef sites. Weakfish are still a ghost story down there. Water's been sitting well above 70 for over two weeks now and I haven't heard of a single legit weakfish report, which tells you warm water alone isn't the trigger everybody thinks it is — there's something else that needs to line up, and it hasn't yet this year. Porgies are solid and reliable on the reef structure off Cape May in 30 to 40 feet, small pieces of clam on a hi-lo rig, good action if you just want bent rods and a fish fry. Sea bass season closed up on the 21st so that's off the table till it reopens, but sheepshead have been showing in the back bays around pilings and bridge structure for anybody running fiddler crabs.

There's real noise offshore too — yellowfin and some bluefin working the 20 to 30 fathom lines and out toward the canyons, plus the first bonito starting to show at the eastern inlets on clean incoming water. That's a bit outside my beat but keep an ear out, because if that bonito push works its way down the coast the way it usually does in July, Manasquan and Shark River could see Spanish mackerel and bonito mixed in with the blues before the month's out.

My plan for the week: fluke at Manasquan on the outgoing with bucktails, blues on bunker off the Hook in the early morning, and I'm saving Saturday night for that new moon flood-sunset window on the rips. If the tide and the light line up like they should, that's where I'd put my rod in the water first.

reports.headline: Bay water pushes into the 70s, and the fluke and bass follow the current out the inlet
reports.subhead: New moon springs build toward a big weekend — Shinnecock Inlet's outgoing tide is where I'm putting my nights.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the bay finally caught up to summer. Shinnecock Bay's been sitting in the mid-to-upper 70s, and that kind of warmth does something predictable if you've fished this water long enough — it pushes the fluke right out of the flats and into anything with current and depth. I watched it happen over four nights on the water: the drift off Tiana that was holding decent fish two weeks ago went quiet, and the channel edges by the Canal and the inlet mouth started producing instead. Warm, slack bay water doesn't hold fluke long in July — they want moving water and a temperature break, and right now that break is sitting right at the inlet where upwelled ocean water, running close to 71 degrees, is meeting the warmer stuff sliding out on the tide. That seam is the whole story this week.

We're heading into new moon, peaking around July 11-13, and that means the tide swings are building — bigger floods, harder outgoing, more water moving through the inlet in less time. For a night guy like me, that's the green light. Bigger springs mean the outgoing rips harder off the jetties, bait gets pulled out with real force, and the stripers stack up in the eddies waiting for it. This is the first true nighttime window we've had since the June full moon set up, and I don't take that lightly. If the wind cooperates — and right now it looks manageable out of the south-southwest, nothing that's going to blow the inlet into chop — Friday through Monday night should be the best stretch we get this month.

Striped bass have been the most consistent thing I can point to, and they're doing it exactly where they're supposed to: the outgoing tide at Shinnecock Inlet, working the north jetty rocks and the back side structure toward the Coast Guard station. Eels have been the closer after dark — a 7-inch live eel, no weight, drifted right along the rock face on the last three hours of the outgoing. Guys throwing bunker-spook style pencil poppers at the top of the tide have picked off a few too, but the eel bite in the dark hours has been the more dependable pattern. Fish have run 24 to 34 inches mostly, with a couple of better ones pushing 20 pounds coming off the deeper pocket where the inlet channel bends toward the ocean side. Nothing blitz-style, but a hookup every 20 minutes on a good tide isn't a bad night by any measure.

Fluke have shifted, like I said, and the inlet mouth and the deeper channel water running out toward the ocean are where I'd put my rod right now instead of the mid-bay drifts that were producing back in June. Four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the last two hours of the outgoing in 12 to 18 feet, have been the ticket. A few boats working the deeper hole just inside the inlet on the ocean side have found keeper-class fish to 22 inches mixed with a lot of short fish, so it's not a fish-a-drift bite — you're covering water and culling through some throwbacks to find the better ones. Chartreuse bucktails tipped with squid strips have worked when the current's really ripping and you need something with more flash to get down.

Ponquogue Bridge has been holding weakfish, though I want to be straight about this one — it's a bite, not a blitz. Working bucktails tipped with a strip of squid or a Fishbites strip along the pilings after dark, on the last of the outgoing when the current sweeps bait past the structure, has produced fish in the 2 to 4 pound range with a scattered 5-pounder mixed in. It's a slow, patient bite, best fished from a boat anchored just up-current of the pilings so your presentation swings naturally into the shadow line. If you're not getting bit within the first 30 minutes of a tide stage, it's usually not going to happen — move rather than grind it out.

Porgies are steady but unspectacular around the inlet rocks and the deeper bay structure near the Canal mouth, clam on a standard rig doing the job for anyone who wants a mixed bag or a chance at a bonus blackfish holdover. Bluefish have been running through the inlet in short pushes, mostly smaller choppers chasing bait on the outgoing — good fun on light spinning gear with a metal lure if you catch the timing right, but they're not staying put long.

Looking ahead, the new moon springs building into the weekend are what I'd plan around. If the current at the inlet really loads up like I expect Friday through Sunday night, that's when I'd fish the eel bite hardest on the outgoing — the harder the current, the more the bass commit to the eddies along the jetty. If that doesn't produce, the backup is the fluke drift right at the inlet mouth where the temperature break is holding — that pattern should stay reliable as long as the bay keeps running warm and the ocean keeps feeding cooler water in on the tide. Worth checking the Canal connection into the Peconic side too if the bay stays sluggish; that link has bailed out plenty of slow weeks for me before.

reports.headline: Bay water pushes 79°, fluke stack up in the inlet throat as new moon springs build
reports.subhead: Moriches Bay got too warm for its own good this week — the fluke bailed for the cut, and a new moon flood-sunset window is lining up for bass by the weekend.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the bay did what it does every July when we get a stretch of light southwest wind and no rain to flush it — it cooked. Great South Bay pushed 78.8°F, and Moriches wasn't far behind on the flats off Tuthill Point and the mid-bay guts. That's warm enough to shut fluke down on the feed, and warm enough that they made the only smart move available to them: they left. Every year I watch this happen and every year guys keep soaking bucktails on the flats wondering where the fish went. They went to the inlet. They went to the channel edges where the current still moves cold water twice a day, and some of them pushed clean out into the ocean where an upwelling event has stacked 71°F water against the beach — eight degrees colder than the bay they just left. That's not a small gradient. That's a wall, and fluke respect it.

This week the moon is doing the heavy lifting. We're running into a new moon with spring tides building toward peak alignment Friday through Monday (7/10-13), and that means bigger swings, stronger current through the inlet throat, and — this is the part I care about — the PM flood stacking right on top of sunset. That western Sound pattern people talk about has its twin here: when the flood tide peaks as the light goes down, bass move up out of the deep cut and feed the drop-off edges hard for that last hour. First real PM window like this since the June full moon. I'd circle Saturday and Sunday evening on the calendar and build the trip around it, not around convenience.

On the fluke: the bite in the bay proper has been mediocre to poor, and I'm not going to sugarcoat it — guys drifting the humps off Pattersquash and the flats inside Cupsogue are working hard for two or three keepers on a good outgoing tide. But move to the inlet itself, work the throat on the last two hours of the ebb when that cold water is ripping out past the jetty rocks, and it's a different story. Ounce-and-a-quarter white bucktails tipped with 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullet, dragged slow along the north side of the cut in 12 to 18 feet, have been putting quality fish in the boat — nothing giant, mostly 18 to 22 inches, but steady. If you're fishing the ocean side off Cupsogue or the Westhampton groins, that 71-degree upwelled water is holding fluke tight to the second bar. Work a high-low rig with squid strips or Gulp on the incoming, right as the water starts pushing back over the bar — that's the window, twenty minutes either side of the tide change, before the surf gets confused.

Stripers have been the more honest fish this week — not blowing up, but present and predictable if you fish the structure right. The inlet's storm-cut geometry hasn't changed much since the last reconfiguration; the main channel still hugs the west side coming out, and that's where the current funnels bait past the rock jetty on the ebb. Guys drifting live eels after dark through that funnel, letting them swing with the current instead of retrieving, have been picking off fish in the 24 to 34-inch range. During the day, bucktails and swim shads worked the eastern bar edge on the last of the outgoing have produced schoolies mixed with a few keepers. Surfcasters at Cupsogue are doing better at first light on the outside bar with topwater — Danny plugs and Gibbs poppers — before the sun gets high and pushes the fish off the structure.

Bluefish have shown in spurts, mostly small to mid-size, chopping bait on top around the inlet mouth and along the Smith Point stretch during the last hour of daylight. Nothing sustained enough to call it a blitz, but if you see the birds working, get a metal lure — a Deadly Dick or a Hopkins — in the water fast, because those windows close in ten minutes.

Here's the one I'm watching closest: the pelagic window for bonito and Spanish mackerel closes out around the 11th, and every signal that needed to line up for a first Moriches/Shinnecock report has lined up — the ocean-side clean water, the incoming tide timing, the bait pushed tight to the beach by that upwelling. If it's going to happen on our stretch this year, it happens in the next three days on a clean incoming tide at the inlet mouth or off the eastern jetty at Cupsogue. I wouldn't build a whole trip around it, but if you're already out there working the fluke bite on the incoming, keep a small metal jig or Deadly Dick rigged and tied off, because that's exactly the kind of fish that shows up unannounced and gone in the same trip.

Look-ahead: if the wind stays out of the northeast through the weekend the way it's been sharpening the offshore breaks, expect it to keep pushing that cooler water against the beach here too — good news for the ocean-side fluke and whatever pelagics show up. Inside the bay, I'd write off the deep flats until we get a real blow to flush the heat out, and I'd spend my bay time working inlet-adjacent structure on the tide changes. Best case for this weekend: the new moon flood stacks on sunset Saturday and Sunday, the bass feed hard in that last hour of light, and somebody connects on the first bonito of the year working the incoming at Cupsogue. Worst case, the bonito window shuts without a report and we're back to grinding bucktails through the inlet throat — which, honestly, has been productive enough on its own to justify the trip.

reports.headline: New-moon springs load the Stratford Shoal rip as bass push back on the moving water
reports.subhead: Bluefish crash bunker off Charles Island, fluke slide into the deep guts, and the first evening bite since June's full moon is set to reopen this weekend.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the Sound sat in that mid-summer lull where the wind never really commits — light sou'westerlies most afternoons, glassy mornings, water building heat every day it wasn't stirred. That kind of pattern spreads bait thin. Peanut bunker and silversides scattered into every harbor mouth from Oyster Bay to Port Jeff instead of stacking anywhere obvious, and the bass and blues followed suit — around, but not concentrated, not predictable. The moon was working against us too. We're coming off the June full moon and sliding through the neap-to-building stretch, current softening at the rips, fish spreading into eddies instead of holding tight lanes. That's the kind of week where you have to go find them instead of having them come to you.

That changes fast. We're running into a new moon around July 13, and the spring tides that come with it are already building — bigger swings at Kings Point and up through the Norwalk Islands, more water moving through the pinch points that make this stretch of Sound what it is. The forecast I like most: the PM flood tide is converging with sunset from Friday the 10th through Monday the 13th, which is the first evening high-water window we've had line up with dusk since before the last full moon. When that flood stacks against the last hour of light, bait gets pinned against structure right when predators want to feed on it, and the whole middle Sound corridor — Stratford Shoal, Middle Ground, the Norwalk chain — narrows down the options for where the bass have to be. Wind looks manageable through the weekend, nothing that should blow the shoal rip apart. If it holds, this is the setup I've been waiting on.

Striped bass are still the most honest read on the week. The Stratford Shoal rip has been giving up fish on the outgoing, right at the top of the drop where the current pours off the shoal into deeper water — 20 to 35 feet, bouncing bucktails tipped with a strip of fresh bunker, working the seam where the sandy bottom breaks toward the channel. Nothing enormous, mostly schoolies to low-20-inch fish with a few better ones mixed in, but consistent enough that three or four boats a morning are camped on it during the last two hours of the outgoing. Trolling umbrella rigs through the same zone has worked too if you're not into jigging — keep it slow, right on the edge where the water color changes.

Bluefish have been the more reliable violence this week. Charles Island and the stretch of beach running toward the Norwalk Islands have had genuine peanut bunker showers at first light, gulls working tight, blues busting through from underneath hard enough to put spray in the air. Poppers and metal — Kastmasters, Ava jigs in white — have been getting hit as fast as you can cast into the melee. It doesn't last long, usually thirty to forty-five minutes before the bait scatters and the blues sound, so if you're running out from Norwalk or Westport, be on the water before sunrise, not after.

Fluke have been the trickier story. Bay and harbor water has been running warm enough that the better fish have been sliding out of the shallow flats and into the deeper guts — the channel edges off Middle Ground Light and the drop-offs around the mouth of Port Jefferson Harbor have both outfished the flats proper. Five-inch white or pink Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow through 25 to 40 feet on the last of the outgoing, have been the ticket. It's not a banner fluke week — I'd call it steady with occasional keepers, not a slam-dunk — but the fish that are biting are quality, several pushing 4 to 5 pounds off the deeper structure.

Porgies remain the dependable bread-and-butter around the Norwalk Islands reefs and the rockpiles off Middle Ground — small hooks, sandworms or clam, anchored up on the last of the drop or the first of the push, and you can fill a cooler without much drama. Simple fishing, but it works, and it's a good call for a slower tide stage when the bass and blues aren't cooperating. Blackfish season is closed through the summer in both states right now, so leave the crab pots in the garage until fall opens back up.

Weakfish, I have to be straight with you, have been a non-event. Water's plenty warm enough on paper, but warm water alone hasn't been translating to fish in the net anywhere I've heard of this year, and that's held true again this week. If you're targeting them specifically, I'd shift that effort to the bass and blues instead — better odds for your gas money right now.

Looking at the bigger picture, the bonito corridor down around Block Island and Newport has been widening as that cold wall broke down, and history says that push eventually walks west along the Sound's eastern approaches by August. Too early to chase them here yet, but it's on my radar for late month. For this coming week, my time is going into that Friday-through-Monday evening flood window at Stratford Shoal and the Norwalk Islands. If the wind stays cooperative and that new-moon spring tide does what it should, sunset on the outgoing-to-incoming transition ought to be the best few hours we've had in a month. Plan B if the bass don't show is the same deep-water fluke drift off Middle Ground — that bite's been honest even when nothing else is.

reports.headline: New moon springs load up Moriches Inlet as fluke funnel out of an overheated bay
reports.subhead: Great South Bay pushing 79°F has fluke stacking in the inlet throat, while a closing bonito window and building tides set up a big week at Cupsogue.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the bay did what overheated bays do in early July — it pushed everything with fins toward cooler water. Great South Bay and the western reaches of Moriches Bay were sitting at 78.8°F by midweek, which is fine for snappers and bunker but starts to shut down the metabolism on fluke and push weakfish deep and lockjawed. That kind of heat doesn't just make fish uncomfortable, it stratifies the water column — warm skin layer up top, cooler water pinned against the bottom in the deeper channels. Fluke don't fight that fight. They ride the outgoing tide down the guts of Narrow Bay and the Forge River channel and stack up where the current funnels them: the inlet throat and the ocean side, where upwelled water sitting around 71°F is a straight upgrade.

This week the moon is doing the heavy lifting. We're building toward new moon, with peak spring tide alignment landing July 11-13. That means bigger tidal exchange through the inlet cut than we've seen in weeks — more water moving faster through a system that's already narrow and scoured out from the last few nor'easters. The west cut off Cupsogue has held its depth better than the main channel this season, running 15 to 18 feet through the throat before shoaling out onto the ebb bar. When the springs peak, that current lane sharpens, and so does the bite window around it. Wind's been manageable, mostly light out of the south and southwest, which keeps the ocean side clean enough to fish the surf without getting worked over by a sloppy groundswell.

The fluke bite is real right now, but it's not a bay bite anymore — it's an inlet-and-ocean bite, and that's an important distinction if you're planning a trip. I've been working the drift from the Coast Guard station down through the throat on the last two hours of outgoing, dragging 3/4-ounce white bucktails tipped with 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullets right along the bottom where the scour drops off. Fish are sitting in that 15 to 18 foot cut, using the deeper water as a highway between the bay and the ocean side sandbars. Nothing enormous — most fish going 17 to 20 inches — but there's enough volume that a two-hour outgoing drift is producing four or five keepers if you're covering ground and not anchoring up. On the ocean side, the same fish are pushing out onto the bar in that cooler upwelled water, and guys drifting bucktail-and-Gulp combos in 20 to 25 feet off Cupsogue are picking off a mix of fluke and the occasional short-to-keeper bass that's using the same current seam.

Stripers are still around Cupsogue and the west jetty, but they're playing the tide stages, not the clock. Best window has been the last hour of the ebb into the start of the flood, right at the jetty rocks where the current compresses and bait gets pinned. Bucktails with white or chartreuse teasers are working, and a few guys throwing bunker chunks off the jetty on fishfinder rigs have connected with fish in the mid-20s. It's not a blitz — you need to be there at the right tide stage, not just fishing the whole day and hoping. Bluefish have been mixed in on the same structure, mostly cocktail-sized, chopping bunker pieces and hitting metal on the outgoing.

Here's the piece worth watching closely: the pelagic window that opened around the Fourth is closing out over the next few days, and Moriches sits right in the zone for it. First bonito and Spanish mackerel reports are trickling in from the ocean side of the eastern inlets, and with clean incoming water pushing that upwelled 71°F water against the beach, this stretch — Moriches and Shinnecock ocean side — is exactly where I'd expect the first real showing here. If you've got light tackle and some small metal or epoxy jigs, the next three or four days on an incoming tide at first light off Cupsogue or the Smith Point bar is worth the gas money. This window doesn't stay open long, and once it closes, you're waiting for a second wave later in the summer that isn't guaranteed to show at all.

Weakfish, I'll be straight with you — nothing worth reporting. The bay's been above 70°F for over two weeks now, which used to be the trigger everybody watched, but it's not producing. I've had zero solid weakfish reports out of this zone, and I'm hearing the same from other bay systems. Temperature alone isn't doing it this year; there's something else missing, probably bait density or an absent year class. I wouldn't burn a tide targeting them right now.

Looking ahead: the new moon springs peaking mid-week should sharpen the inlet drift for fluke and give the striper bite at the jetty a stronger push on the tide changes. If the wind stays out of the south and the ocean stays clean, I'd spend my mornings on the incoming working bonito metal off Cupsogue, then shift to the fluke drift through the throat as the tide turns. Plan B if the pelagics don't show — there's always fluke stacked in that scour hole, and that bite isn't going anywhere as long as the bay stays this warm.

reports.headline: Springs building toward the new moon — bass setting up on the Stratford Shoal rip
reports.subhead: Fluke slide out to the inlets, bluefish chop bunker off Charles Island, and the first PM flood window in weeks opens this weekend.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the Sound sat under a light southwest breeze most days — nothing that tore the water up, but enough to keep a chop running through the afternoons and push surface temps up another notch. That's typical for early July here: the middle Sound narrows between Port Jeff and the Connecticut shore and holds heat once it arrives, and by the weekend the harbor thermometers around Oyster Bay and Norwalk were reading properly summer-warm. The moon's been waning toward new, which this week turns into building spring tides — bigger swings, more current through the pinch points, and that's the piece that matters most for how I'm going to fish the next seven days.

We're heading into new moon on the 13th, and the springs build hardest Friday through Monday. That's significant because the PM flood now lines up with sunset for the first time since the June full moon — the tide stage and the light are stacking instead of fighting each other. On a beat like this, where Stratford Shoal and Middle Ground Light live and die by how hard water rips over the structure, that alignment is the difference between a slow drift and a real bite window. I'd circle Friday evening through Monday evening as the best stretch to be on the water for stripers.

Speaking of stripers — the reports out of Stratford Shoal have been honest, not spectacular. Guys working bucktails and swim shads on the last two hours of the outgoing have picked at fish in the 24-30 inch range, holding tight to the boulder edges on the west side of the shoal where the current breaks and folds. Slack water there has been mostly dead; you need the rip actually moving to pull fish up off the bottom. Same story at Middle Ground — a few keeper bass came off bunker chunks fished on the bottom during the last hour of outgoing, but it's been a grind, not a blitz. With the springs building this week, that current is going to run harder and longer through both spots, and that usually concentrates bait against the rock piles better than a lazy neap tide does. I'd fish the last two hours of the ebb at Stratford and the first hour of the new flood at Middle Ground, working 5-inch white or bone Storm Shads on 3/4-ounce jig heads, bounced slow along bottom.

Bluefish have been the more reliable player. Peanut bunker have been thick around Charles Island and pushed into the coves off Norwalk, and the blues have been chopping them on the surface most mornings before the wind fills in. Poppers and metal — Deadly Dicks, half-ounce Kastmasters — have worked when you can find the surface activity, but a lot of the better fish have come on bunker chunks fished mid-column off Charles Island reef, especially on the first two hours of the incoming when bait gets pushed up against the structure. Nothing huge, mostly 3-5 pounders, but steady enough that it's worth having a rod rigged for them any time you're out.

Fluke have done exactly what you'd expect with the water this warm — they've slid out of the shallow bay pockets and settled onto the channel edges and drop-offs near the inlets. Port Jeff Harbor mouth has been better than the inner harbor all week, with keeper-class fish coming off the 20-25 foot drop just outside the breakwater on white Gulp Swimming Mullets teamed with chartreuse bucktails, fished on the last of the outgoing when the current sweeps bait off the flats. Norwalk Islands has produced similarly — the channel between Sheffield and Copps has held fish on the drift, though you have to cover water; it's more a fifteen-drift-for-three-keepers pattern than an easy pick.

Porgies have been steady and honest, which is about all you can ask from scup in July. Sandworms and clam on high-low rigs over the rock piles at Middle Ground and around Charles Island have kept rods bent for anyone willing to anchor up and chum a little. Not glamorous, but it's a bite you can count on when the bass and bluefish go quiet mid-day.

Weakfish — I have to be straight with you here — still aren't showing. Water's plenty warm enough on paper, but that threshold alone hasn't meant anything the last few seasons, and this year is no different so far. I'm not spending tide time chasing them until someone actually puts one in a cooler.

One thing worth watching quietly: the warm-water corridor that's been pushing bonito and Spanish mackerel toward Rhode Island and eastern Long Island has widened this week as that cold wall out that way broke down. Central Sound bonito are an August event historically, not a July one, but with water this warm this early, I wouldn't be shocked if we get an early scout report from the Norwalk Islands or Charles Island in the next couple weeks. Nothing confirmed yet — just something I'm keeping an eye on.

For this week: I'd build around the Friday-through-Monday PM flood window for bass at Stratford Shoal and Middle Ground, work the bluefish early before the wind builds off Charles Island, and treat fluke as an inlet-and-channel game rather than a bay game until the water cools back down. If the wind stays manageable and the springs build the way they should, this is the best current setup we've had in weeks — worth putting a full evening into it.

reports.headline: Bay Fluke Push Out to the Inlet as Shinnecock Heats Up Toward the New Moon
reports.subhead: Warm bay water is shoving fluke into the channels and the inlet mouth while the first bonito scouts show up on clean incoming tide.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the bay ran warm and slow. Light southerly wind for four straight days, not enough to build any real chop, but enough to keep the surface glassy and the bay water stacking heat. I had a thermometer reading pushing into the high 70s in the guts off Tiana and up toward the canal, and that's too warm for fluke to sit still in six feet of water all day. They didn't disappear — they moved. By Thursday the drift in the bay had gone quiet and the action shifted hard toward the channel edges and the inlet itself, which is exactly what you'd expect when the flats turn into a bathtub. The moon's been sliding down toward new, which was already tightening up the tide swings by midweek, and that thinner current made the fish even less willing to fight for a meal in open bay — they wanted structure and moving water, not a flat drift over sand.

This week the moon goes new, and that means spring tides building right through the weekend — bigger swings, stronger current in the inlet, more water moving on the outgoing. That's the single biggest thing I'm watching. A bigger outgoing means more bait getting flushed out of the bay and past the rocks at the inlet, and that's when the stripers stack up on the drop. I'd also keep an eye on the ocean side — the incoming tide has been running clean the last few days, no discolored runoff, and that clean water at the inlet mouth is prime territory for the first Spanish mackerel or bonito showing up this time of year. It's late in that window — first LI bonito reports usually taper off after mid-July — but the water's right for it right now.

The fluke bite has been honestly mixed in the open bay, and I'm not going to sell you otherwise. Guys drifting the flats off Tiana Beach with bucktail and Gulp combos were getting a lot of short strikes and undersized fish for most of last week — too much bait, too much heat, fish just picking. But move to the channel edges near the canal entrance, or drift the deeper cuts inside the inlet itself on the last two hours of the outgoing, and the size picks up. Chartreuse bucktails, half-ounce to three-quarter depending on current, tipped with a 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullet, worked slow along bottom in 12 to 18 feet — that's been the combination putting keepers in the box, mostly 19 to 22 inches, with the occasional fish pushing 24. The bite window is tight, usually the two hours around the tide change when the current slows enough for the fish to commit but hasn't gone fully slack.

Striped bass are where I spend my nights, and the inlet on the outgoing remains the most honest bet in this entire zone. I've been working the rock jetty on the west side an hour after sunset, casting swimming plugs and darters into the current seam where the outgoing meets the deeper hole, and connecting with schoolies and a few bigger fish in the 28 to 34 inch range, mostly on bunker-colored swimmers worked with a slow, steady retrieve right along the edge of the white water. Live eels drifted on a fish-finder rig through that same seam have also been producing after midnight, when the smaller boat traffic clears out and the fish settle back into their lanes. With the new moon spring tides building through the weekend, that outgoing current is going to run harder and longer than it has in weeks — I expect the bite window to widen, not just at the peak of the drop but for a solid hour before and after. If you can only fish one night this week, I'd pick Saturday or Sunday when the tide swing is near its biggest and the current through the inlet channel is really ripping.

Weakfish at Ponquogue Bridge have been quiet, and I want to be straight about that rather than pretend otherwise. A few scattered fish came off the bridge lights at night on bucktail-and-twister-tail combos worked slow along the pilings, but it's nothing like a real push yet. Worth a stop on your way to or from the inlet, especially right at the bottom of the outgoing when the current slackens around the pilings, but don't build a whole trip around it right now. Porgies are still mostly a daytime, high-tide affair around the bridge structure and the deeper holes toward the canal — standard hi-lo rigs with clam are getting steady action in the one to one-and-a-half pound range, nothing spectacular but reliable if you want bent rods for the kids. Blackfish are still mostly holding on the deeper structure toward the ocean side and haven't turned on in any real way yet — that's a September story, not a July one.

Looking ahead, the new moon spring tides are the whole ballgame this week. Bigger swings mean a stronger flush through the inlet, which should keep pulling bait — and stripers behind it — out of the bay and into that current seam at night. If the incoming stays clean on the ocean side, I'd make at least one run to the inlet mouth with a light spinning rod and small metal jigs just in case those bonito or Spanish mackerel show up in numbers before that pelagic window closes. My plan for the week: nights at the inlet jetty on the outgoing for bass, mornings working the channel edges near the canal for fluke before the sun gets high and pushes them back into the depths. If the bass don't show on a given night, the fluke in the channel are my fallback — and if both are slow, there's always a bucket of clams and the bridge pilings for porgies while I wait for the tide to turn.

reports.headline: Bay bakes past 78, and the doormats bail for the inlet
reports.subhead: Great South Bay ran hot enough to push the fluke out to Fire Island Inlet and the ocean side — and a building new-moon tide should only sharpen that bite this week.
reports.body_markdown:
Let me tell you what the bay looked like last week — flat, hazy, and warm enough to make you want to jump in with your clothes on. Great South Bay pushed up to 78.8 degrees in the shallows, which sounds great until you remember fluke don't love bathwater. That heat sat on the flats around Nicoll Bay and off Sayville for the better part of a week with light wind and not much to stir it, and by Thursday the guys who'd been picking at keepers on the West Fire Island flats were coming back with nothing but snappers and sea robins. The fish didn't disappear. They just did what smart fluke do — they slid for cooler water, and the cooler water right now is in the channels and out at the inlet.

That's set up the week ahead nicely, because we're building toward a new moon on the 13th, and that means spring tides stacking in through the weekend. Bigger swings at Fire Island Inlet, more water moving on the outgoing, and more of that upwelled ocean water — sitting around 71 degrees off the beach — getting pulled through Democrat Point and up into the channel edges off Robert Moses. When the bay's too warm and the ocean's noticeably cooler, that thermal seam right at the inlet mouth becomes the highway. Bait gets squeezed through it, and so do the fluke that are chasing it. I'd rather fish a strong outgoing at the inlet this week than putter around the bay flats hoping for a fluke that's already left the building.

And that's exactly how it's fished. The Robert Moses bridges — both the Route 27 span and the causeway pilings — have been holding fluke stacked on the outgoing, 25 to 35 feet depending where you set up on the drift. Four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails have been the honest producer, dragged slow right along bottom, with a few guys upsizing to chartreuse when the water's got any color to it after a tide change. Fish to five and a half pounds have come off that structure in the last week, mixed in with a lot of shorts, so it's not a pin-your-limit bite — it's a work-for-it bite, but the quality fish are legitimately there when you find the right piece of structure on the drift.

Democrat Point has been the better story for stripers, though I want to be straight with you — it's early mornings only right now, and it's not every morning. The bass are working the surf line off the point and down toward the lighthouse jetty on the last of the outgoing and into the start of the incoming, chasing bunker schools that have been pushing bait right up against the beach. Bucktails with white or pearl curly-tail trailers, and if you've got peanut bunker on hand, a fish-finder rig cast just outside the wash has been the better bet at first light. Bluefish have been mixed in with those schools too — nothing giant, mostly 2 to 4 pounds, but they'll test your leader and keep the rod bent while you're waiting on a bass to show. That bite has a short window. Once the sun's up and the wind picks up off the ocean, it shuts down fast.

Porgies have held steady in the bay — not exciting, but honest fishing if you want a bucket of fish for the pan. Bloodworms or clam on a hi-lo rig around the reef structure off Patchogue and the deeper holes toward Nicoll's Point have been producing steady action, better on the last two hours of the incoming when the current slows enough for the porgies to sit and feed instead of getting pushed around.

Weakfish, I'll be honest with you — it's been quiet. The water's been warm enough for weeks now, well above what we usually think weakfish need, and I keep hearing guys say "any day now," but any day hasn't come. I'm not writing them off completely for late summer, but if you're planning a trip around weakfish specifically this week, I'd have a strong Plan B.

Worth keeping an eye on for those of you who run east: the ocean-side eastern inlets have started throwing the season's first bonito and Spanish mackerel reports, riding clean incoming water. That's not squarely our patch out of Captree, but if you're trailering toward Moriches or beyond on a clean day, don't be shocked if something fast and silver hits your spoon.

Looking at the week ahead, I'm watching that new moon build through the weekend and thinking about the outgoing at Fire Island Inlet — bigger tide swings should push more of that 71-degree ocean water through and keep pulling fluke off the bay flats and onto the channel edges where we can actually catch them. If I had one morning to fish, I'd be at Robert Moses on the start of the outgoing with bucktails rigged and ready, and I'd have the surf rod in the truck just in case those bunker schools are still working the beach at first light. Two different bites, same tide window — that's about as good as July gets out here.

reports.headline: New moon springs build toward Jones Inlet as fluke abandon a bathwater bay
reports.subhead: Great South Bay hit the high 70s and pushed the fluke out — the inlet and the outgoing tide are carrying the load right now.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the bay did what it does every July — it got too warm for its own good. Great South Bay pushed close to 79 degrees in the shallows, and that's bathwater for a fluke. When that happens I don't fight it, I follow the fish, and the fish went where they always go when the flats turn into soup: the channels, the humps, and the inlet itself. We had a decent stretch of southwest wind through the middle of the week that kept things stirred but not blown out, and the moon's been building since the last new moon back in mid-June — we're past full, waning toward the next new moon, and the tides have been climbing every day toward what's going to be a real push this weekend.

That's the story for the week ahead too. New moon lines up around July 13, and that means spring tides stacking in hard from Friday through Monday — bigger exchange, more water moving through the inlet on both ends of the tide, stronger current at the jetties and in Sloop Channel. When the moon does that, I stop thinking about the bay as one big flat piece of water and start thinking about it as a plumbing system — the inlet's the drain, and everything the bay doesn't want gets flushed through it twice a day. Water's still trending warm, but the ocean side is getting a boost from upwelling — we're seeing cleaner, cooler water pushing in on the incoming, something in the low 70s, and that's exactly what a fluke wants after baking in 79-degree bay water for two weeks.

So here's where I've been putting my time, and where I'd send you. The fluke bite has shifted hard into Jones Inlet proper and down into Sloop Channel — the drop-offs along the edges, 15 to 25 feet, where the channel bends off Short Beach and where the current rips past the old workboat cuts. Outgoing tide is the play, no question. That's when the warmer bay water gets pushed out and the fluke stack up right in the seam where it meets the incoming ocean water — think of it as a dinner bell. Three-quarter-ounce white bucktails tipped with a five-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullet have been the go-to, dragged slow along bottom on the drift, and don't be afraid to bounce it — these fish have been a little lazy in the heat and they want it right in their face. A few boats working the deeper hole off the inlet mouth, close to 30 feet, have had better luck with a heavier jig, an ounce or more, just to hold bottom against that new-moon current once it really starts running this weekend. Size has been mixed — plenty of 16 to 18-inch fish that go back, but there've been keepers in the 20 to 22-inch range mixed in, and I heard of one better fish pushing 5 pounds taken on a chartreuse bucktail-and-Gulp combo right at the turn of the tide.

Striped bass are still around but this isn't a blitz — don't let anybody tell you it is. What we've got is resident fish working the inlet mouth and the edges of Jones Beach on bunker that's scattered through the surf and the back bay. Best window has been dawn, right at first light, working topwater plugs and darters along the Short Beach jetty rocks and the outside bar at Jones Beach. If you can find a pod of bunker getting nervous, a bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig fished tight to the bottom in that same 15 to 20-foot zone off the inlet has been picking off a few better fish in the 28 to 34-inch class, mostly on the last two hours of the outgoing. It's not consistent — I've had trips where I worked three different stretches of beach for one bass, and trips where I got two keepers in twenty minutes. That's where we are right now: fish are there, but you have to find the bait first.

Weakfish — I want to be straight with you here because there's a lot of hope floating around about a comeback, and hope isn't the same as fish in the boat. The water's been warm enough for weeks now, plenty above 70, and that's necessary but it clearly isn't enough on its own. I've heard of exactly one solid weakfish taken in the bay recently, a nice one over 7 pounds, but that's one fish, not a pattern. If you want to chase them, work the deeper holes in South Oyster Bay on the last hour of the outgoing with a bucktail and squid strip, but go in with realistic expectations.

Snapper blues have shown up in the back creeks around Freeport and Wantagh, which is a good sign bigger blues aren't far behind — small metal lures and Kastmasters will keep the kids busy while you work bigger stuff.

Looking ahead: that new moon spring tide building through the weekend is the thing to watch. Bigger tides mean a harder flush through the inlet, which should concentrate bait and predators right in that mouth on the outgoing. If I had one shot this week, I'd fish the Friday or Saturday evening outgoing at the inlet, right into dusk — that's when the current's strongest and the bass have shown the most willingness to commit. Plan B is the Sloop Channel fluke drift if the bass don't cooperate, because that bite's been the more dependable of the two.

reports.headline: Bay water runs hot, fluke slide to the inlet, and the new moon sets up a sunset striper window
reports.subhead: Jamaica Bay's flats are cooking past 78 degrees — the real action this week is where moving water meets the heat.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the bay basically turned into a bathtub. Flat calm, sun beating down, and the shallow flats off Canarsie and up in the back creeks climbed into the high 70s — I heard 78, 79 degrees from a couple guys running temp gauges off Beach Channel. That's warm enough that fluke don't want to sit still on the flats anymore. They get lethargic, oxygen gets thin, and they slide toward whatever's got current running through it — the inlet mouth, the bridge channels, anywhere water's actually moving and staying a touch cooler. That's exactly what I saw happen this week. The bay bite that was solid back in May and June has thinned out on the shallow stuff and pushed hard toward Rockaway Inlet and the ocean side.

Here's what's coming: we're building toward a new moon on the 10th, which means spring tides stacking up through the weekend, peaking around the 11th through the 13th. Bigger swings, stronger current, and — this is the part I like — the PM flood is going to line up almost perfectly with sunset those evenings. That's the first evening window like this since the June full moon, and it's the kind of setup that gets bass moving and feeding hard right at last light instead of just picking at bait in the dark. If you've got one evening to fish this week, Friday through Monday at the Marine Parkway Bridge on that building flood, right into dusk, is where I'd be.

Stripers have been working the bridge pilings on the outgoing, same as always this time of year, but with the new moon current building, the outgoing's going to run harder and push more bait past those pilings than it has in weeks. I'm throwing a white bucktail, an ounce and a half, with a white curly-tail trailer, and working the downcurrent seam off the pilings — that's where the ambush happens, not right up against the concrete. Guys are also doing well with darker swimming plugs at dusk when the light gets low. Sizes have been schoolie-heavy, 18 to 24 inches, but there's been enough mid-20s mixed in that a slot fish isn't a surprise. Nobody's telling me about a run of true keepers yet, but with that sunset flood window coming, I wouldn't be shocked if this week changes that.

Bluefish have shown up with some teeth on them. Breezy Point and the Rockaway Beach surf line have had blitzes in the early morning — bunker peanuts and silversides getting run right up into the wash, gulls diving, the whole show. If you catch it, metal is the move: Deadly Dicks, Kastmasters, anything you can chuck far and retrieve fast through the mess. Snapper blues are also thick in the bay proper right now if you've got kids who want steady action off Canarsie Pier — small stuff, but it keeps a rod bent.

Fluke is the one where I have to be straight with you: the bay bite is inconsistent right now, and it's because of that heat I mentioned. I fished the flats off Canarsie two days this week and it was slow going, a few short fish and one keeper over three hours. But guys working the Rockaway Inlet mouth and the deeper cuts along Beach Channel are doing noticeably better — 15 to 25 feet, drifting the outgoing with white or chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid if you've got it. There's upwelled ocean water pushing in on that outgoing tide that's running cooler than the bay, and that's exactly where the bigger fish have relocated. If you're set on fluke this week, fish the inlet and the ocean-side drifts off Breezy Point, not the shallow flats. That's not where the fish are living right now.

Porgies have actually been a bright spot inside the bay — structure around the Cross Bay Bridge and the rock piles near Canarsie Pier have given up decent numbers on bloodworm and clam, moderate depth, nothing fancy needed. If you want a stress-free evening with a bucket of bait and a simple high-low rig, that's your play.

Weakfish — I'll be honest, I haven't heard a single real report out of the bay or the inlet despite the warm water. The temperature's been there for weeks now and it just hasn't translated into fish showing up. I wouldn't plan a trip around them right now.

Looking ahead, that new moon spring tide building into the weekend is the story. Bigger current, more bait getting flushed through the inlet and past the bridge, and a sunset flood window Friday through Monday that's the best alignment we've had in a month. If I only had one evening, I'd be at Marine Parkway working the outgoing into that flood, switching over to bucktails as the light dies. Backup plan if the bass don't show — head to the inlet mouth and drift bucktails for fluke on that same tide change, because that bite's been the more reliable one lately even if it's not blowing up. Keep an eye on the ocean side too — bluefish have been aggressive enough in the surf that a dawn trip to Breezy Point could pay off on its own, blitz or no blitz.

reports.headline: New moon springs load The Race as fluke push out of the bays and bonito knock on Fishers Island's door
reports.subhead: Bigger current, colder edges, and a widening bonito corridor mean this week's fishing is about picking the right five-minute window, not the whole tide.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the Sound was in a holding pattern — post-solstice current still building toward these new moon tides, and a run of NE wind put a chill on the surface layer that pushed the thermocline around more than I like to see in July. That upwelling is exactly why the fluke bailed out of the back bays. Water sitting near 78 degrees in the shallow flats got uncomfortable fast, and the fish slid to the channels and inlet mouths where that cooler 71-degree water was stacking up underneath. I saw it happen at Plum Gut first — a Tuesday outgoing that felt more like October than July, current ripping and bottom temp noticeably cooler than the drift I ran two days earlier. That's your fluke water now. Forget the flats until this settles.

This week the moon is the story. New moon spring tides build through Friday into the weekend, peak alignment landing July 11-13, and that means the current through The Race and Plum Gut is about to get meaner than it's been in three weeks. More exchange means harder push, which means the eddies behind Valiant Rock and off the Orient Point rip reload faster and hold bait longer on the slack. If you've been getting bored fishing that structure on neap tides, this is your reset. I'm also watching the cold wall that collapsed between Block Island and Rhode Island Sound — water jumped over ten degrees on that boundary, which is opening a real bonito and Spanish mackerel corridor stretching from Newport down toward Point Judith. Fishers Island sits right on the doorstep of that. The LI bonito window that opened July 4th is closing out over the next few days, but with that cold wall gone, I wouldn't be surprised if the first fish show up on the east end of the Sound before it's officially shut.

Striped bass fishing has been real, but it's not automatic. I've had two solid nights out of four working the Race on foot from the Orient rocks — big paddletails and 2-ounce Gibbs pencils worked through the seam where the rip meets the eddy, best from an hour before high through the first hour of the drop. Fish have run mixed, mostly schoolies and mid-20s, but there's chatter of real cows showing up in pockets up toward Block Island and Cape Cod this past week, and eastern Sound structure like this holds the same class of fish when the current's right. Plum Gut has been more of a boat game — drifting bucktails, half-ounce to one-ounce depending on the stage, tipped with a strip of fresh bunker, worked along the 30 to 40 foot edge on the west side of the Gut on the outgoing. That's produced better than the slower, weaker tides did two weeks back. The takeaway: bigger tides equal a shorter, harder bite window, but a better one. Don't fish the whole six hours — fish the ninety minutes around the turn.

Fluke have been the more consistent player, just not where guys expect. Inlet and channel drifts are outfishing the open bay right now. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow through the deeper cuts off Plum Gut and the mouth of Orient Harbor, have been putting keepers in the box — nothing giant, mostly 18 to 21 inches, but steady on the outgoing when that upwelled ocean water is flushing through. If you're marking bait stacked tight to bottom in 30-plus feet, slow the drift down and go heavier on the head. That cooler water is concentrated fish instead of spreading them out.

Porgies are exactly where you'd expect — Fishers Island structure, the rockpiles off the Race, bottom rigs with squid and sandworm working 20 to 35 feet on the last two hours of the incoming. That bite has been reliable all season and hasn't changed with anything above. Bluefish have been more show than substance so far — a few chopper-sized fish busting bait on the surface out toward the Gut at first light, gone as fast as they showed. If the bonito corridor pushes this way like I expect, the blues and albies will start overlapping, and that's when things get fun fast — small metal, Deadly Dicks, half-ounce Deceivers, keep them in the bag.

Weakfish — I'll be straight with you, nothing. Water's been warm enough for two-plus weeks now and there's still not a single report worth mentioning. That old rule about hitting 70 degrees triggering a bite clearly isn't the whole story anymore. I'm not chasing that one this month.

Here's what I'd do with the week ahead.
