If the wind stays out of the northeast through the weekend, I'm fishing the outgoing at Plum Gut Friday and Saturday for bass and fluke both, working the same drift twice — bucktails deep on the first pass, then switching to plugs along the surface eddy as the tide slackens. Sunday and Monday, with the moon at its peak, I want to be on the rocks at Orient at first light watching for surface activity — if bonito or albies have pushed into the corridor, that's when they'll show. Best case, the cold wall keeps collapsing east to west and Fishers Island gets its own pelagic run before the month's out. If it stalls at Block Island, I'll keep grinding bass and fluke on the bigger tides, which on their own are worth the trip.

reports.headline: New moon springs reopen the sunset striper window from Kings Point to Execution Rocks
reports.subhead: After a sluggish, bunker-heavy week of daytime lockjaw, building tides and a converging evening flood set up the best striper window since the June full moon.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the Sound gave us exactly what mid-summer neap tides usually give us: warm, slick water, plenty of bait, and bass that wanted no part of daylight. Little Neck Bay and Manhasset Bay have been running hot on the surface — I don't have a hard number but it felt like bathwater on top, the kind of warmth that pushes stripers down and out rather than up and in. A weak system rolled through midweek and put a little chop on the water for a day, nothing that really turned things over, just enough to dirty the surface film off Matinecock for 24 hours before it laid back down. The moon's been waning toward new, which means the tides have been running small — slow current at Execution Rocks, slack water sitting around too long at Stepping Stones, and bass that had no reason to commit to any one piece of structure.

That changes this week. New moon lands Saturday, and with it come the spring tides — bigger swings, faster current, more water moving through the pinch points that make this zone what it is. The piece I'm circling on the calendar is Friday through Monday, when the PM flood tide starts converging with sunset at Kings Point. That's the first evening window we've had like this since the June full moon, and it's the kind of alignment that turns a mediocre bay into a striper highway for about ninety minutes a night. Bigger tides also mean more bait getting flushed out of the back bays and funneled past Hart Island and through the Throgs Neck pinch — that's going to wake fish up that have been sitting on bunker schools all week without really feeding.

Speaking of bunker — they're stacked up off Matinecock Point again, thick pods sitting just off the point in 15 to 20 feet, and where there's bunker in July there's usually something under them. Problem is, most of the action on those schools has been early — first light, before the boat traffic and jet skis push everything down. I've had reports of bass and blues shadowing the pods at dawn, then going quiet by 8 AM once the sun gets up and the water flattens out. If you're going to work that bunker school, get there before the sun clears the trees, snag one on a weighted treble and freeline it back into the school, or run a bunker spoon on wire behind the boat at a slow troll. By mid-morning it's mostly just bait balls with nothing interested.

Execution Rocks is still doing what Execution Rocks does — it's just been on a smaller clock with these neap tides. The outgoing has been the better stage, current sweeping bait off the rockpile and down toward the channel, and guys working bunker chunks on fish-finder rigs or bouncing bucktails tipped with white Gulp along the down-current side have picked at schoolie-to-mid-30-inch bass. Nothing blitz-worthy, but steady if you're patient and fish the full stage of the outgoing rather than just the first hour. Stepping Stones has been similar — a slower current window meant fish were sitting in the eddies rather than stacked on the current lane, so drifting live eels or bunker chunks right along the edge of the light's rockpile, letting them sit rather than working them hard, has been the better play. Once these spring tides kick in this weekend, I expect both spots to tighten up and get more predictable — faster water means fish committing to ambush points instead of loafing.

Fluke have been an interesting story. The bay water's gotten warm enough on the surface that the fluke have been sliding out of the shallow flats in Manhasset Bay and Hempstead Harbor and setting up on the deeper channel edges — 25 to 35 feet off Hart Island and along the Throgs Neck Bridge drift. That's actually produced some decent action, fish to 4 and 5 pounds on white Gulp Swimming Mullets rigged on ¾-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the last of the outgoing where the current stacks bait against the channel wall. If you've been fishing the shallow grass flats and coming up empty this week, that warm surface layer is your answer — the fish didn't leave, they just went down and out.

Porgies have been the reliable bread-and-butter this month — Hart Island reef and the rockpile at Execution Rocks are both holding good numbers, sandworms or clam on a hi-lo rig in 20 to 30 feet, best on the last two hours of the incoming when the current's still got some push but isn't ripping. Weakfish, I'll be honest, are a non-story again this year — water's plenty warm enough on paper, but I haven't had or heard of a single credible report out of this zone, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. Warm water alone doesn't bring weakfish back; something else has to click, and it hasn't in years.

If I had one shot this week, I'd take the Saturday or Sunday evening flood at Kings Point or the Stepping Stones light, right as the tide peaks into sunset. That's the alignment the calendar's been building toward, and building spring tides plus low light plus a concentration of bait is about as good a striper setup as this zone offers in July. Plan B if the wind kicks up out of the southwest and muddies the surface — fall back to the fluke drift along Throgs Neck in that deeper water, where the fish don't care as much what's happening on top.

reports.headline: New moon springs building — bass window reopens as bonito push into Narragansett Bay
reports.subhead: The cold wall between the Island and the Sound finally broke, and that's changing everything from the North Rip to Beavertail.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the wind did what it usually does in early July — it went southwest and sat there, five, six days of it, pushing warm surface water up against the Island and stirring the upper water column just enough to keep the stripers honest but not stupid. Tides were still on the tail end of the last cycle, moderate swings, nothing dramatic. But the real story wasn't the wind — it was what happened to the cold wall that usually sits between Block Island Sound and Rhode Island Sound this time of year. That thermal barrier collapsed, better than ten degrees in the RIS side, and when that wall goes down, everything south of Newport gets an invitation it doesn't usually get until August. Bonito and Spanish mackerel don't read charts, they read water, and right now the water between here and Point Judith says come on in.

This week the moon is going dark, working toward new phase around the 11th, and that means the tides are building toward springs — bigger swings, stronger current, and a sunset flood that's going to stack up perfectly with high water on the western approaches by Friday through Monday. That's the window I'm circling. Big fish don't move on comfort, they move on current speed and light angle, and a new-moon spring flood hitting right at dusk is about as good a combination as this Island produces. Water temps have been stable to slightly warming inshore, mid-60s holding around the ledges, upwelled water running closer to 60 out on the North Rip edge where the bottom drops fast — that seam is exactly why the biggest bass in the Northeast show up here every July and nowhere else.

Striper fishing has been solid, not explosive, but solid — which at this point in July is exactly what I expect. The North Rip is still holding fish on the drop of the tide, working eels and 3-ounce bucktails with white curly tails down through 25 to 40 feet where the rip stacks bait against the ledge. Southwest Ledge has been better on the last two hours of the incoming, live scup and pogies drifted naturally through the structure in 30 to 50 feet — I had a 38-pounder come off there Tuesday morning on a live scup fished on a fish-finder rig with 60-pound fluoro leader, and that fish came right up out of the rocks on the last surge before the tide went flat. Once it slacks off, the bite dies fast out there — you've got maybe a ninety-minute window before the current quits and the fish drop back into the deeper holes and stop feeding. Southeast Light and the Chaunterelle have been quieter, more of an evening bite, umbrella rigs and tube-and-worm trolled slow along the drop-off in 60 to 90 feet.

Fluke have pulled a classic mid-summer move — out of the Great Salt Pond and the back-bay water, which has been running warm, and out into the inlet mouths and open ocean structure where that upwelled water is holding closer to 60 degrees. That colder, cleaner water is loaded with sand eels and squid right now, and the fluke know it. Best drift has been off the Coast Guard station on the outgoing, four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, bounced slow along bottom in 25 to 35 feet. A few keepers to 5 pounds, more shorts than keepers if I'm honest, but the quality fish have been legitimately quality — thick, healthy, full of sand eels when we cleaned them.

The bonito news is real and it's spreading. With that cold wall gone, the corridor now runs from Block Island right up through Newport and into Point Judith, which is new for this early in July — usually we don't see that until the back half of the month. Small hardtails have been showing on the surface off Brenton Reef and around Beavertail on calm mornings, chasing bay anchovies in tight, fast-moving pods. If you see the birds working low and jumpy rather than diving hard, slow down — that's bonito, not bluefish, and they'll spook off a boat running full speed into the school. Small epoxy jigs and Deadly Dick spoons, cast ahead of the pod and worked fast on a straight retrieve, have been the ticket. It's not an all-day bite, more a dawn-and-dusk window, but the fact that it's happening at all this early tells me the water's ahead of schedule.

Bluefish have been scattered but present around Southwest Ledge and off the Charlestown breachway, mostly cocktail-sized fish on the troll, though a few boats have found bigger choppers mixed in with the bass on bunker chunks fished on the bottom during the last of the outgoing near the North Rip. Porgies remain the reliable bread-and-butter — sandworms and squid strips on double-hook rigs, anywhere there's structure in 20 to 40 feet, Great Salt Pond entrance and the rock piles off New Harbor both holding good numbers. Blackfish season's still closed here, so leave them be for now.

Looking ahead, the new-moon springs building toward the weekend are what I'd plan around. If the wind lays down Friday night like it's forecast to, I'd want to be on the Southwest Ledge for the sunset flood — that combination of maximum current and low light is when the true trophy fish show themselves. Plan B if the bass don't cooperate is running the fluke drift off the Coast Guard station on the same tide, because that water isn't going anywhere either way. And keep an eye on the surface inshore — if this bonito push holds, Point Judith and Narragansett could be seeing steady action a full month ahead of the calendar.

reports.headline: New moon springs building off Block Island as the bonito corridor widens toward Newport
reports.subhead: Giant-class bass are still working the Southwest Ledge and North Rip while a collapsed cold wall in Rhode Island Sound opens the door for early bonito east of the Ledge.
reports.body_markdown:
We're coming off a week where the moon was waning down toward new, which meant smaller tidal swings and a slower current at the rips — the kind of stretch where you have to work harder for your bites but the fish that do show are usually quality. That's exactly what played out. The Southwest Ledge fished better on the last two hours of the ebb than on the flood, and the North Rip wanted a slack tide bite instead of the usual full-current push. Water out on the Ledge has held clean and cool, the way it always does out here in July when the Gulf Stream eddies and the cold pool underneath us keep doing their job. But there's a real story developing to our west: the cold wall that normally separates Block Island Sound from Rhode Island Sound has come apart — we're talking about a jump of better than ten degrees in RIS water temps over the last couple weeks. That's not a subtle shift. It means warm water that used to stay pinned east of Newport is now spreading, and it's already showing up in the bonito reports.

This week the moon swings new on the 11th, and that means building springs right through the weekend — bigger tidal exchange, stronger current at every rip and ledge from the Southwest Ledge to the Race. New moon springs are when Block Island does what it does best: it flushes bait hard through the rips and gives the bass something to lean into. I'd expect the bite to sharpen back up as the tidal push increases through Thursday and Friday, with the best window Saturday through Monday when the current's really moving and the fish stack up in the eddies behind the boulders. If you've fished the SW Ledge before you know the drill — anchor up-current of the structure, live-line an eel or drift back a chunk of fresh bunker, and let it swing into the wash. That's still the money program.

Bass fishing has actually been solid, not spectacular, but solid — and a couple of genuinely big fish have come off the Ledge and out around the North Rip in the last ten days, giants in the 30-to-40-pound class mixed in with a good number of schoolies and mid-20s fish. Eels are still king after dark, fished on a fish-finder rig with just enough weight to hold bottom in 25 to 40 feet of water on the down-current side of the boulders. During the day, bucktails in the 2- to 4-ounce range tipped with a strip of squid have been drawing strikes when you can work them slow along the rock piles on the Ledge's western edge. Umbrella rigs trolled at 3 to 4 knots through the deeper water off the North Rip have also been putting bigger fish in the boat for guys willing to make the run out there and grind it out over a tide change.

Fluke have shifted, and this is worth knowing if you've been fishing the same spots with no results. The bay-side fluke bite has cooled off as inshore water has warmed into the high 70s, which pushed the better fish out to the channels, the inlets, and now into the ocean proper where upwelled water sitting around 71 degrees is holding bait tight to structure. Great Salt Pond's outflow and the deeper water off Old Harbor have both been producing keeper fluke on the outgoing tide — white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom contours where the sand meets rock. Doesn't take much finesse, just patience and a slow drift. Some fish to 6 pounds have come out of that stretch in the last week, though it's not an every-drift bite — more like three or four keepers out of a full tide if you're covering ground.

Bluefish have been around but scattered — chopper-class fish mixed with smaller ones blitzing bait pods off Point Judith and along the Narragansett beaches, mostly at first light. Nothing sustained, but when you find the birds working you can load the boat fast on top-water plugs or tin.

The bonito news is the one to watch closest. With that cold wall gone soft between here and the mainland, the corridor that used to be strictly a Block Island phenomenon is stretching west toward Point Judith and Newport. I haven't seen numbers yet that make me want to plan a whole trip around it, but the water's right, and if the pattern holds through the weekend I'd expect the first real showing of bonito working bait schools off the Southwest Ledge and out toward the Newport Bridge area. Small metal — half-ounce to one-ounce Deadly Dicks — cast into diving birds is the move if you find them.

Looking ahead, the new moon springs building through the weekend are the whole story. Bigger current means bait gets pushed harder through the rips, and that's when the Ledge and the North Rip both wake up. If the wind stays out of the southwest and light like it's been, I'd plan to fish the last two hours of the outgoing tide Saturday and Sunday morning — that's where I'd put my money. Plan B if the bass don't cooperate is running the fluke drift off Old Harbor on that same tide. Either way, the water's healthy and the fish are here — the only question this week is timing it to the tide.

reports.headline: New moon springs stack the tide at Plum Gut as bass and porgies both show
reports.subhead: Bigger water builds toward the July 11-13 peak, fluke get shoved out of the warm bay into Mattituck's mouth, and the Gut starts working again on the push.
reports.body_markdown:
Sixty years on this shoreline and I still pay attention to the moon before I pay attention to the weatherman. We're running down toward new moon, and you can feel it in the current already — the tide's been building each day this week, bigger swing morning and night, and by the weekend we'll be into full spring tides. That matters more here than almost anywhere else on the Island, because my water lives and dies on current. Plum Gut and the Race don't fish on slack. They fish on push. Last week was mixed — we had some blow come through mid-week that roiled things up along Horton Point and Rocky Point, dropped visibility to soup for a day or two, and the fish scattered off the structure until it settled. By Sunday it had cleaned back up and the current started doing what current does — stacking bait against the rocks.

This week the tides keep building right through the new moon, with the biggest exchanges lining up Friday through Monday. That's not just a Sound Shore thing — I'm hearing the western end of the Sound is set up the same way, with the evening flood converging right on sunset for the first time since the June full moon. Out here it means the same thing: moving water late in the day, right as the light goes gold, right when the bass want to work. If you've got one window to fish this week, that's the one I'd take — the last two hours of the incoming, running into dusk, anywhere current stacks against structure. Horton Point's boulder field, the rip off Rocky Point, and the top of the Gut approach where the reef breaks the flow — those are the three places I'd put a boat or a set of waders.

Fluke have been the more reliable story the last ten days, and it's not really a Sound Shore pattern so much as a squeeze. The bay's been running warm — warm enough that the fluke that usually spread out over the flats have bailed for cooler, cleaner water, and that means they're stacking at the mouths where bay water meets Sound water. Mattituck Inlet has been the beneficiary. Fish are holding right where the outgoing current dumps warm water into cooler Sound water, and there's a temperature seam you can practically see as a color change on a calm morning. Four to five pound fluke have come out of that seam on the last two hours of the outgoing, fished with three-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on half-ounce bucktails, dragged dead slow along bottom. Don't work it fast — these fish are sitting in a comfort zone, not chasing. Let the bait do the work.

Bass have been spotty, and I'll say that plain instead of dressing it up. Guys working Plum Gut on the last two weeks have had good days and dead days, and the difference has almost always come down to current strength. When the tide's weak, the fish sit deep and sulk. When it's ripping — and it's about to start ripping harder as we build toward the new moon — they come up on the reef edges and feed hard for a short window. Eels have been the go-to there, drifted or slow-trolled through the Gut on the last of the ebb, and bucktails tipped with a strip of squid have worked the same water when the current's too strong to hold an eel straight. Bluefish have been mixed in with the bass at the Gut, not thick, but present enough that if you're fishing bait you'll get bit by something with teeth sooner or later. Nothing wrong with that this time of year — a few slammers in the 4-6 pound range have come through on diamond jigs worked fast through the rip.

Porgies are the one thing out here that hasn't let anybody down. Structure fishing off Rocky Point and the rock piles east of Horton Point has been steady — not spectacular, but steady, which for porgies is exactly what you want. Squid strips and clam on a hi-lo rig, bottom fished right on the rocks, and you'll fill a bucket most mornings. Blackfish have started showing on the same structure as water settles, though it's early for them yet — a few keepers to three pounds on green crab, nothing to build a trip around but worth a rod in the spread if you're anchored up for porgies anyway.

Weakfish I'll mention only because people keep asking. They're just not here in numbers worth chasing. Water's been plenty warm enough for a while now, and the fish haven't followed the temperature the way the books say they should. I wouldn't burn a tide targeting them — if one shows up mixed in with the bass at the Gut, treat it like a bonus, not a plan.

Looking ahead, I'm watching Friday through Monday close. If the wind stays out of the south and lays down at night the way it's been trending, that sunset flood at the Gut and off Horton Point should be the best current-and-light combination we've had since spring. I'd fish the last two hours of the incoming into dark, eels or bucktails at the Gut, bucktails and Gulp at Mattituck's mouth on the fluke. If the wind kicks up out of the northeast instead, I'd shift inside to the porgy grounds and wait the blow out — that bite doesn't care much what the sky's doing.

reports.headline: Porgies stack up around Shelter Island as new-moon springs build toward Plum Gut
reports.subhead: Fluke slide out of the bay and into the channels while bass wait on the building tide for the weekend's big push.
reports.body_markdown:
The Peconic's been doing what it does every July — running hot ahead of the open Sound, and last week that gap widened again. Shallow flats off Southold and Noyack have been soaking up sun since sunrise, and by afternoon high the water up in the coves feels more like bathwater than bay. That's pushed bait shallow and pulled some of the bigger fluke out of the skinny stuff and into the channels where they can sit in cooler moving water — the same pattern we're seeing bay-wide this summer, just compressed here because the Peconic warms faster than anywhere else on the East End. We're heading into a new moon Thursday, and that means the tides are building into true springs through the weekend, peaking around the 11th through 13th. Bigger swings, faster water, more exchange through the Gut and around Shelter Island's points — that's the kind of current that stacks bait and gets predators moving on a schedule instead of just picking at random.

What that means practically: the days of lazy slack-tide bass are numbered for a few days. I'd be planning trips around the moving water, not fighting it. Morning outgoing at Orient Point and Plum Gut has been the best window for stripers, and with the tides building bigger this week, that current is going to rip harder and pull more bait through — sand eels and small bunker getting squeezed against the rocks on the Orient side. Bucktails in white or chartreuse, 1 to 1.5 ounce depending on how hard it's ripping, worked along the rock edge on the drift, have been picking up bass in the 26 to 32-inch range. A few better fish — one angler I talked to at the Orient ramp had a 38-incher on a bunker chunk fished on the bottom in the deeper water off the point right at the top of the tide, right before the current really got moving. Night guys running eels through the Gut on the last two hours of the outgoing have had the more consistent shots at bigger fish — that's still the money play there, especially with darker skies heading into the new moon.

Porgy fishing has been the bright spot all week, and it usually is this time of year — the Peconic is about as reliable as it gets for scup once the water settles into summer temps. Cedar Point reef, the drop-offs off Jessup's Neck, and the rock piles around Robins Island have all been holding good numbers. Bloodworms are still king but squid strips and clam are doing plenty of damage too, fished on a simple high-low rig with size 6 or 8 hooks, right on bottom in 15 to 25 feet. Anchoring up and chumming a little clam or crushed mussel shell has been worth the extra effort — it concentrates the schools and turns a decent afternoon into a limit trip. Sizes have been solid, plenty in the 12 to 14-inch range with enough 15s mixed in to keep it interesting. If you've got kids or you just want a bend-in-the-rod kind of day, this is still the play in this bay.

Fluke have been more work than usual. The bay stretches that were producing in June — the flats off Southold, the grass edges in Noyack — have gone quiet as that water's warmed past what fluke want to sit in comfortably. The better bite has shifted into the channels: the North Ferry cut between Shelter Island and Greenport, the deeper water off Jessup's Neck, and the edges of the Orient channel where the bottom drops into 20-plus feet and stays cooler on the moving tide. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the drift through those channel edges on the outgoing, have been the most consistent producer. Sizes have been mixed — a lot of shorts mixed with keepers in the 18 to 20-inch class, occasional fish pushing 22. It's not a bay full of doormats right now, but a patient drift through the deeper cuts is putting fish in the box.

Weakfish, I'll be straight with you — they're just not here in any real numbers. Water's been warm enough for weeks now that the old temperature theory doesn't hold up anymore; it's just not the season for them in this bay the way it used to be. If you're targeting them specifically, I'd spend that time on porgies or fluke instead. Bluefish have shown up in pockets chasing bait around Gardiners Bay and off Shelter Island's south side — nothing sustained, but when you find a school working bunker on top, small metal jigs or poppers will get bit fast and hard for twenty minutes before they move on.

Looking ahead, the building springs into the weekend are the story. If the wind stays reasonable, I'd be at Plum Gut or Orient Point on the outgoing Friday through Sunday morning, working the rock structure hard as that bigger tide starts really moving bait. Porgy trips around Shelter Island are close to a sure thing right now regardless of moon phase — that bite doesn't care much about tide timing the way the bass do. And for fluke, stick with the channels until this heat breaks; the bay flats won't turn back on until we get a stretch of cooler nights to knock the surface temps down.

reports.headline: Bass Holding on the Boulders as New Moon Springs Build Toward the Weekend
reports.subhead: Stripers are scattered but present in the rips, bluefin are showing off the back side, and the real window opens with Friday's tide push.
reports.body_markdown:
We're in that stretch of July where the Point makes you work for it, and this week has been no exception. Last week's tides were unremarkable — nothing extreme, nothing to write home about — but the water's been doing something worth noting. The thermal edge out past the shelf sharpened up considerably after the blow earlier in the week, and that kind of structure doesn't happen every season. We're looking at close to a ten-degree differential out on the shelf-slope break, which is about as pronounced as I've seen it. That's canyon water, not Point water, but it matters to us because it tells you the whole regional system is stacking bait and pushing warmth around in ways that eventually filter back toward the reefs and rips.

What's coming is the piece that actually changes my plans. We're building toward a new moon, and that means spring tides — bigger swings, stronger current, more water moving through North Bar and Shagwong on both stages. The window I'm circling is Friday through Monday, when the evening high stand starts lining up with sunset. That's not just a pretty picture — that's the moment stripers stack against structure and feed hard as the light drops and the current is still working. If you've fished the Point long enough you know that alignment doesn't happen every week, and when it does, you don't sleep in.

As for the bass fishing itself — I'll be straight with you, it's been a grind. Not a bad grind, but a grind. The boulder field on the south side, the stretch I've fished since I was a kid, is holding fish but they're not stacked the way they were during the June push. I worked the incoming tide there three mornings this week and connected each time, but it was one or two fish per trip, not a parade. Best action came right at first light, bucktails in the 1.5 to 2-ounce range, white or olive, bounced slow along the boulder tops in eight to fifteen feet of water. One 28-pounder came off a boulder seam on the incoming Tuesday, taken on a swim of a black GT Eel fly worked just under the surface at first light — proof the bigger fish are still around, just not schooled up tight.

Shagwong Reef has been more consistent for numbers, if not size. Guys trolling umbrella rigs and single bucktails through the reef on the last two hours of the outgoing have been picking at schoolies and a few mid-20s fish, mostly in that 15 to 25 foot depth range where the reef breaks up the current. Live eels after dark off the Lighthouse rocks have produced too — nothing gaudy, but a couple of solid mid-30s fish came off there this week on the last of the incoming, right in that classic white-water zone where the current wraps the rocks.

Bluefish have been mixed in with the bass at North Bar, chopper-class fish up to ten pounds hitting poppers and Hopkins jigs worked fast over the sandbar on the outgoing. If you want steady action without the bass grind, that's been the more reliable play — blues don't care about moon phase the way stripers do, they just want moving water and bait pushed up shallow.

Offshore, there's real buzz worth passing along even though it's not strictly Point water. Bluefin have been showing on the 20 to 30 fathom breaks south of us, and small boats running out that direction have connected on schoolie-class fish using diamond jigs and trolled Mojos. If you've got a center console and a decent weather window, that's worth a look — but I'd call it a bonus trip, not the bread and butter.

Fluke have shifted hard toward the harbor mouth and Fort Pond Bay inlet as the back bay water's warmed up more than the fish like. Drifting white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails through the deeper cuts near the inlet on the outgoing has been the play — fish to five pounds, nothing enormous, but steady enough to fill a cooler if you keep moving and hit the deeper holes where the cooler ocean water is pushing in.

Porgies and blackfish remain a summer afterthought right now — most guys aren't targeting them seriously until the water cools in fall, though a few porgies have come over the side incidentally while bottom bouncing for fluke near Turtle Cove.

Looking ahead, Friday through Monday is where I'm putting my chips. New moon springs building, the evening high stand lining up with the last light, current still working the boulder field and Shagwong hard enough to pin bait against structure. If that alignment holds and the wind stays reasonable out of the southwest, I expect the bass bite to tighten up — more fish, closer together, feeding with some urgency instead of the scattered picture we've had. I'd start at the boulder field on the incoming Friday evening with bucktails and eels, then shift to Shagwong on the last two hours of the outgoing Saturday morning if the Point doesn't produce. Worth remembering — this window doesn't come around often, and if you can only make one trip this month, I'd make it this one.

reports.headline: Bay water hits 79°F and pushes the fluke straight to the inlet
reports.subhead: Great South Bay is too warm for its own good this week, so the doormats and the smart anglers are both heading for Fire Island Inlet.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the bay basically turned into bathwater. I ran a thermometer off the transom out past the Nicoll Bay flats on Thursday and it read pushing 79 degrees on the surface — that's summer-camp-pool warm, not fluke-holding warm. We had a stretch of light southerly wind that just sat on the water for days, no mixing, no relief, and it cooked the shallow flats and the channels off Sayville and Patchogue into soup. Fluke don't like that. Neither do the bass, honestly. So the fish did what smart fish do — they left.

What's coming this week changes the equation a little. We're building toward a new moon on the 13th, and that means spring tides are stacking up — bigger swings, stronger current, more water moving through Fire Island Inlet on both the flood and the drain. That's the best thing that could happen for us right now. Stronger current means more exchange between that overheated bay water and the cooler, cleaner stuff coming in off the ocean side, which the analyst data has been showing running around 71 degrees where the upwelling's been working the beach. When that cold water gets pulled through the inlet on the outgoing, it drags bait and predators with it, and it gives the fluke and the bass a reason to stack up right where the funnel narrows. Watch for that current to really turn on Friday through Monday as the new moon tightens its grip — that's your window.

So here's what's actually happening on the water. The fluke bite in the open bay has gone soft — guys drifting the flats off West Sayville and the Nicoll Bay channel are picking at short fish and losing patience fast. But move to the inlet itself, anywhere from the Democrat Point side down through the Robert Moses bridges, and it's a different story. I had a solid morning last outgoing tide working 25 to 35 feet just west of the second bridge span with a 3/4-ounce white bucktail teased with a 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullet in pearl white, dragging it slow along bottom on the drift. Picked up two keepers in the 4-to-5-pound class and lost what felt like a bigger fish right at the boat. The pattern is consistent — fluke are stacking on the edges of the channel where that cooler ocean water is pushing in against the warmer bay flow, and the outgoing tide two hours either side of dead low has been the most productive window. If you're not marking bait on the sonar down around 20-30 feet near the bridge piers, keep moving — they're bunched up tight this week, not spread thin.

Striper action is a night game right now, which is normal for July but worth saying plainly — daytime bass fishing in the heat has been mostly a bust. Guys working bunker chunks off Democrat Point after dark on the last two hours of the incoming have been connecting with fish in the mid-20s to low 30-inch range, some better mixed in. If you want a shot at something bigger, fish the sandbar drop right off the point where the current rips hardest on that new moon flood — that's where the bait gets pinned and the bigger fish sit in the wash waiting. Live eels fished on a fish-finder rig, or just chunked bunker on a fireball rig, both been working. Don't bother during the day unless there's real cloud cover and a stiff breeze breaking up the surface.

Bluefish have been the reliable player this week when everything else got moody. Bunker schools pushing through the inlet on the tide changes have chopper blues in the 3-to-6-pound range busting bait right on the surface, especially around sunrise off the south side of the Fire Island Lighthouse rip. Metal — Kastmasters, Hopkins, anything silver you can rip through the surface — will get bit fast. It's not subtle fishing, but it's fun, and it's about the only guaranteed action if the fluke and bass are being difficult.

I want to be straight with you about weakfish — they're basically not happening. Water's warm enough, has been for weeks, and there's just nothing showing up in the bay or off the inlet. I know some of you remember when the weakfish run here was a real event; this isn't that year. I'd stop planning trips around them until something changes.

Porgies are a modest bright spot for the bay-bound crowd — light action over the reef structure off Sayville and around the Robert Moses causeway rocks, small pieces of clam on a hi-lo rig taking a mix of decent-sized scup, nothing spectacular but steady if you need a bucket of fish for dinner without fighting the inlet current.

One more thing worth watching — there's chatter about bonito and Spanish mackerel starting to show on the ocean side of the eastern inlets this week, riding that same warm push that's been moving west along the south shore. Nothing confirmed at Fire Island yet, but if that pattern keeps sliding our way, Democrat Point and the outer bar could see the first fish of the year sooner than usual. Worth keeping a rod rigged with small metal on the ready if you're out there working bass or blues.

Looking ahead, I'd put my time at the inlet through the weekend. The new moon spring tides building into Monday should sharpen up that current exchange and keep pulling fluke and bait through the bridges — that's where I'm starting every trip. If the wind stays reasonable, the outgoing tide Friday through Sunday morning is the play. Plan B if the inlet gets crowded or the current's too ripping to hold bottom — work the porgy grounds off Sayville for something to show for the day.

reports.headline: Bay Water Runs Hot, Fluke Push Into Jones Inlet on the Outgoing
reports.subhead: Spring tides build toward the new moon this weekend, and the fish that matter are following the current out of a bay that's gotten too warm for comfort.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the bay told you everything you needed to know just by looking at it. Hempstead Bay and the Great South Bay side pushed up into the high 70s — I heard 78.8 off one of the buoys inside, and that's warm enough to shut fluke down on the flats where they'd been sitting all June. When the bay gets that soupy, those fish don't sit around and suffer. They move. And where they move to, every single year, is the channels and the inlet mouth, where the outgoing tide is dragging cooler, cleaner water off the ocean side back through. That shift has already started, and it's the single biggest thing driving my week.

This week the moon is doing its part too. We're building toward a new moon around the 11th to 13th, which means bigger tidal swings — stronger current through the inlet on both ends of the cycle. Bigger outgoing means more bait getting flushed out of the back bay and stacked up right where the channel necks down past Short Beach and the Jones Inlet jetties. Bigger incoming at night means bunker and spearing pushed back up into the guts, which is when the bass that are holding around structure decide to feed hard instead of just sipping. Wind's been mild out of the south-southwest most days, no real blow to roil things up, so the water clarity on the ocean side has stayed decent — that upwelled water running around 71 degrees is a lot more comfortable for a fluke than the bathwater they were sitting in two weeks ago.

So here's what that means on the water. Sloop Channel and the West Channel drift have both turned back on for fluke, and it's specifically an outgoing tide bite — you want that current moving good, dragging your bucktail with the flow instead of fighting it. I've been running 3/4-ounce white bucktails tipped with a 5-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullet in 18 to 25 feet, slow-dragging bottom, and there's a deeper pocket off Short Beach pushing 30 feet where the bigger fish have been holding — that's where I picked up a 6-pounder Tuesday on a chartreuse bucktail with a Gulp Nemesis trailer. Not every drift produces. I made probably a dozen passes through Sloop Channel over two days to put together four keepers and a handful of shorts, so don't expect a five-minute limit. But the fish are there and they're eating, which is more than I could say for the bay two weeks ago.

Striped bass are still around Jones Inlet, mostly the resident summer fish holding tight to the jetty rocks on both sides, and the play right now is bunker. There's still bait moving through — not the fall blitz-scale schools, but pods big enough to hold fish under them. I've had the best luck snagging a bunker off the east jetty on the tail of the incoming and drifting it back with a fish-finder rig into the current seam where the rocks meet the channel edge. Night tide, especially that push right around and after high water, has been the window — a couple of fish in the mid-20-inch range and one better fish pushing 34 inches came off that program this week. Daytime has been mostly quiet for bass unless you're right on the structure at first light.

Bluefish have been mixed in under those bunker pods, nothing huge, mostly cocktail blues in the 2 to 4 pound range, but they'll hit a diamond jig or a bunker spoon worked fast along the jetty tip at first light, and they'll save a slow morning.

Weakfish are the one I keep getting asked about, and I want to be straight with you — the comeback everyone's hoping for hasn't shown up in the reports yet, at least not around here. Water temp alone isn't the trigger people think it is; the theory on Delaware Bay weakfish this summer was that warm water above 70 degrees would flip the switch, and it's been sitting there for over two weeks with basically nothing to show for it. That tells me temperature is necessary but it's not the whole story — there needs to be bait concentration and the right current to go with it. If you want to gamble on weakfish, I'd try the deeper holes near the Wantagh Bridge on the last two hours of the outgoing at dusk, working a bucktail tipped with a strip of squid slow along bottom. Don't build your whole trip around it yet.

Porgies have been steady and reliable if you just want meat for the cooler — the reef structure off the Jones Inlet sea buoy has been giving up 9 to 12 inch porgies all week on standard high-low rigs with clam, fished right on bottom in 20 to 25 feet. Not glamorous, but it's a bite you can count on when everything else is being stubborn.

Looking ahead, I'm watching that new moon spring tide build through the weekend. If the outgoing keeps flushing bait like it has, I expect the fluke bite at the inlet mouth and Sloop Channel to hold or even improve, and I want to be at the jetty right at that peak night flood on the 11th through 13th when the current's ripping hardest — that's historically when the bigger resident bass decide to really commit. If the wind stays out of the south like it has, the ocean side should stay fishable and clean. My plan for the weekend is jetty bunker at night for bass, fluke drift on the morning outgoing, and I'll keep a rod rigged for weakfish just in case that back bay current finally flips them on. Worth the gas, not worth betting the whole trip on any single species right now.

reports.headline: Bay water's cooking — fluke slide to the inlet as new moon springs build
reports.subhead: Jamaica Bay's flats are too warm to hold fish, but the inlet channels and the Bridge current are picking up the slack.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the bay sat under that thick July haze — light southwest air, barely a ripple most afternoons, and the flats cooking in the sun. That kind of stagnant, warm-water stretch is exactly what pushes fluke off the shallow bay bottom, and that's what happened. The moon's coming off full and sliding toward new on the 11th, which means the tides have been slack and unremarkable the last several days — small swings, weak current, water sitting instead of moving. That's the setup that lets bay water climb into the mid-to-upper 70s on the flats, and fluke don't want any part of that once it gets much past 75. They've been sliding toward the channels, the inlet, and anywhere there's a little more exchange and a little less heat.

This week changes that picture. New moon lands July 11, and that means building spring tides right through the weekend — bigger highs, lower lows, and a lot more current pushing through Rockaway Inlet and under the Marine Parkway Bridge. Bigger tide swings flush the bay harder, pull cooler, cleaner ocean water in on the flood, and get everything moving again. I'm watching Friday through Monday, the 10th through the 13th, as the best stretch of the month so far — that's when the evening flood starts stacking up right around sunset, and that's prime time at the Bridge.

Fluke has been the real story, but it's a moved story. The bay flats — Grassy Bay, the flats off Ruffle Bar, the stuff that's usually money in June — have gone quiet as the water's warmed. The fish that made the trip didn't disappear, they relocated to the inlet channel and the deeper cuts around Breezy Point and the Rockaway Inlet buoys, where there's current and cooler water pushing in off the ocean side. I've been dragging white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails through 18 to 25 feet in the inlet channel on the outgoing, tipping with a strip of squid, and connecting with keeper-class fish in the 18 to 21-inch range, with the occasional better one mixed in — nothing like that 12-plus-pounder they weighed in at Bayonne a couple weeks back, but solid, legitimate fluke fishing if you're willing to leave the flats behind. The bite's been best on the first two hours of the outgoing, when the current is still building and dragging bait out of the bay past the bridge pilings.

Striped bass have been a dusk-and-dawn proposition right now — daytime heat has them tucked deep and sluggish, but the Marine Parkway Bridge is still doing its thing on the outgoing tide, especially the last two hours before low. Bunker chunks fished on the bottom near the pilings have been picking up schoolies and the occasional mid-20-inch fish, and guys throwing swimming plugs and paddletails through the current seams after dark have had better luck than the bait guys some nights. With the new moon building the tide swings this week, I expect that bridge bite to sharpen up — more water moving means more bait getting pushed through the current lanes, and bass stack up right where that funnel narrows.

Bluefish have been scattered but present. Rockaway Beach surf has had pockets of activity early and late in the day when bunker schools push close to the beach — metal like a Deadly Dick or a Kastmaster worked fast through the wash has been the ticket when the blues show, though it's not an every-day thing yet. Inside the bay, Canarsie Pier has had a decent run of snapper blues for anyone with a light spinning rod and small Kastmasters or spearing — good action for kids and a nice change of pace, even if nobody's filling a cooler with them.

Porgies are around Cross Bay Bridge and the humps off Beach Channel in modest numbers — nothing spectacular, but a bucket of bait, some sandworms or clam, and a couple hours on the bottom during the tide change will put a mess of them in the cooler. Weakfish, on the other hand, have basically been a non-event. Water's warm enough on paper, but the reports just aren't there this year — same story up and down the coast. I wouldn't plan a trip around them right now.

Looking ahead, I'd put my time at the Marine Parkway Bridge on the outgoing this weekend as the new moon builds those spring tides — Friday through Monday evening, right as the flood stacks up with sunset, is where I'd expect the bass bite to firm up. If that current gets moving the way I think it will, the inlet fluke bite should get a boost too, with cleaner ocean water pushing further into the channel on the flood. If the bass don't cooperate, I've got the fluke drift in the inlet as my backup — either way, the bay's telling you plainly where the fish went. Follow the current, not the flats, until this heat breaks.

reports.headline: New moon springs load up The Race and Plum Gut as fluke abandon the baking bay
reports.subhead: Stripers stack the eddies on max current, bluefish chop through Orient, and the fluke bite has gone from Peconic mud to cold ocean water pouring through the inlets.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the Sound did what it always does heading into a new moon — the current built every tide, and by Sunday The Race was running like a river. Wind had been out of the northeast for a stretch, which kept some chop stacked against Fishers Island but also pushed a slug of cooler water up against the eastern grounds. That mattered, because Gardiners Bay and the Peconics have been sitting up near 78 degrees, borderline uncomfortable for fluke, while the ocean-side water pushing through Plum Gut and Orient on the incoming has been running closer to 71. That 7-degree gap is the whole story of the week — everything that can leave the warm shallow water for the cold moving water has been doing exactly that.

This week the moon goes new on the 11th, which means we're building toward spring tides right through the weekend — bigger swings, harder current, and a PM flood that starts stacking up against sunset from Friday through Monday. That's the window I'm circling. When the evening high tide lines up with last light at Plum Gut and Orient Point, the bass come up out of the depth and feed the last hour of shrinking light into full dark. It's not a guarantee, but I've fished that convergence enough summers to know it's the best two hours you'll get all week if the wind cooperates.

Striper fishing right now is a current game, full stop. The bite at The Race and Plum Gut is happening on the meat of the tide, not the slack — find the eddy behind Valiant Rock or off North Dumnpling where five knots of water folds back on itself, and that's where the bass are parked, facing into the current waiting for whatever gets swept past. Eels fished on a fish-finder rig, weighted just enough to hold bottom in that current, have been the most consistent producer after dark. Guys throwing big Danny-style swimmers and bucktail-and-eelskin combos off the rocks at Orient Point State Park have connected too, mostly on the last two hours of the incoming into the top of the tide. Sizes have been mixed — plenty of schoolies and mid-20s in the mix, but there are still pockets of genuinely large fish showing up in that current, the kind that make your drag sing when a 40-incher decides it doesn't want to come off bottom. Nothing guaranteed, but the fish are there — you need to be on the water when the current's running hardest, which usually means 10 p.m. to 2 a.m. right now.

Bluefish have been the more reliable player. Choppers in the 8-to-12-pound class are working bunker schools through Plum Gut and off Orient Point on the ebb, and they're not subtle about it — surface blitzes with birds working overhead, easy to spot from the boat or even from the rocks at first light. Bunker spoons trolled behind the boat at 3-4 knots have been money, and if you want to cast, a Hogy popper or a chrome Kastmaster worked fast through the froth will get bit. This bite has been the most dependable thing in the zone the past ten days — less finesse than the bass game, more about being in the right piece of moving water when the bait gets pushed through the funnel.

Fluke is where the story's changed the most. The bay bite has gone soft as that Peconic water climbed into the high 70s — fish just don't want to work that hard in warm water when there's cooler stuff nearby. What's happened instead is a real push of fluke out of the bay and into the current-swept edges: Orient Harbor's outer channel, the deeper cuts inside Plum Gut, and the drop-offs on the ocean side of Fishers Island. Fishing the last two hours of the outgoing in 25 to 40 feet with a 3/4-ounce white bucktail and a chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullet has been the play — drift slow, keep contact with bottom, and expect the bite to come as a subtle tick rather than a slam. Sizes have been decent, some fish pushing 4 to 5 pounds mixed in with a lot of shorts, so it's not a keeper-every-drift situation, but the fish are there if you put the time in on the right piece of structure.

Porgies have been quiet and dependable at the same time — not exciting, but a sure thing if you want dinner. The rock piles off Fishers Island and around Bug Light are holding good numbers in 20 to 30 feet, and a simple high-low rig with sandworms or clam strips will keep you busy on any stage of the tide. Weakfish, on the other hand, I'm not seeing. Water temps have been right for weeks now and there's still nothing worth reporting — I'd put my money elsewhere.

One more thing worth watching: the warm-water pelagic window that's been building along the South Shore inlets is in its final days, and there's a real chance the first bonito or Spanish mackerel push into the strong current at Plum Gut or The Race before it closes out. I haven't seen it yet in our water, but the current here is exactly the kind of structure those fish like to work, and the timing lines up. If I had a morning open this week, I'd be running light spinning gear with small metal jigs just in case, while still working the main program — bass on the current, blues on the blitz, fluke on the drift. That's the reliable stuff. The bonito would just be a bonus.

reports.headline: New moon springs build toward a sunset flood window at Stepping Stones
reports.subhead: Bass have been scattered and lockjawed on the slack tides all week, but bigger water arriving Friday through Monday should turn the lights back on at last light.
reports.body_markdown:
Let me tell you what the last seven days felt like out here: warm, flat, and stingy. We came off the June full moon into a stretch of neap tides — small swings, weak current, water that just sat there instead of moving. Add in a run of light southwest wind and stable warm air, and you get exactly what I saw off Execution Rocks and the Stepping Stones light all week: bass that show for twenty minutes around the tide change and then vanish. When the current's soft, stripers don't have to commit. They can sit in the rockpiles and pick at whatever drifts by instead of setting up on a rip and feeding hard. That's been the story since last weekend — good marks on the machine, quiet rods.

That's about to change. We're building into a new moon, and the tides are already stacking bigger day over day. The real news for this zone is the PM flood window lining up with sunset from Friday the 10th through Monday the 13th, with the tightest alignment Saturday and Sunday. High stand at Kings Point is going to hit right around last light those two evenings, which is the exact recipe that turns Stepping Stones and the mouth of Manhasset Bay into a striper highway. Bigger spring tide, more water moving, current stacking bait against structure right as the light drops — that's when the bass that have been sulking all week get up on the reef and feed with some authority. If you've only got one evening to fish this month, Saturday or Sunday night on that incoming tide is the one I'd take.

In the meantime, the bite hasn't been dead, just honest work. Bass to 28 inches have been coming off Execution Rocks on the outgoing, fished tight to the rockpile in 15 to 20 feet with 1-ounce bucktails dressed in white or chartreuse, tipped with a strip of fresh bunker belly. Slow-rolled right along the bottom edge where the rock drops into the channel — that's where they're sitting, using the structure to break the current and ambush whatever's getting swept through. A few guys working live eels after dark at the base of Hart Island have done well too, especially on the last two hours of the outgoing when the current's still got some push but isn't ripping.

The bunker schools I told you to watch back in June are still stacked up off Matinecock Point, and they haven't thinned out much — pushed a little tighter to the beach with the warm water we've had. Where you find bunker balled up like that, bass and blues are shadowing them, especially at first light. Bluefish have actually been the more reliable player this week — 3- to 5-pound choppers blowing up on top off Matinecock and around the Throgs Neck Bridge pilings, chewing through anything metal. Diamond jigs in the 1- to 2-ounce range, or a topwater popper worked fast through the froth, and you're hooked up. That bite's been consistent morning and evening regardless of the tide funk, because blues don't care as much about current as bass do — they just want the bait ball.

Fluke have been a mixed bag, and here's why: the bay and harbor water has gotten warm — I've seen mid-to-upper 70s readings in the back harbors, Manhasset and Hempstead both — and that's pushed the better fluke out of the shallow bay water and into the deeper channels and toward the inlets where there's cooler water moving through. If you're drifting Little Neck Bay or the shallow flats and getting nothing but shorts, don't fight it — slide out to the channel edges and the mouth of Hempstead Harbor, work 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, and drag them slow on the last of the outgoing. That's where the keeper-class fish have been sitting, staged in the deeper cooler water waiting on bait to get pulled out of the bay with the tide.

Porgies have been steady and reliable, which is more than I can say for most everything else this week — Hart Island and the rockpiles off City Island are holding good numbers on bloodworms and squid strips, high-low rigs, fishing the bottom of the tide when the current eases up enough to keep bait on the hook. Blackfish season's closed in the Sound right now, so leave the tog gear home — those fish are off the menu until the fall opener.

And weakfish — I'll be straight with you, I haven't heard a single credible report out of this zone despite water temps that should be right for them. Warm water alone doesn't make weakfish show up; you need the bait and the right structure lining up too, and right now it just isn't happening here. I wouldn't burn a tide targeting them specifically.

So here's my read heading into next week: the neap tide funk breaks as the new moon builds bigger water, and that PM flood window converging with sunset Friday through Monday is the best shot we've had since before the June full moon. I'd be at Stepping Stones or working the drift off Kings Point Saturday evening with bucktails and eels ready, watching that tide come up as the light drops. If the bass don't cooperate there, Matinecock's bunker schools are the fallback — where there's bait, there's usually something willing to eat it.

reports.headline: Bay Cooks Past 78, Fluke Slide Into Jones Inlet on the Outgoing
reports.subhead: New moon springs building toward the weekend are trading warm bay water for cold ocean water right through the inlet — and that trade is the whole story this week.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the Great South Bay got soupy. I had a thermometer reading up near 78.8 degrees in the back channels off Freeport, and that's too warm for a fluke that likes his water in the low 70s. What that does is push the fish — it doesn't shut them off, it relocates them. Fluke that were sitting on the flats and channel edges all June started sliding toward moving water where it's cooler and better oxygenated, and that means the inlet itself, Sloop Channel, and the ocean side structure off Jones Beach and Short Beach. I fished three tides last week trying to find where they'd settled and the pattern held every time — nothing in the shallow bay water, and then you hit the deeper cuts near the inlet mouth and you're back in business. The wind didn't do us any favors either, sitting out of the south and southwest most days, which kept the bay a little chalky and pushed extra warmth in on the flood.

This week the moon's the story. We're building toward a new moon around the 13th-14th, and that means the tidal swings are getting bigger every day between now and the weekend — bigger range, stronger current, harder push both ways. At Jones Inlet that translates directly into a stronger outgoing tide, which is exactly what we want right now. That outgoing drags all that warm, stale bay water out past the jetties and lets the cooler ocean water — I'm hearing upwelled readings around 71 degrees just outside — sneak back in on the flood behind it. That exchange is the whole ballgame for fluke and for bait movement this week. Bigger springs also mean a harder-running current through the inlet channel itself, which is going to concentrate bait against structure instead of letting it spread out over the flats. That's good news if you're a jetty guy or a boat guy working the deeper cuts, tougher if you're used to picking at fish over open sand.

Fluke fishing has been honest work, not easy work. The bay bite has gone quiet — I had two drifts inside South Oyster Bay last week that didn't produce a single knock — but the inlet and ocean-side program has been salvaging the trip. Best water has been the deeper edge of Sloop Channel and the stretch just inside the inlet mouth on the outgoing, working 3/4-ounce white bucktails tipped with a five-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullet, dragged slow along bottom in 15 to 25 feet. Chartreuse has been drawing more strikes than white on the dirtier tides, so I keep both tied on and switch depending on how the water looks that day. Nothing giant — most fish 17 to 20 inches, with a few keepers mixed in — but enough action to make the drift worthwhile if you're patient about finding the exact seam where that cooler water is stacking bait.

Stripers have been a night and dawn game right now, which is normal for the middle of July. The bigger fish are holding around the inlet rocks and the deeper holes off Short Beach, and I'm hearing solid reports of bunker schools starting to show along the beach front, which always gets my attention this time of year — that's usually the first hint of things to come once the water starts trending the other way in September. For now, the play is eels after dark fished tight to the Jones Inlet jetty rocks and the bridge pilings on the last of the outgoing, and diamond jigs or bucktails worked the same structure at first light before the boat traffic picks up. Nothing frantic, but consistent — a couple of slot fish a trip if you put in the time.

Bluefish have filled in the gaps nicely. Snapper blues are thick in the Freeport canals and back creeks, and the cocktail-sized blues are chasing bait right at the inlet mouth on the outgoing tide, which makes for a fun break between fluke drifts — small metal or a Deadly Dick will get bit fast if you find the surface activity.

Weakfish I want to be straight with you about. There's chatter about a comeback and I've had a few scattered reports of weakfish in the deeper holes of South Oyster Bay and around the Wantagh Bridge pilings, taken on grass shrimp jigs and bloodworms fished slow on the bottom at night. But it's spotty — a fish here, a fish there, not a pattern yet. Warm water alone doesn't bring them back; I've seen that story before and it takes more than a warm reading to build a real fishery. I wouldn't plan a whole trip around them yet, but I'd keep a rod rigged light just in case you're in the right creek at the right time.

Porgies are steady and reliable around the Jones Inlet rock piles in 20 to 30 feet — standard high-low rig, clam bait, and you'll pick at them all tide if you've got nothing better going.

Looking ahead, I'd fish the building springs through the weekend and target the outgoing at Jones Inlet for fluke and bass both — bigger current should push more bait through the cut and concentrate it right where the jetty guys and drifters can get at it. If the inlet gets too strong to fish clean on the peak of those new moon tides, my backup is working the slower stages, first hour of the outgoing or last hour of the incoming, when the current's still moving bait but hasn't turned into a firehose.

reports.headline: Bay water pushing 78 degrees sends the fluke running for the inlet
reports.subhead: New moon springs load up the Marine Parkway rip while bluefish crash bunker in the Rockaway wash.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the bay did what it does every July when we get a stretch of sun and light wind — it cooked. I was seeing 78 and change on my temp gauge in the back channels off Grassy Bay by Thursday, and that's too warm for fluke to sit comfortably on the flats where they were feeding in May and June. They didn't disappear, they just packed up and moved to where the water still moves and stays cooler — the deeper channels, the Beach Channel drop, and out through Rockaway Inlet itself. That's the story of the whole bay right now: warm, mostly slack, green water inside, and a cleaner, cooler push wherever the tide is actually working. The moon's swinging toward new on the 10th, which means we're building into spring tides through the weekend — bigger swings, stronger current, and that's exactly the medicine this bay needs right now to flush some of that heat and get bait moving again.

Wind's been out of the south and southwest most days, which keeps the ocean side a little bumpy but doesn't hurt the bay much — if anything it's helped push a little cooler water in through the inlet on the bigger tides. With the new moon spring tides peaking Friday through Monday, look for the flood to run harder and longer at Marine Parkway Bridge, and the outgoing to really rip through the inlet by the channel markers off Breezy. That's the window I'm circling. Stronger current means bait gets pinned against structure instead of drifting lazy, and that's when the bigger bass and the blues decide it's worth their while to show up and eat instead of just cruising.

Fluke fishing in the bay proper has gone from good to patchy — guys who were limiting out in May on the flats off Ruffle Bar and Big Egg Marsh are working a lot harder for fewer fish now that the water's warm and slack. The move has been out toward the inlet and the deeper cuts. I had a solid afternoon last week working the drop-off just inside Breezy Point in about 18 to 22 feet, dragging a 5-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a 3/4-ounce bucktail nice and slow on the last two hours of the outgoing. Picked up three keepers and lost a good one at the boat that felt bigger than the 12-pound doormat that got weighed in over on the Jersey side a couple weeks back — that fish is still the one everybody's talking about at the shops, and it's a reminder that the big girls are out there if you put the right bait in the right depth. If you're fishing from a kayak or small boat, don't waste your time on the shallow bay flats right now — head for Beach Channel or work the edges where the current still runs, even at low water.

Stripers are where the new moon tide is going to matter most. Marine Parkway Bridge has been staging fish on the outgoing all week, and with the bigger spring tides coming in through the weekend, I expect that bite to sharpen up. Live eels drifted through the pilings on the last two hours of the outgoing have been the ticket, along with bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig for the fish holding deeper in the current seam. Nothing enormous yet — mostly schoolies to mid-20-inchers — but the current's about to get a lot more serious, and stronger flow usually means the better fish start showing up to work the rip instead of just the small ones. I'd be at that bridge on the Friday through Sunday outgoing this week, right as the tide starts really moving, and I'd stay through the last hour before dead low.

Bluefish have been the most reliable thing in the surf. Rockaway Beach has had real bunker schools pushing through close to the beach in the mornings, and when the blues find them it's fast and violent — poppers and metal like a Kastmaster or an Ava jig worked at speed have been drawing crashing strikes right in the wash from Beach 90th down toward Beach 116th. It's not an all-day thing — it's short windows, usually first light and again right before dark, so don't sleep in if you want in on it. Porgies are still a solid, honest bite for anyone fishing bottom rigs with sandworms or clam off Cross Bay Bridge and in the Beach Channel — nothing glamorous, but steady, and a good option for family trips off Canarsie Pier where the kids can get bit without much fuss.

Weakfish, I'll be straight with you — despite the warm water, I'm still not hearing real reports out of the bay or inlet. The water's plenty warm enough on paper, but warm water alone hasn't been enough to trigger them the last couple seasons, and this year's no different so far. I wouldn't plan a trip around them yet.

Looking ahead, the new moon spring tides building through the weekend are the story. If the current comes on as strong as it should at Marine Parkway and the inlet, I'd fish the outgoing there over the next four or five days before anything else — that's where the stripers and the bigger blues are going to concentrate. Plan B if that bridge bite doesn't materialize: work the Breezy Point drop-off on the last of the outgoing for fluke, because that pattern's been consistent even while everything else in the bay sorts itself out.

reports.headline: New moon springs load up The Race as first bonito show at Fishers Island
reports.subhead: Bigger tides and ripping current are stacking bass in the eddies while bluefish and porgies keep the rail bent from Plum Gut to Orient.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the Sound was still shaking off the June full moon hangover — current running hard but not violent, water in the low 70s and holding steady, and the bass scattered between the classic structure instead of stacking anywhere reliable. Wind sat out of the northeast for a few days, which is usually a gift out here because it sharpens the thermal breaks along the edges of The Race and Plum Gut, but it also kept the surface a little lumpy for the guys running small boats. I fished four tides, connected on two, and both times it was about finding the exact seam where the moving water met the slower stuff — not the middle of the rip, the edge of it.

This week changes the math. We're building into new moon springs, peaking around July 11-13, and that means bigger tidal exchange than we've seen since before the last full moon. More water moving through Plum Gut and The Race in less time — current that'll run harder and longer on both the ebb and flood. For a guy who fishes current for a living, that's not a inconvenience, that's the whole game. Big springs push bait out of the back bays and eelgrass flats and funnel it straight through the pinch points. Stripers know this. They don't fight 4-5 knots of water head-on — they sit in the eddies behind Race Rock, behind the humps off Orient Point, behind the down-current side of the reef at Fishers Island, and let the current deliver dinner. The harder the water runs, the tighter those fish hold to structure, and the better the eddy bite gets right at the tide change when the current starts to slacken just enough for them to leave the shadow and feed.

Fluke have already started making the move we expect this time of year — out of the warm, stagnant bay water and into the inlets and channels where there's exchange and oxygen. Gardiners Bay and Orient Harbor water has been sitting warm and a little soft, and the fluke that were spread through there are pushing toward Plum Gut and the deeper cuts off Orient Point where the tide keeps things clean. Best fluke action this week has been on the outgoing at Plum Gut, working 4-ounce bucktails tipped with a strip of squid or a 5-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullet, bounced along bottom in 25 to 40 feet. You want to be right on the edge of the main channel where the current slows just enough to hold bottom without your bucktail skipping off into the rocks. Keeper-size fish, some pushing 5 pounds, mixed with a lot of short fish you're throwing back — a decent bite but not a slam-dunk, so cover water and don't marry one drift.

Striped bass have been the story at first light and last light, which tracks with where we are on the moon. Working the rocks at Orient Point in the dark hours, big soft-plastic swimbaits and Danny-style surface plugs have drawn strikes from fish in the 20 to 30 pound class, mostly on the last two hours of the incoming when the current softens enough to let a plug swim instead of getting swept sideways. The Race has fished better by boat — drifting bunker chunks and live eels through the rip on the last hour of the ebb, right where the current dumps into the deeper basin south of Race Rock. That's classic big-bass water, and with springs building, that current lane is going to get more violent before it gets easier, which means the eddy game becomes even more important. If you're throwing plugs from the rocks, fish the slack pockets tight to structure — don't waste casts into the screaming middle of the rip.

Bluefish have been the reliable bite when the bass go quiet, and they're not shy about it. Chopper blues in the 8 to 12 pound range have been busting bait on the surface off Fishers Island and out toward the Race on calm mornings, and if you see the birds working, a simple Hopkins or Kastmaster thrown into the melee will get bit on nearly every cast. Porgies remain a dependable bottom bite around Plum Gut and the rockpiles off Fishers — small hooks, sandworms or clam, fished on a hi-lo rig in 20 to 35 feet on the slower stages of the tide when they're not getting pushed off structure by current.

The most interesting development is what's showing up at the edges of the zone. The cold wall that's normally kept warm-water pelagics penned up around Block Island broke down hard, and that's opened a corridor for bonito and Spanish mackerel to spread west toward Newport and Point Judith. That warm water is close enough to Fishers Island that it's worth watching — I haven't seen confirmed bonito inside Sound proper yet, but the signs are lining up, and the first fish showing anywhere near Fishers wouldn't shock me before the pelagic window closes out this weekend. Worth running light spinning gear rigged with small metals if you're already out there chasing blues.

Looking ahead: if the new moon springs build the way they should through the weekend, I'm fishing the eddies at Race Rock and the down-current side of the Orient reef on the last two hours of the incoming — that's where the current math favors big bass without punishing the angler. If the bass don't cooperate, the fluke bite at Plum Gut on the outgoing is the fallback, and it's been solid enough to fill a cooler even on a slow bass day. Either way, respect the current this week — springs like these can turn a comfortable drift into a genuine hazard fast, especially through the Gut.

reports.headline: New Moon Springs Reopen the Sunset Striper Window from Norwalk to Charles Island
reports.subhead: Bigger tides and bunker pods are reshaping the Central Sound bite as fluke bail out of warming harbors for the cooler edges of Stratford Shoal.
reports.body_markdown:
We're coming off a stretch where the harbors got soft and the Sound stayed honest. Oyster Bay, Northport, Port Jeff Harbor — all of them have been running warm in the back corners, warm enough that the fluke that were happy sitting in eight feet of water on a sand bottom two weeks ago have picked up and moved. That's not a guess, that's what I'm seeing on the drift — empty water where there used to be marks, and marks now stacking on the hard edges where warm harbor water bumps into the cooler main-Sound flow. Stratford Shoal is the textbook example of that right now. The thermal break sitting off the western drop is doing exactly what a thermocline is supposed to do: holding bait, holding fluke, holding porgies, and making the shoal fish tighter to specific depth bands instead of spread all over the plateau.

The bigger story this week is the moon. We're building into new moon springs, with the tightest alignment landing Friday through Monday, July 10–13. Bigger tidal range means stronger current through the pinch points — Stratford Shoal rip, the gaps between the Norwalk Islands, the tip of Charles Island — and stronger current means bait gets pushed hard into the eddies where predators don't have to fight for it. The piece that's got my attention specifically is the PM flood lining up with sunset on those spring tide days. That's the first evening high-water-into-dark window we've had since the June full moon, and in the western half of my beat — Oyster Bay out through the Norwalk chain and down to Charles Island — that combination has produced some of the better bass nights of the last two summers. If you can only fish one window this week, that's the one I'd take.

Striper fishing itself has been honest but not easy. Guys working the Norwalk Islands humps on the last two hours of the incoming into dusk are finding schoolies mixed with better fish — bass to low 30-inch class — on white and chartreuse bucktails, one to two ounces, worked slow along the rock edges, and on soft-plastic swimbaits skipped over the same structure once the light drops. Nothing has been a blitz. It's been pick-your-spots fishing: find where the current is breaking around a specific rock or point, work it thoroughly, move on if nothing happens in twenty minutes. There have also been quieter reports of some genuinely large fish mixed into the bunker schools working Port Jefferson and around Middle Ground Light — not a pattern you can plan a whole trip around yet, but worth having a bigger rod rigged if you're marking bait balls getting nervous on the surface. When those peanut bunker and adult bunker schools get pushed tight by blues on top, that's when the bigger bass show up underneath to clean up what gets dropped.

Bluefish have been the most reliable thing in the middle Sound the last ten days. Port Jeff, Middle Ground, and the water off Charles Island have all had bunker getting worked over hard, blues in the 3 to 6 pound range mostly, some better mixed in. Diamond jigs — half-ounce to one-ounce, bare or with a tube — cast into the surface commotion is about as complicated as it needs to be right now. If the blues get finicky, dropping a bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig behind the melee usually pulls a few more.

Fluke has been the honest disappointment of the last two weeks for guys fishing the traditional harbor spots, but the Stratford Shoal push has been a bright spot if you know where to look.
