Four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on three-quarter-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the western edge in 25 to 35 feet on the last of the outgoing, have been putting keeper-class fish in the boat — nothing huge, mostly 18 to 21 inches, but steady enough to call it a pattern. Spearing tipped on the same bucktail has been the better producer when the current slacks and the drift gets lazy. Middle Ground Light has fished similarly on the smaller tides but got noticeably better once the bigger water started moving through this week.

Porgies remain the most dependable thing I can point you to right now. Stratford Shoal and Middle Ground Light on the anchor, high-low rigs with sandworm or clam, and it's a numbers game — good for keeping a rod bent when the bass and blues aren't cooperating. Blackfish, honestly, is a non-story this time of year — that bite belongs to October and November, not July, and I wouldn't waste a trip on it now. Weakfish continue to be more theory than reality in this zone; I haven't heard a credible report worth passing along, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

Looking ahead, the July 10–13 spring tide window with that PM flood-sunset convergence is where I'd put my money if I only had one shot this week — Norwalk Islands and Charles Island rock structure, working the last two hours before dark into the first hour of true dark. If the wind stays reasonable out of the south or southwest, that setup should hold. Plan B if the bass don't show is the Stratford Shoal fluke drift, which has been the more consistent producer regardless of moon phase. As for bonito — it's too early for Central Sound yet, that's an August pattern once the water pushes past 68 degrees through the narrows, but the pelagic corridor east of us is already stirring, and it's worth watching how fast that warmth works its way down the Sound this month.

reports.headline: Post-blow edge lights up Veatch and Hydrographer as the shelf break widens to 10 degrees
reports.subhead: A dirty week of weather finally cleared into the best thermal setup of the season, and the yellowfin found the seam first.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week was a write-off for most of the fleet out of Montauk and Block Island — a stretch of onshore wind and a couple of frontal passages kept the canyon boats tied up or running short trips to the closer grounds. But that blow did something useful out on the edge: it mixed the water hard enough that when it finally cleared out Tuesday night, the shelf-slope break sharpened up instead of smoothing over. I'm looking at a differential of better than 10 degrees between shelf water and the Gulf Stream filaments pushing up against Veatch and Hydrographer — the widest gap I've seen all season. That's not a subtle edge. That's a wall you can practically see on the plotter before you see it on the temp gauge, and fish stack against walls like that because the bait does first.

The moon's sliding toward new — we're dark by the 12th or 13th — which means squid lighting at night is going to get better every night this week, not worse. No moon glow to wash out your underwater lights, no moon glow pulling squid away from the boat. And the Coimbra corridor, that 20 to 30 fathom stretch where a northeast upwelling has been sharpening the temperature breaks all week, is holding a real concentration of school bluefin. That's a midshore run, not a canyon run, and it matters for fuel math — if the bluefin are eating good at 20 fathoms, there's no reason to burn the extra hours and diesel to get to the 100-fathom line unless the yellowfin are stacked up enough to justify it. Right now, with this edge as sharp as it is, I think they are.

Wednesday and Thursday this week are shaping up as the first real canyon window since the blow, and I'd call it the best structural setup of the year so far. The warm seam running out toward the Hudson east wall and down through the Wilmington-Poor Man's stretch has yellowfin holding right on the 100-fathom curve — we marked good sign trolling the temp break in 900 to 1,100 feet off the southwest corner of Veatch, working a mixed spread of green machines and cedar plugs off the short riggers with a bar of Ilanders down the center. Fish in the 40 to 60 pound class, nothing giant, but a consistent pick through the morning before the bite went quiet with the sun high. When the troll dies at midday, that's when I switch over to vertical jigging — a 200 to 300 gram Shimano Butterfly worked with a long stroke through the thermocline has been drawing strikes right at the edge of where the warm and cold water shake hands, usually somewhere between 250 and 400 feet on the sounder.

Bigeye have been a nighttime program, same as always this time of year. Anchor or drift right on the edge at Hydrographer with the underwater lights down and squid jigs working, and once you've built a bait ball, switch to a chunk line with butterflied squid on a long fluorocarbon leader, no swivel, letting it sink naturally. We've had a couple of quality bigeye in the 150 to 200 pound range come off that program over the last ten days, but I want to be straight with you — it's a low-percentage game. You might sit on the edge all night and get one bite. That's the nature of bigeye fishing out here. You do it because when it connects, it's the best fish of the year, not because it's consistent.

Wahoo have shown up sporadically on the high-speed trolling spread — planers and deep-diving stretch lures worked at 12 to 15 knots along the same warm seam — but they're a bonus fish right now, not a target you can plan a whole trip around. Same story with mahi: a few fish came off a weed line drifting east of Oceanographer, nothing big, 5 to 10 pounds, but if you find any floating structure or a good rip line with clean water on one side and dirty on the other, it's worth a few casts with a small hookless teaser and a naked ballyhoo behind it.

White marlin are still a watch item, not a report. The warm plume that needs to push onto the bank hasn't gotten out this far east yet — that's a mid-Atlantic story for now, expected in the next week to ten days at the canyons south of us. I wouldn't plan a trip around marlin at Atlantis or Veatch this week. Plan around the yellowfin edge and the midshore bluefin, and treat any marlin sign as a bonus.

Looking ahead: if that 10-degree differential holds through the weekend — and Georges Bank's second warming surge this month suggests it might strengthen rather than fade — I'd keep pushing Veatch and Hydrographer on the troll at first light, then work the vertical jig once the sun gets up. If you can only get one night out there, make it a dark-moon squid light session at the edge; that's where the bigeye earn their reputation. And if the fuel math doesn't favor the long run, the bluefin at 20 fathoms in the Coimbra corridor are a legitimate consolation prize, not a fallback. Either way, watch the wind — another front is worth keeping an eye on before you commit to the run.

reports.headline: Post-blow window opens the Washington Canyon wall — yellowfin stack the warm seam
reports.subhead: A 10-degree thermal break at the shelf edge and a darkening moon set up the best two-day stretch of the young season, but you had to be there Wednesday to cash it.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week beat us up a little before it paid us back. We had a stiff blow roll through over the weekend that put a 3-4 foot chop on the canyon and kept most of the fleet tied to the dock Sunday into Monday. That kind of wind mixes the top of the water column, and I was bracing for the usual hangover — cloudy green water, scattered bait, a slow week of hunting. Instead the blow did us a favor. It pushed the shelf-slope thermal break wide open, and by Tuesday afternoon we were reading a 10.3-degree differential between the shelf water and the slope water off the canyon edge — the widest gradient I've seen all year. That's not a subtle seam. That's a wall of warm water stacked against cold, and anything with a swim bladder knows exactly where that line is.

The moon's been waning down toward new — dark nights right now, and dark nights on the canyon mean squid. The Illex and shortfin have been thick on the meter after sundown, and with no moon washing out the water column, the squid-light bite off the stern has been about as reliable as anything we've got right now. New moon lands mid-week ahead, which means springs building, more current push through the canyon, and — if the warm seam holds — a shot at getting bigeye to show on the night drop. That's the setup. Wednesday and Thursday were the payoff.

We worked the warm seam running from the Wilmington-Poor Man's stretch down across the top of Washington, riding the 100-fathom curve where it bends around 38°10'N, 74°12'W. That's been the honest edge line — troll it east to west on the drop from 90 fathoms out to about 130, and you're crossing the thermal break instead of running parallel to it, which matters. Yellowfin were sitting right on that edge, mixed classes, mostly 30-50 pounders with a few bigger fish mixed through, and they wanted a green machine or a small Ilander pulled tight in the shotgun position, ballyhoo strings out further back. Nothing exotic — small spreader bars worked when the fish were finicky, straight ballyhoo-and-hookless-teaser combos worked when they were fired up chasing bait balls we could actually see on the surface.

The bluefin have been a different story and honestly the more interesting one right now. NE upwelling has sharpened up the 20 to 30 fathom breaks well inshore of the canyon proper, and the corridor running north of the Coimbra wreck has been holding a real concentration of school-class bluefin — 20 fathoms of water, tighter troll spread, cedar plugs and small Mojos doing the damage on the troll pass, and then at night the squid lights bring them up shallow enough to jig cut squid strips right off the transom. That's been more consistent than the offshore bite, honestly — three trips out to that corridor this week, connected on all three, though not every fish stuck and we had our share of pulled hooks on light drags set for the smaller class fish.

Wahoo have been quiet for us — one fish, a decent 45-pounder, came off a high-speed Yo-Zuri along the east wall drop where the current rips hardest, but that's one bite in four trips, not a pattern yet. Mahi have shown in ones and twos around any floating debris or weed line we crossed on the run out, nothing to build a day around but worth a stop if you see color under a paddy. And I'll say this plainly — the bite has not been a gimme. We had one trip this week where we worked the whole edge from Poor Man's down to Washington and only had two bites all day. The fish are there, but they're locked onto that thermal seam with real precision, and if you're not running your temp gauge and paying attention to where that line actually sits that day, you can burn a tank of fuel trolling warm water on both sides of the fish.

White marlin is the one I'm watching hardest right now. The warm plume that's been feeding this thermal setup is the same signal that usually pushes the first flags up onto the bank, and with the canyon complex running this warm this early, I'd put the window at seven to ten days out — call it the back half of next week. If I had one day to burn on that bet, I'd run the ballyhoo spread light and small, dinks and split-tail mullet on 20-pound class gear, working the 50-fathom edge inshore of the canyon head where the bait's been stacking.

Here's the honest read heading into this week: the Wednesday-Thursday window was the best structural setup we've had all season, and if that thermal break holds through the weekend — big if, since another front is lurking behind this one — I'd keep running that same seam off Wilmington-Poor Man's into Washington. If the gradient collapses back down, I'm sliding inshore to the Coimbra corridor and fishing bluefin in 20 fathoms with the squid lights after dark, because that pattern doesn't need the canyon to be perfect to produce. Either way, work the dark nights while you've got them — the new moon squid bite has been the most dependable thing on my boat all week.

reports.headline: Post-blow warm seam splits Wilmington and Poor Man's — yellowfin stacking the 100-fathom line
reports.subhead: A season-wide temperature break born out of last week's wind is holding tuna tight to the canyon walls, with bluefin filling in the midshore gap at 20 fathoms.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week's blow did us a favor, even if it didn't feel that way while we were stuck at the dock watching the anemometer. Two days of hard northeast wind churned the shelf water and let a Gulf Stream eddy tuck up against the break, and what it left behind is the sharpest shelf-slope edge I've seen all year — better than a ten-degree swing between the cold shelf water and the warm water sitting up against Wilmington and Poor Man's. That's not a subtle line. That's the kind of wall that stacks bait against the canyon face and holds it there instead of letting it wander. We haven't had structure like this since last September, and it showed up in the middle of summer instead, which tells you the eddy that spun off the Stream this year came in hot and early.

The moon's sliding toward new over the next several nights, which means less light in the sky and more comfort for squid pushing up out of deep water after dark. That matters more than people think out here — the overnight chunk and jig bite lives and dies on squid activity, and a darkening moon is exactly the kind of window that gets bigeye and bluefin working the surface glow off your underwater lights instead of staying pinned to the bottom. Combine that with the warm seam sitting right where it is, and Wednesday and Thursday shaped up as the best structural setup of the year so far. Anyone who made the run out reported the kind of temperature break you could see change color off the transom.

Yellowfin have been sitting right on that seam between Wilmington and Poor Man's, working the 100-fathom curve where the warm push meets the shelf edge. Boats trolling a mixed spread — naked ballyhoo skirted in green-and-yellow, small Ilanders behind, a couple of cedar plugs run long for the smaller fish — have been connecting steady through the morning bite, mostly 30 to 50 pound class with a few bigger mixed in. The Hudson's east wall has produced the same pattern a little further north, same warm-water signature pushing right up onto the wall. Don't waste time trolling the middle ground between the canyons right now — the fish are locked to the temperature break itself, not roaming the flat water in between. Find the color change, work it slow, and be ready to pitch a bait the second you see nervous water.

Midshore, the bluefin have set up around 20 fathoms in the Coimbra corridor, and that one's been a little more honest work than the canyon bite. The northeast upwelling this week sharpened up the 20 to 30 fathom breaks, which is pulling bait tight against that structure, and the school bluefin — mostly 40 to 60 pounds — have been sitting on it. This is squid-jig-and-light water at night: get anchored or drifting slow over the break after dark, drop the underwater lights, and give the squid time to show up on the sounder before you start jigging. When they come, the bluefin usually aren't far behind. It's not a guaranteed bite every night — I'd call it two good nights out of three this week — but when it goes, it goes fast and it's over just as quick, so have rods rigged and ready before the squid show, not after.

Wahoo have been mixed in on the high-speed troll along the drop-off edges, especially where the temperature break holds tightest — a couple of nice fish in the 40 to 60 pound range came off deep-diving lures run at 12 to 15 knots right on the color change itself, not out in the blue water beyond it. Mahi have been scattered rather than concentrated — a few fish off debris and scattered weed lines riding that same warm seam, nothing like a solid mahi bite yet, more of a bonus fish while you're trolling for tuna. If you want mahi specifically, work any floating junk you find sitting on the break, but don't plan a whole trip around it right now.

Bigeye have shown at night on the chunk, mostly in that same warm-water zone off Wilmington, working butterfish chunks fished on long fluorocarbon leaders down in the 100 to 200 foot range once the sun's off the water. It's a patience game — bigeye don't show up on command, and some nights you sit there feeding chunks into black water and nothing happens until 2 a.m. This week the odds have been better than average because that warm seam is holding bait deep, but it's still a grind fishery, not a sure thing.

White marlin haven't shown yet, but the setup is building toward it. The warm plume that's been pushing toward the bank all week is the trigger everyone watches for, and if it keeps advancing the way it has, I'd expect the first flags in the mid-Atlantic canyons within the next week to ten days — Wilmington and the Baltimore Canyon complex both look like early candidates given where this water's sitting now. I wouldn't build a trip solely around marlin yet, but I'd have the dink baits and a dredge rigged and ready, because when that plume locks onto the bank, it tends to happen fast.

If I had one shot this week, I'd run out Thursday morning before the wind has a chance to rebuild, work the Wilmington-Poor Man's seam early for yellowfin, then sit on the color change into the evening hoping for a wahoo or a mahi bonus, and finish with lights down over the Coimbra break after dark for bluefin. That's three shots at three different fisheries off one temperature break, which is about as efficient as this canyon system gets. Watch the wind forecast closely — if it swings back onshore hard, that break can slide or soften fast, and this window closes as quick as it opened.

reports.headline: Widest thermal edge of the season fires up yellowfin on the Hudson's 100-fathom line
reports.subhead: A mid-week blow sharpened the shelf-slope break to a 10-degree differential, and the tuna know it — here's where to find the seam and what's biting on it.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week's blow did what a good blow always does out here — it made a mess for two days and then handed us the best structural setup we've seen all season. Southwest wind pushed hard Sunday into Monday, kicked up a sloppy 4-6 foot sea on the shelf, and for a minute it looked like a lost week. But underneath that chop, the wind was doing real work — piling warm slope water up against the cooler shelf water and sharpening the edge between them instead of blending it out. By Tuesday the differential across that break hit roughly 10.3°F, shelf to slope, which is the widest thermal wall I've measured all year. That's not a subtle gradient — that's a line you could practically draw with a ruler on the chartplotter, and it's sitting right where it should: along the shelf-slope transition east of the Hudson's main channel, from around Wilmington-Poor Man's over toward the canyon's east wall.

That edge is why Wednesday and Thursday of this week are the window I'd circle if I could only pick two days. Seas are settling behind the blow, the seam is holding rather than sliding, and yellowfin have already found it. The moon is working in our favor too — we're waning down toward the new moon around the middle of the month, which means darker nights building through the week. That matters more than people think out here, because darker skies mean the squid-light bite at night gets better fish reaction, less moon glow washing out the underwater lights. Combine that with a sharpening 20 to 30 fathom break from the NE upwelling and you've got a legitimate two-species week — yellowfin in the canyon by day, bluefin on the inside grounds after dark.

We worked the Wilmington-Poor Man's seam Tuesday and had a mixed morning turn into a strong afternoon once we found where the color changed from that dirty green shelf water into the cleaner blue slope push. Yellowfin from 45 to about 70 pounds came on a standard spread — naked ballyhoo on the long riggers, a green machine and a small Ilander/ballyhoo combo down the shotgun, cedar plugs in close on the flat lines. Nothing fancy, but the fish were sitting right on that thermal wall and once we located it the bite stayed consistent for a solid three-hour stretch on the troll. The east wall of the Hudson itself, out past the Dip, produced smaller class fish mixed with a couple of bigeye-looking marks on the sounder that we couldn't get to eat — worth a jig drop if you've got the crew for it, but I wouldn't plan a trip around it yet.

The real story for the back half of the week might be the bluefin, not the yellowfin. The Coimbra corridor — that 20-fathom stretch on the inside edge of the canyon grounds — is holding a legitimate concentration of school-to-mid-size bluefin, and the NE upwelling sharpening that break is stacking bait right where the fish want it. With the moon darkening through the week, this is squid-light water at night: get anchored or drifting over the break after dark, lights down, and let the squid show up on their own schedule. We've seen 40 to 70-pound class bluefin working those bait balls consistently, and jigging into marks with a Shimano Butterfly-style jig or a smaller vertical iron has been more efficient than trying to troll them up in the dark. If you're not a night owl, working that same stretch at first light with a small spread of cedar plugs and green machines has still produced a fish or two before the sun gets high.

Mahi have been a bonus rather than a target this week — a few gaffers in the 8 to 15 pound range came off scattered weed patches on the troll near the seam, nothing concentrated enough to call a pattern yet. No real wahoo activity to report, and I'd be lying if I told you there was — the water's warm enough for them but we haven't seen the high-speed strikes that usually tip us off. White marlin is the one everybody's asking about, and the honest answer is: not yet. The warm plume that needs to push up onto the bank hasn't fully arrived — we're looking at a 7 to 10 day window before that trigger sets up properly at the mid-Atlantic canyons, the Hudson included. I wouldn't build a trip around marlin this week, but I'd have the pitch bait rigged just in case, because when that plume shows up it tends to show up fast.

If I had one day this week, I'd take Wednesday or Thursday, run straight for the Wilmington-Poor Man's seam first, and work the color change hard before shifting east toward the Dip if the bite softens. If the crew can handle a night trip, Friday into Saturday at Coimbra under lights is the play for bluefin, especially with the moon continuing to darken. Either way, this is a week to trust the thermal break over any single set of coordinates — that 10-degree wall is going to move a little day to day, and the fish are going to move with it. Find the edge, don't fish the spot.

reports.headline: Doormat fluke stack the inlets as summer springs build toward the new moon
reports.subhead: Barnegat Bay got too warm for its own good, the fluke bailed for the inlets, and the canyon window out of Cape May might be the best shot of the year.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the back bays cooked. Barnegat Bay pushed into the upper 70s — I heard 78 and change out toward the causeway — and that snot grass algae bloom that's been choking the flats did what it always does: it ran the fluke right out of the shallow structure and into anything with current and a hard bottom. That's not a bad thing if you know where to look. Manasquan Inlet, Barnegat Inlet, the channel edges up in Raritan Bay off Keansburg and Great Kills Light — that's where the doormats went, and that's where the guys putting fish in the box have been working all week. Meanwhile offshore, the upwelling that's been sharpening the shelf break has opened up a real temperature seam out around Wilmington and Poor Man's — 10 degrees of contrast on the edge, which is about as good as it gets for a canyon trip.

This week the moon's the story. We're building toward new moon on the 11th-13th, which means bigger springs — more water moving through the inlets on both the flood and the drain. That's good news for fluke guys because more current means more bait getting pushed off the flats and stacked in the deeper holes and channel bends where the doormats sit and wait. It's also good news for anybody chasing bait-driven blitzes on the beach, because bigger tides tend to flush peanut bunker and mullet out of the bays right past the jetties. Watch the evening high stand this weekend — with sunset lining up close to the top of the tide Friday into Sunday, that's your window if there's any bass left holding around Sandy Hook or the Highlands bridge structure. I wouldn't call it a sure thing this deep into July with the water this warm, but it's worth a rod in the sand for an hour.

Fluke has been the most honest bite in the zone. Boats drifting the Manasquan Inlet channel on the outgoing, working 20 to 35 feet with 3/4-ounce white bucktails tipped with Gulp Swimming Mullet, have been putting together limits with fish mixed in to 6 and 7 pounds. Same story at Barnegat Inlet — the deeper holes on the bay side of the Route 72 bridge have been holding better grade fish than the open bay has all month. If you can get live spot, that's still the ticket for the bigger models; guys soaking them on a fishfinder rig tight to the channel drop-offs have been separating the doormats from the dinks. Up in Raritan Bay, the fluke bite off Great Kills and along the Old Orchard Shoal channel has been a mixed bag — some days it's a slow pick, some days you get a stretch where three keepers come over the rail in twenty minutes. Pink Gulp Shrimp on a light jig head has been the better call than bucktails in the muddier bay water, especially on the last two hours of the outgoing when the current's still got some push but the water's clean.

Bluefish have been the one bright spot for anybody who likes a fight. Jumbo blues, some pushing double digits, have been working the surf line from Sea Bright down through Long Branch, chasing bunker schools that are still thick along the beach. Metal — Ava jigs, diamond jigs — cast into the wash at first light has been getting bit hard. If you see the bunker balling up and nervous, that's your cue. Don't sleep on chunking bunker off the Sandy Hook rocks either; the blues have been holding tight to structure there on the last of the incoming.

Weakfish, I'll be straight with you, have been a ghost. Water's plenty warm enough — that threshold everybody points to has been cleared for over two weeks now — but warm water alone isn't doing it. I've had exactly zero solid weakfish reports out of Raritan Bay or the back bay flats this week. If you want to burn a tide looking for them, work the deeper edges of the flats at last light on a swimming grub, but go in with your expectations in check.

Offshore is where the real headline is sitting. The temperature break out around Wilmington and Poor Man's Canyon is the widest seam we've seen all season, and yellowfin have been showing on that 100-fathom line. Boats running out of Cape May and Atlantic City hit that seam Wednesday and Thursday and connected. If you've got a canyon trip on the books this week, this is the window — that kind of structural setup doesn't sit still for long, and if the seam tightens back up by the weekend I'd expect the bite to slide with it. Closer in, there's been chatter of bluefin working the 20-fathom breaks off the Jersey coast on the overnight squid drift, worth a look on the darker nights before the moon fills back in.

Looking ahead: the new moon springs peaking the 11th through 13th should keep the fluke bite honest in the inlets — bigger current, more bait movement, better drifts. I'd fish the outgoing at Manasquan or Barnegat with bucktails and Gulp, and if I had a boat capable of the run, I'd be looking hard at that Wilmington/Poor Man's seam before it closes up. Bonito and Spanish mackerel have started showing up the coast at the eastern Long Island inlets — if that pattern keeps sliding south the way it usually does, Manasquan and Shark River could see the first fish any day now. Nothing's shown here yet, but I'd have a small metal rod rigged and ready just in case.

reports.headline: New moon springs load up Plum Gut as fluke push out of the bays
reports.subhead: Big tides building for the weekend flood, and the current lines from Horton Point to Orient are starting to show life again.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the Sound did what it usually does the week after a full moon — it settled down. Current went slack in the middle of the tide cycle, the wind sat out of the southwest most days and pushed a little chop against the north-facing beaches, and the water along my stretch held steady, not cold, not blazing, just working its way toward summer temperature the way it does every July. Nothing dramatic happened, and that's fine by me. Slack water after a full moon usually means the fish stop chasing bait around and start digesting it, which is exactly what I saw — a lot of marks on the fish finder sitting tight to bottom structure at Rocky Point and not doing much about anything you threw at them.

That's about to change. We're sliding into a new moon this weekend, and new moon means spring tides — the biggest swings of the month. More water moving through Plum Gut, more current stacking up against Orient Point, more push through the Race. That current is the engine for everything out here. When it starts ripping again, bait gets displaced off the flats and funneled into the rips, and the bass and blues that have been holding deep and lazy start working the seams. The window everybody ought to have circled is Friday through Monday, the tenth through the thirteenth — the peak of the spring tide lines up with the evening flood, which puts a strong push of water moving into the Gut right around sunset. That's the first real PM window we've had since the June full moon, and it's the kind of setup that gets stripers moving up into the current lanes to feed instead of just holding under it.

On the fluke side, the story this month has been bay water running warm — warm enough that fluke have been sliding out of the back bays and into anything with moving, cooler water: inlets, channels, current-scoured bottom. Mattituck Inlet has been the beneficiary. Guys working the outgoing tide right off the jetty rocks with three-quarter-ounce bucktails and white Gulp Swimming Mullets have been finding keeper fluke stacked in that deeper cut where the inlet dumps into the Sound — nothing gaudy, but a few fish in the 20 to 22-inch range mixed with a lot of shorts that need to get thrown back. Slow-drag it right along bottom on the drop, and don't be afraid to tip the bucktail with a strip of squid when the current's really moving; the scent seems to matter more when the water's a little stirred up.

Bluefish have been scattered but present — small to mid-size blues showing up in blitzes off Horton Point and Rocky Point early and late in the day, chasing bunker pods that have been thick along that stretch. Nothing sustained, more like fifteen-minute windows where the water turns to white foam and then goes quiet again. If you see the gulls diving, get on it fast — diamond jigs, an ounce and a half, silver or chartreuse, worked fast through the melee, or a topwater popper if you want the visual. Don't waste time on a spot once the birds lift off; they don't come back for round two out here most days.

Stripers have been the tougher nut. A few fish have come off the boulder fields near Rocky Point on live eels fished on the bottom during the last two hours of the outgoing, and there's been better action right at the mouth of Plum Gut itself for guys willing to work bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig in the deeper water where the current really funnels. But it's been a fish here, a fish there — not a pattern you can set your watch by. I expect that to sharpen up with the new moon current. When that Gut starts ripping the way it does on a big tide, bass stack up in the eddies behind the rocks and feed hard for a short window right at the peak of the flood and again on the first hour of the drop. That's when I'll be out there, working bucktails tipped with pork rind along the seams, letting the jig fall into the slack pockets behind structure rather than fighting the main current.

Porgies have been steady and reliable if unspectacular — small to medium scup off the Orient breakwalls and around the rock piles near the Point, taking sandworms and pieces of green crab fished on a simple high-low rig in fifteen to twenty-five feet. Good action for anybody who wants a guaranteed bend in the rod without a lot of running around. Blackfish are out of season on this stretch through the summer, so leave the crabs for the porgies and save the tog game plan for when the water cools and the fall opener rolls around — I'll be scouting rock piles for that starting in September like I do every year.

Weakfish, I'll be honest, have been a non-event. The water's warm enough on paper, but warm water alone doesn't make weakfish show up, and I haven't heard of a single one taken along this whole stretch this year. I wouldn't plan a trip around them right now.

For the week ahead: if the wind stays reasonable and doesn't blow hard out of the north, I'd fish the Friday and Saturday evening flood at Plum Gut and right off Orient Point, working the current seams as the spring tide builds toward its peak. That's where I'd put my money. Backup plan is the Mattituck Inlet fluke drift on the outgoing if the bass don't cooperate — that fishery's been the most consistent thing going, and consistent beats exciting most weeks out here.

reports.headline: Fifty-Pound Bass Still Prowling the Boulders as New Moon Tides Build
reports.subhead: The Point keeps giving up big fish on bucktails and eels while the fleet watches for the first bonito push and a bluefin run that's suddenly close enough to matter.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the Point ran on that classic July rhythm — clean water, steady southwest air in the afternoons, and a tide that built through the week as we worked toward this new moon. The rips off the Lighthouse were setting up hard on both the ebb and the flood, and that current is exactly what turns boulder fields into feeding stations. Water out there has been holding in that comfortable low-to-mid 60s range at the surface, with a noticeable temperature break where the reef structure meets deeper water off North Bar — that's the kind of edge that stacks sand eels and silversides against rock, and where sand eels stack, bass follow.

This week the moon goes new on the 10th, and that means building spring tides right through the weekend — bigger swings, stronger current in the rips, and more water moving through Turtle Cove and around the Elbow than we've seen in a couple weeks. Peak tidal push lines up Friday through Monday. For us that's not just a number on a tide chart — a bigger spring tide at the Point means the current lane through the boulder field runs faster and longer, which pins bait against structure instead of letting it drift free. That's when you want to be positioned in the eddies behind the big rocks, not out in the main current, because the bass sit in the slack pockets and let the tide bring dinner to them. I'd rather fish the first two hours of a building tide right now than fight slack water with nothing moving.

The bass fishing itself has been the real story. We've had fish up to 50 pounds coming off the Point on bucktails, topwater, and fly gear — those numbers aren't hype, that's what's actually been landed working the boulder field on the outgoing tide, first and last light. White or bone-colored 2-ounce bucktails bounced slow along bottom in 15 to 25 feet off the Lighthouse rocks have been the most consistent producer, but the topwater bite at dawn — big pencil poppers and Danny-style swimmers worked over the white water — has been giving up some of the better fish, the ones that push 40 and up. If you're throwing fly, sinking lines and big Deceivers or Hollow flies in the 6- to 8-inch range, worked through the wash where the boulders break the surface, will get you tight to fish that other guys are walking past. Night tide has still been an eel game — live eels drifted through the rip off North Bar on the last two hours of the incoming have put quality fish in the boat, nothing huge but steady 20s to low 30s.

Bluefish have been mixed in with the bass, mostly in the 4- to 8-pound range, chopping bait on the surface off Shagwong Reef and out toward the Elbow in the mornings. If you want blues specifically, small metal — half-ounce to ounce Deadly Dicks or Kastmasters — worked fast through visible surface activity will connect quick, but don't expect a sustained blitz like September. This is scattered, opportunistic stuff right now, not the fall gorge.

Fluke have been shifting the way they always do this time of year — out of the warmer bay water and into the harbor mouth and the ocean side drifts. Fort Pond Bay has gotten too warm and stale to hold quality fish consistently, so the better fluke action has moved to the deeper water off the harbor entrance and out toward the rips, working the outgoing tide when clean ocean water is pushing through. Four- and 5-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, drifted slow in 25 to 40 feet, have taken fish to 6 pounds, with the occasional better fish mixed in. If the bay bite's been dead for you, stop fighting it — the fish already left, and the inlet and ocean-side drifts are where they went.

Porgies and blackfish have both been steady bottom producers if you need to fill a cooler — porgies on clam and squid strips over the reef structure around Shagwong and off the south side rocks, blackfish still legal-adjacent and biting green crab in the deeper boulder pockets, though that fishery really turns on later in the fall. Right now it's a bycatch fishery more than a target trip, but worth knowing if the bass go quiet on a tide change.

The thing everybody's talking about at the dock is what's happening just south of us. Small boats have been running out and connecting with schoolie bluefin — not a fishery you plan a trip around yet, but it tells you something about what's pushing up the edge of the shelf and how warm that offshore water has gotten. I wouldn't chase it in anything without range and a weather eye, but it's a sign the season's building toward something bigger out there. Closer to home, keep half an eye out for the first bonito showing at the Point. The cold wall that's normally been penning bonito up around Block Island collapsed hard this week, and that corridor's opening wide — Newport to Point Judith, and Montauk sits right on the doorstep of that push. If clean water and bait line up right on an incoming tide off the Lighthouse or North Bar, don't be shocked if the first small albies or bonito of the season show up chasing sand eels through the white water. I wouldn't build a whole trip around it yet, but I'd have a bag of epoxy jigs and small metal in the truck just in case.

For the weekend, with the new moon building those bigger tides, I'd fish the boulder field on the last two hours of the outgoing Saturday morning, then switch to the fluke drift off the harbor mouth once the sun gets high and the bass bite goes quiet. If the wind stays out of the southwest and light, that's a good combination — moving water for the bass, clean push for the fluke. If it kicks up hard from the south, I'd rather work the more protected water around Turtle Cove and take what the bluefish give me instead of grinding it out in a chop.

reports.headline: Bay water pushing 79°F shoves the fluke into Shinnecock Inlet as spring tides build
reports.subhead: New moon currents are loading up this weekend — the outgoing at the inlet is where the smart money's fishing right now.
reports.body_markdown:
I've been out here past midnight three of the last five nights and I can tell you what the thermometer's been telling everybody all week — the bay's cooked. Shinnecock Bay is sitting up near 78-79 degrees in the shallows, and that's too warm for a fluke to sit still in. They know it before we do. Every fluke that was spread out over the flats off Tiana and the flats behind Hampton Bays two weeks ago has pulled off into the channels, and a good chunk of them have already run for the inlet itself, where the ocean's pumping in water in the low 70s on the incoming. That's a real thermal wall — bay water baking, ocean water upwelled and cool — and it's stacking bait and fluke right where the two meet. That's the story of the week, and it's not subtle if you're paying attention to where the boats are anchoring up.

Tide-wise, we're building into a new moon — peak spring alignment lands right around July 11-13 — and that means bigger swings, faster water, and a harder pull through the inlet on the outgoing than we've seen since the June full moon. For me that's the whole ballgame. Bigger tides mean the current lane through the inlet gets stronger and longer, which pins bait against the jetty rocks and gives the bass and blues a reason to stack up instead of scattering. If you fish here regularly you know the pattern — neap tides make the bite lazy and spread out, springs make it violent and concentrated. This week's leaning toward violent. Wind's been mild out of the south-southwest most nights, which has kept the inlet clean, and that's a gift — dirty water on a spring tide is a mess to fish, clean water on a spring tide is when you load the cooler.

Striped bass have been the most consistent thing I can put my name behind this week, and it's strictly a night game right now. I've been running the outgoing starting about an hour before peak ebb, working bucktails tipped with pork rind and swimming plugs — SP Minnows and Danny-style swimmers — tight against the north jetty rocks where the current curls into an eddy. Fish have been mostly schoolies to mid-20s, but there've been a few nights with a couple of fish pushing 30-plus inches mixed in, especially in that dead-black hour after the tide really starts ripping. Live eels drifted on a fish-finder rig through the main channel have out-produced the plugs on the slower nights — if the current's not moving much yet, an eel swims itself into a strike zone better than anything I can cast.

Fluke is where the volume's been, and the inlet mouth and the deeper edges of the channel running out past the Coast Guard station are the spots right now. Boats drifting the outgoing with 3/4-ounce chartreuse bucktails tipped with white Gulp Swimming Mullet, working 15 to 25 feet of water, have been putting decent numbers in the box — nothing epic, but steady keeper-class fish in the 18-20 inch range with the occasional 4-pounder mixed in. The bay drift off Tiana still has fish on it if you want to stay shallow, but it's thinned out noticeably from three weeks ago, and I'd rather burn the gas to fish the inlet where the water's actually comfortable for them.

Weakfish at Ponquogue Bridge have been a mixed bag, and I want to be straight with you about that instead of blowing smoke. The bite's real but it's thin — a handful of solid fish, including at least one better than 7 pounds weighed in locally this month, but for every good report I hear about three quiet nights. I've had luck working the up-current side of the pilings on the last two hours of the outgoing with bucktails tipped with squid strips, fished slow and bounced off bottom, but you need to put in the time. This isn't the kind of bridge bite where you show up and it happens for you in twenty minutes. Treat it as a bonus fish while you're really there for bass or fluke.

Bluefish have shown up in flurries at the inlet on the last of the incoming, chopping up spearing and rainfish pushed against the rocks — poppers and small metal have worked when they're up, but it's been on-again-off-again, not a sustained blitz. Porgies and blackfish are around the usual structure — the rocks off the inlet and the reefs out toward Shinnecock proper — standard clam baits on a high-low rig, and that bite's been reliable if unremarkable, good for a mixed bag when the marquee species aren't cooperating.

One more thing worth watching — with the pelagic window still open through this weekend, there's been chatter about early bonito and Spanish mackerel showing on the ocean side, working the clean incoming water off the inlet and toward Moriches. I haven't connected myself yet, but the conditions line up — warm plume pushing in, clean water, bait present. If I had a morning free this week I'd have a small tin rigged and ready just in case they show inside casting range of the jetty.

Looking ahead: if the wind stays out of the south and doesn't kick up chop through the inlet, I like the outgoing tide Friday and Saturday night as the window to be there — the new moon spring should have that current ripping harder than it has all month, and that's when the bigger bass show themselves. Plan B if the bass don't cooperate is sliding into the fluke drift right at the inlet mouth on the same tide — you're already there, and the fish have already told us that's where they want to be.

reports.headline: New-moon springs flush the bay — fluke and bass stack at the Moriches Inlet cut
reports.subhead: Great South Bay water pushing into the high 70s has shoved the fluke out to the channels, and this weekend's new-moon tides are about to turn the inlet into a conveyor belt.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the bay did what bays do in the first week of July — it cooked. Great South Bay pushed into the high 70s, touching 78.8 in the shallow flats off Tuthill Point and East Moriches, and that kind of water doesn't hold fluke. It holds sea robins and bathtub-warm slop. What it did do was push every keeper fluke in the system toward cooler water, and in this system that means one of two places: the main channel through the bay or the inlet itself, where the ocean is still feeding in cleaner, cooler water on every tide. That migration is the single biggest story on my beat right now, and it's not subtle — guys who were picking at fluke on the flats two weeks ago are getting skunked there now and finding them stacked in the cut.

This week the moon does the rest of the work for us. We're building into new-moon springs, peak alignment landing right around July 11-13, which means bigger tidal range and more water moving through a system that's already narrow and touchy after last fall's shoaling. Moriches Inlet doesn't have the luxury of a wide throat like Shinnecock — every extra foot of tidal push gets squeezed through that cut and accelerates. That's good news if you're fishing structure. The outgoing on those spring tides is going to run harder and longer than it has in weeks, which flushes bait — spearing, small bunker, grass shrimp — out of the bay and stacks it against the sandbar off Cupsogue and the rock jetty on the Smith Point side. Predators know this. Stripers and blues will set up in the eddies behind the bar and let the current do their work for them.

The striper bite through the inlet itself has been steady, not spectacular — I'd call it a solid mid-tier week. Best window has consistently been the last two hours of the outgoing, fished tight to the west side of the cut where the deeper scour channel runs against the Cupsogue side. Bucktails in the 1- to 1.5-ounce range, white or chartreuse, worked slow along bottom in that 12- to 15-foot trench, have been drawing fish in the 24- to 32-inch range with the occasional better fish mixed in on bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig right where the current breaks off the tip of the bar. Live eels after dark have also produced, particularly on the last of the outgoing into the start of the slack, fished off the rocks at the east jetty. Nothing has been a blitz. You're working for these fish, and on a lot of tides you're getting two or three fish in a session, not a dozen. That's honest — the bay isn't stuffed with bass right now, but the ones passing through the inlet on that flush are eating.

Fluke is where the real story is. With the bay fish pushed toward structure, the drift through the inlet channel itself — from the Coast Guard station down through the cut and out to the sea buoy — has been the most consistent producer on my beat. Four- and 5-inch white Gulp swimming mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the outgoing in 15 to 25 feet, have taken fish to 6 pounds, with a good number of keepers mixed into a lot of short fish. The bite window tightens up around the last two hours of the outgoing and first hour of slack — once the tide turns and starts flooding back in, the fluke seem to lose interest and scatter. Ocean-side drifts off Cupsogue in that upwelled 71-degree water have also been worth the run, particularly for guys willing to work the deeper humps a quarter-mile off the beach.

Porgies have shown consistently at Pattersquash and in the deeper holes off Tuthill Point, standard high-low rigs with clam, nothing to write home about but a reliable box-filler if the bigger stuff isn't cooperating. Weakfish, I'll be straight with you — I haven't had a real report worth passing along. Water's been warm enough on paper for weeks now and the fish just haven't shown in numbers here, which tracks with what's happening system-wide. I wouldn't plan a trip around them right now.

The development I'm watching closest is the pelagic push. The bonito and Spanish mackerel window that opened around the Fourth is in its final days, and the early signs are pointing at Moriches and Shinnecock on the ocean side picking up fish on clean incoming water. If you've got a boat that can work outside the bar, small metal jigs and Deadly Dicks worked fast around bait pods off Cupsogue on the incoming are worth a look through the weekend before that window likely closes.

Looking ahead: if the new-moon springs build the way the tide charts suggest, I'd be at the inlet cut Friday through Monday working the last two hours of the outgoing, bucktails for the fluke, chunks and eels for the bass in the deeper scour. If the current gets too strong to fish clean — and on a big spring tide through this pinched inlet, that's a real possibility — I'd shift inside to the flats around Tuthill Point on the front half of the incoming, where the bait gets pushed back in and the bass and fluke follow it. Either way, the water's moving with purpose this week. That's usually when this inlet gets interesting.

reports.headline: Bay water tips 79°, and the fluke are bailing straight for the inlet
reports.subhead: Great South Bay got too warm for its own good this week, so the doormats moved to the bridges and Democrat Point — and that's exactly where you should be too.
reports.body_markdown:
I checked the bay temp Sunday morning and about spit out my coffee — 78.8 degrees off Sayville flats. That's bathwater. Great South Bay runs shallow and it heats up fast once we get a string of calm, sunny days like we had last week, and that's precisely what happened: light winds, high pressure sitting on us, tide swings modest under the waning moon. Comfortable boating weather, uncomfortable fish weather. Warm, sluggish, low-oxygen water in the back bay pushes fluke and bait right out the door, and that's the story of my week — everything funneling toward the inlet and the ocean side where there's still some cold water coming up off the shelf.

This week the moon's sliding toward new, and that's the piece everybody needs to pay attention to. New moon lands right around the 11th to 13th, which means we're building into spring tides — bigger swings, more water moving, stronger current through Fire Island Inlet on both the push and the drain. For a bay-runner like me that's good news two ways: bigger outgoing tides flush more bait and cooler water out through Democrat Point, and bigger incoming tides push fresh, cleaner ocean water back up into the bay channels. If you've been getting nowhere in the skinny water off Nicoll Bay or West Sayville, stop fighting it — go where the tide is doing the work for you.

Fluke first, because that's the honest headline this week. The bay bite has gone soft — I had two trips off the Meadow Island flats that produced short fish and not much else, water too warm, fish too lazy. But shift to the Robert Moses bridges — the Fire Island side, in that 25 to 35 foot slot between the second and fourth pilings — and it's a different world. Upwelled ocean water sitting around 71 degrees is stacking up against the warmer bay water right at the inlet mouth, and the fluke are parking right on that seam. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the outgoing, have been putting keepers in the box, with a few pushing 5 and 6 pounds mixed into the shorts. Don't be shy about tipping the bucktail with a strip of squid — on the slower current stages that extra scent has made the difference between a bite and a look. Democrat Point itself, out past the Coast Guard station where the inlet dumps into the ocean, has also been holding fish on the last two hours of the outgoing — bounce a chartreuse bucktail bounced tight to the sandbar drop, 15 to 20 feet, right where the rip forms.

Stripers have been a mixed bag, which is about right for early July. Dawn patrol on the Fire Island beach — I walked from the Lighthouse Tract east toward Kismet twice this week — turned a handful of schoolies on bucktails and small metal, nothing to write home about, mostly 22 to 26 inches. The better fish are still showing after dark or right at first light, and they're following bunker. There's a decent pod of peanut bunker holding in the bay off Oak Beach and pushing through the inlet on the tide, and where you find bunker balled up tight, especially near the Robert Moses Causeway bridge pilings on the last hour of the incoming, you'll find bass and bluefish working underneath. Snag-and-drop a bunker on a fishfinder rig, or just chuck a big Savage Gear Sandeel through the school and let it sink — I had a solid 31-inch bass do exactly that off the Captree side of the bridge on Tuesday's morning tide.

Bluefish have been the more reliable of the two — choppers in the 3 to 6 pound range are chewing through the inlet on both tides, and they don't seem to care much about the temperature the way the bass and fluke do. Poppers off the surf at Democrat Point at first light have been fun, and if you're bottom fishing for fluke at the bridges, keep a wire leader rigged and ready because the blues will find your bait eventually.

Weakfish — I'll be straight with you, still nothing. The bay's been warm enough for long enough that if they were coming, they'd be here. I'm not chasing that story anymore this summer; warm water alone isn't the trigger everyone hoped it would be. Porgies are around the usual structure — Robert Moses Causeway rocks and the Fire Island Inlet jetty rip — small stuff on sandworms and squid strips, decent action if you just want bent rods with the kids, nothing tournament-worthy. Blackfish season's closed and they're not what you're after in July water anyway.

There's chatter building to our east about the first bonito and Spanish mackerel showing on the ocean side around Moriches and Shinnecock, riding that same clean incoming water everyone's talking about. It hasn't shown at Fire Island Inlet yet, but the water temperature signature moving through matches what we've got, and inlets like ours have a way of getting these fish eventually if the bait stays put. Worth keeping a light spinning rod rigged with a small Deadly Dick in the truck just in case, but I wouldn't plan a whole trip around it yet.

Looking ahead: with the new moon building through the weekend and into next week, I'm expecting the outgoing tide at Fire Island Inlet to run harder and colder, which should keep pulling bay fluke toward the bridges and Democrat Point. If I've got one day to fish, I'm running the Robert Moses bridge on the two hours around peak outgoing, then finishing at Democrat Point for the last of the light with bass and blues on my mind. Bigger tides mean a tighter window to hit it right, but they also mean the fish will know exactly where to be.

reports.headline: New moon springs push GSB fluke into Jones Inlet as bay water tips 78 degrees
reports.subhead: The bay's too warm for summer flounder to sit still — they're stacking in the channels and inlet mouth on the upwelled water, and the building tides this week should only help.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the bay did what it does every July — it cooked. Great South Bay pushed up to 78.8 degrees in the shallows, and that's too warm for a fluke that wants oxygen and moving water, not a bathtub. What that did was shove fish out of the flats and into the channels and the inlet itself, where the tide keeps things turning over. The ocean side of Jones Inlet has been running cooler — upwelled water sitting around 71 degrees at the mouth — and that temperature break right where bay meets ocean is exactly the kind of edge fluke set up on. I've been watching this pattern build for two weeks now and it's not subtle. If you were still grinding sod flats in South Oyster Bay last week wondering where the fish went, this is why.

This week the moon's the story. We're running into new moon on the 11th-13th, which means spring tides — bigger swings, stronger current through the inlet in both directions. That's good news for anybody drifting Jones Inlet or Sloop Channel because the extra push moves more bait and pulls fluke up out of the mud to feed. It also means the ebb out of Jones Inlet is going to be flushing serious volume late in the week, which is the tide I want to be fishing. Wind's been manageable, nothing that's blown the water to milk, and I don't see a front lined up to change that through the weekend. Water temp trend is stable to slightly warming in the bay, stable to cooling at the inlet mouth on the incoming — that seam is where I'm putting my time.

Fluke fishing has actually been solid, not spectacular, but solid — which this time of year I'll take. Best marks have been the deeper bend of Jones Inlet on the channel side toward Short Beach, 18 to 24 feet, drifting the last two hours of the outgoing into dead low. Three-quarter ounce white bucktails with a 5-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullet trailer have been the money combo, dragged slow along bottom with just enough hop to keep the tail kicking. Guys working Sloop Channel with the same setup are getting a mixed bag — keeper fluke to 4 pounds mixed with a lot of teen-inch fish you're throwing back. It's not a five-fish-limit-by-nine-AM bite, but if you put in a couple hours on the right stage of tide you're bringing something home. The West End 2 grounds and the deeper hole off the Jones Beach Coast Guard station have both produced better-grade fish on the outgoing — that's where the current concentrates bait against structure.

Stripers have been a night game right now, which is normal for mid-July once the sun's been baking the surf all day. Resident bass are holding tight to the jetty rocks at Short Beach and the inlet breakwater, and the better fish are coming after dark on the incoming tide, eels drifted right up against the rocks on a fish-finder rig with just enough weight to hold bottom without snagging. Nothing huge — mostly 20 to 28 inches, with the occasional mid-20-pound fish mixed in for guys who stick it out past midnight. This isn't fall-blitz bass fishing yet. That's two months out. But it's a real bite if you're willing to lose sleep for it, and the new moon current this weekend should sharpen it up — more water movement means more bait pushed past those rocks.

Bluefish have shown up as the usual July nuisance and I mean that as a compliment — snapper-sized blues and some harbor cocktail blues in the 2 to 4 pound class are chopping bait up and down the bay side, especially around the Wantagh Bridge pilings and the Freeport channel markers on the last of the incoming. Small metal — half-ounce Deadly Dicks or Kastmasters — thrown into the surface activity will get bit fast. Good action for kids or anybody who wants bent rods without overthinking the presentation.

Weakfish I want to be straight with you about, because there's been a lot of talk about a comeback and I'm not going to oversell it. Water's been above 70 degrees in the bay for over two weeks now, which is supposed to be the trigger, and I'm just not seeing the reports to back it up yet. A few marks on the sonar drifting Cedar Creek at dusk, one report of a decent fish caught on a bucktail meant for fluke — that's about it. The temperature is right, but temperature alone clearly isn't enough. I'm still checking the marina lights at night on light tackle because that's historically where they show first, but I wouldn't plan a trip around weakfish this week. Treat it as a bonus, not a target.

Porgies are keeping rods bent on the structure spots while everybody waits on bigger things — the reef markers off Jones Beach and the rock piles inside the inlet are stacked, and a simple high-low rig with clam will keep you busy between fluke drifts.

Looking ahead: I want the outgoing tide Thursday through Saturday at Jones Inlet, right as the new moon springs build the current to its strongest push of the month. If that current stays clean and doesn't get blown apart by wind, I expect the fluke bite to tighten up and the bass to feed a little more aggressively at the jetty after dark. Plan B if the fluke get finicky on the strong current — slide into Sloop Channel where the flow's a touch softer and the bucktail stays in the strike zone longer.

reports.headline: Bay's too warm for fluke, so they ran for the inlet — and found company
reports.subhead: New-moon springs are stacking up behind Breezy Point, and the outgoing at the Marine Parkway Bridge is starting to look like the best address in the borough.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the bay basically cooked itself. We had that stretch of light, southwest air sitting on top of the flats and the surface water in the back bay pushed close to 79 degrees — I heard 78.8 off one of the buoys and I believe it, because the fluke told me the same thing without saying a word. Fluke don't like bathwater. When the shallow flats get that warm, they slide for anything with current and depth — the channels, the bridge rips, and eventually right out through Rockaway Inlet into the ocean, where an upwelling event over the last week and a half dropped that nearshore water down into the low 70s. That's not a coincidence, that's a thermometer doing the talking. The fish left a hot bathtub for a cooler pool with moving water, same as any of us would on a July afternoon.

Now we're heading into new moon, and that's the piece everybody needs to pay attention to this week. The moon goes dark around the 10th to 13th, which means spring tides — bigger swings, harder push on both the flood and the drain. In practical terms for us, that means the outgoing at the Marine Parkway Bridge and through Rockaway Inlet is going to run harder and longer than it has in weeks, and that current is going to drag bait — spearing, small bunker, grass shrimp — right out of the marsh creeks and past every rip and piling between Floyd Bennett Field and Breezy Point. Big springs also mean the dark-of-the-moon bite at night gets better for bass, because less ambient light means they'll sit tighter under the bridge lights and the structure and wait for the current to bring dinner to them instead of chasing it around in open water.

Fluke first, since that's the story of the last two weeks. If you're still poking around the deeper holes inside the bay — off Ruffle Bar, the flats by Motts Basin, the usual July spots — you're going to find some but it's been a grind, a keeper here, a bunch of shorts there. The better, more consistent fish have been coming from the inlet itself and just outside it, drifting the channel edge on the Breezy Point side and working the deeper cuts where the outgoing dumps into the ocean. Three-quarter and one-ounce bucktails tipped with 4-inch white or pink Gulp Swimming Mullets, dragged slow along bottom in 20 to 35 feet, timed to the last two hours of the outgoing — that's been the play. A few guys working the same water with live killies on a fluke rig have done fine too, especially in that softer water right where the inlet current starts to fan out past the bridge.

Stripers have been a mixed bag, which is honest, not a knock. Schoolie-sized bass are all over the bay right now — Canarsie Pier, the flats off Ruffle Bar, the mouth of Motts Basin — and they'll eat small soft plastics and bucktails all day if you find the bait pods, but very few of those fish are going over 24, 25 inches. The better-class fish, the ones worth the trip, are staging where they always do this time of year: right at the Marine Parkway Bridge on the outgoing, sitting in the current seams off the pilings from dusk into the first couple hours of dark. Bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig fished tight to structure has been the most consistent producer, with eels working better once it's fully dark. With the new moon building through the weekend, I'd expect that bridge bite to sharpen up — bigger tide, more current, more bait getting pushed through, less moonlight for the bass to worry about getting picked off from above.

Bluefish are starting to show some teeth in the back bay, which tracks with what I've heard from farther south — the chopper blues moving inshore as the water settles into summer pattern. We've had reports of blues busting on peanut bunker and spearing around Cross Bay Bridge and off Canarsie Pier, mostly in the last hour of daylight. Metal — Deadly Dicks, half-ounce Kastmasters — cast into the surface activity has been the ticket, and if you're fishing from the rocks at Breezy Point on an outgoing tide with bait moving, keep a popper rigged and ready, because those blitzes can materialize and vanish in twenty minutes.

Porgies are steady if unspectacular — Ruffle Bar and the reef structure around the Silver Hole channel have been giving up decent numbers on clam and sandworm, high-low rigs on the bottom, best on the last of the incoming into the top of the tide. Nothing to write home about size-wise, but a fun bucket of fish if you want dinner and don't need a story.

Weakfish — I'll be straight with you, I haven't heard a real report out of the bay yet this season. Water's been warm enough for a while now, but warm water alone doesn't seem to be pulling them in like it used to. If you're specifically hunting weakfish, I wouldn't plan a trip around it right now.

Looking ahead: with the new moon springs peaking around the 11th through the 13th, I'd be at the inlet or the bridge on the back half of the outgoing, betting the bigger current pulls more bait and more bass with it. If that doesn't produce, my backup is the same drift for fluke right off Breezy Point where the cooler ocean water is holding — that pattern's been more reliable than the deep bay lately, and I don't see a reason for it to flip back until this heat breaks.

reports.headline: New moon springs load the Race and Plum Gut as fluke push to the rips
reports.subhead: Bigger tides, tighter current lines, and the first bonito chatter off Fishers Island — here's where the bite's stacking this week.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the Sound got worked over by a stretch of NE wind that upwelled the ocean side of the Race and Plum Gut — cooler, cleaner water shoved in against the warmer stuff sitting in the bays. That's a big deal out here because it sharpened the temperature break right where the current lines set up. I felt it in the water column off Valiant Rock: cold on the bottom, warmer skin water on top, and bait pinned right at that seam. Meanwhile the bay side kept cooking — Great South Bay style temps pushing toward 79 on the flats — which is exactly why fluke have been bailing out of the back bays and running for the inlets and the Sound-side channels where that upwelled 71-degree water is stacking up. That shift isn't subtle. If you were still working shallow bay structure last week, you were probably fishing empty water.

This week the moon's the story. We're building into new moon springs, peaking July 11-13, which means the biggest tides of the month are about to rip through the Race, Plum Gut, and the Fishers Island rips. More current means more bait getting flushed off the structure and stacked in the eddies — that's where I'm putting my time, not out in the main current lane. The other piece: a PM flood-sunset window is realigning with the high stand as these springs build, the first one since the June full moon. That's prime striper time — low light, big water movement, bait pushed hard against structure. Expect the bite windows to compress around that sunset-to-dark flood rather than spreading out over a slow tide like we've had the past couple weeks.

Bass fishing has been real but you have to work for it. I've been running the backside eddy at Plum Gut on the last two hours of the ebb, into the turn, throwing big Danny-style swimmers and Guppy plugs in bone and black — fish from 28 to low-40s inches coming off the bottom of the eddy where the current dumps out and slows. Depth's 30 to 55 feet there depending where you sit relative to the rip line. At the Race, I've had better luck drifting the downcurrent side of Valiant Rock at first light, live eels on a fish-finder rig, letting the current do the work instead of retrieving — that's a 40 to 70 foot bite with fish holding tight to the pinnacle structure where the eddy folds back on itself. North Dumpling's south side has been giving up a few too on bucktail-and-eel-strip combos worked slow on the last of the outgoing.

Blues have been the more consistent player right now — schools chopping bunker on top off Orient Point and along the Fishers Island north rip, especially on the morning outgoing when bait gets pushed out of the harbors. Bunker chunks on wire leader, or just blind-casting big poppers into the surface commotion, and you're in fish inside ten minutes. Nothing huge — mostly 3 to 6 pounds — but steady, and they'll save a slow bass morning.

Fluke are where the real story is this week, because of that bay-to-inlet shift. The Orient Point rip and the channel edges through Plum Gut have turned on for keeper-class fish — 18 to 22 inches, some pushing bigger — on white Gulp Swimming Mullets rigged on 3/4 to 1-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom on the last two hours of the outgoing when that cooler water is funneling through. I'm marking bait stacked at 35 to 45 feet right where the channel drops off, and that's exactly where the fluke are sitting, ambushing whatever gets swept off the shelf. If you're still poking around in the shallow bay grass, you're behind the fish at this point — go find the moving water.

Porgies have been a nice consistent backup on the days the bass and blues go quiet — sandworms and clam on high-low rigs over the rock piles off Fishers Island and around Bartlett Reef, 20 to 35 feet, and they've been thick enough to fill a bucket in an hour if you're anchored right on the structure.

Weakfish, though — I'm not going to pretend they're here. Water's been warm enough for weeks and I haven't heard of a single one caught in this zone. That threshold everyone points to clearly isn't enough on its own; something else needs to line up, and right now it hasn't. I wouldn't burn a tide targeting them.

The one thing I'm watching closely: bonito and false albies. The cold wall that usually pins them down around Block Island has broken down, and that corridor's spreading west toward Point Judith and Fishers Island Sound. It's early — this is a short window, typically gone by mid-July if it doesn't hold — but if you see diving birds and nervous water off the Fishers Island rip or the east end of the Race, have an epoxy jig or a small Deadly Dick ready. That's not a guarantee of a blitz, but the setup's better than it's been in a couple seasons.

Look-ahead: Friday through Monday is where I'd put my best effort. The new moon springs peak, the PM flood lines up with sunset, and that's the kind of current-and-light combo that gets big bass moving out of the eddies to feed. I'd start at Plum Gut on the evening flood with a black Danny plug, and if that's quiet, slide over to the Race at first light on the eel drift. Fluke guys — work the inlet edges on the outgoing, not the bay flats. And keep one rod rigged light for albies if you're running past Fishers Island — this window won't last.

reports.headline: New moon springs build toward a sunset striper window as fluke slide off the flats
reports.subhead: Central Sound bass are staging for the July 11-13 high-tide dusk bite while porgies and blues fill the daylight hours.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the Sound settled into that mid-summer holding pattern where nothing dramatic happens but everything quietly repositions. Water in the harbors — Oyster Bay, Port Jeff, the back of the Norwalk Islands — has been running warm enough that you can feel it through the hull, mid-70s in the shallow coves, while the main body of the Sound out past Stratford Shoal stays noticeably cooler underneath. That split is the whole story right now. Wind's been the typical July pattern, calm mornings, building southwest in the afternoon, nothing that's torn up the water but enough to keep bait pushed into the lees of the islands and the harbor mouths. Tides have been unremarkable the past several days — we're coming off a quarter moon, current's been moderate, nothing forcing fish to move with urgency.

That changes this week. We're building toward a new moon on the 11th-13th, and that means spring tides stacking up fast — bigger swings, stronger current, and critically, the high stand of tide starting to line up with sunset on the western end of our beat. That's the window I'm circling on the calendar. When a big incoming tide crests right as the light goes down, bass that have been sitting deep and sulky through the heat of the day get a reason to move — the current stacks bait against structure right as their most comfortable feeding light shows up. I'd be looking at the Norwalk Islands funnels, the drop at Stratford Shoal, and the mouth of Port Jeff harbor on that Friday-through-Monday high water at dusk. It's the first real evening window we've had since the full moon back in June, and if the wind lays down like it's supposed to, it should fish.

Daytime, the bass bite has been honest but not easy — scattered fish, not stacked fish. Guys working bucktails and swim shads along the Norwalk Islands rips on the last two hours of the outgoing have been picking off schoolies to maybe 28 inches, with the occasional better fish mixed in when the current really rips through the cuts. Live bunker under a balloon off Charles Island produced a few better fish last week, one report of a fish pushing 20 pounds, but that was one good afternoon out of several quiet ones — don't go out expecting that to repeat on command. The pattern that's actually consistent is first-light and last-light around structure with moving water. Middle of the day, middle of the tide, forget it — those fish are down and not interested.

Bluefish have filled in the gaps nicely and they're not shy about it. Middle Ground Light and the rips off Charles Island have both had choppers blowing up on top during the outgoing, and they'll hit anything that moves fast — Hopkins spoons, poppers, bucktails retrieved with some speed. If you want steady action rather than quality, this is where you get it right now. Bring wire or heavy fluoro leader because they're shredding light mono without hesitation.

Fluke are the interesting story this week. The bay-side water has warmed enough that the flats fish have cleared out — I'm not finding them in the shallow coves of Oyster Bay or the back bays the way we were in June. They've slid to the channels and the deeper cuts, which tracks with what's happening Sound-wide as the warm surface layer pushes bait and fluke alike toward cooler bottom structure. The Norwalk Islands channel edges in 25 to 35 feet have been the better bet, drifting white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, working them slow along the bottom on the last of the outgoing when the current's still moving enough to keep the bait swimming naturally. Stratford Shoal's deep side has also given up a few quality fish to guys dragging squid strips tipped with Gulp. Nothing has been a slam-dunk — you're covering ground and culling through shorts to find keepers — but the fish are there if you commit to working the deeper structure instead of the shallows.

Porgies are doing exactly what porgies do in July — piling up on structure and biting steady. Charles Island rocks, the Middle Ground reef, and the rubble around Stratford Shoal have all been giving up good numbers on sandworms and clam, fished on the bottom with light tackle. If you want a guaranteed bend in the rod for the kids or you just want dinner, this is your play right now, no drama required.

Weakfish, I'll be honest, are close to a non-event this season so far. Water's plenty warm enough on paper, but I haven't heard of a single solid weakfish report out of the river mouths or back bays that usually hold them this time of year. That warm-water threshold everybody points to clearly isn't the only ingredient — something else isn't lining up, whether it's bait, salinity, or just numbers being down. I wouldn't build a trip around them right now.

As for bonito — too early for us. That's an August pattern here in the Sound proper, once the water really settles and bait gets pushed hard into the funnel at the Race. The early reports coming out of the ocean side are worth watching as a leading indicator, but I wouldn't rig for them yet inside our beat.

If I had one shot this week, I'd take the Saturday or Sunday evening high around the Norwalk Islands, timed to that new-moon spring tide meeting the sunset. Bring bucktails for the bass, something fast for the blues that will inevitably show up, and don't be shy about working the deeper channel edges after dark if the bite up top goes quiet — that's where the bigger fish have been sitting all week.

reports.headline: New moon springs reopen the sunset flood bite off Kings Point
reports.subhead: Warm bay water is pushing fluke to the channel edges while bass wait on the rock piles for the tide to turn — here's where to be this weekend.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the Sound did what it always does in the dead heat of early July — it went quiet in the middle of the day and came alive at the edges. We had a stretch of settled weather after the last front pushed through, seas laid down flat, and the water in the back bays climbed hard. Little Neck Bay and Manhasset Bay have been running warm, shallow-water warm, the kind that pushes bait and gamefish out looking for something cooler.
