That's not a guess — the bay-side pattern we're seeing mirrors what's happening across the whole South Shore, where surface temps pushing toward 79 degrees have shoved fluke out of the skinny water and into the channels. Same story here. The fluke that were sitting in Hempstead Harbor and the mouth of Manhasset Bay two weeks ago have slid out to the current lines — Throgs Neck Bridge channel, the drop along Stepping Stones, the deeper humps off Execution Rocks. Anywhere the tide runs harder and the bottom holds cooler water, that's where they went.

Now here's what matters for this week: we're running up on a new moon, and that means building spring tides through the weekend. I've got my eye on Friday through Monday, the 10th through the 13th, because the PM high stand at Kings Point starts converging with sunset right in that window — peak alignment looks like the 11th and 12th. This is the first evening flood-into-dark setup we've had since the full moon back in June, and if you've fished this beat as long as I have, you know that combination — big spring tide, high water arriving right as the light drops — is when the resident bass stop sulking on the bottom and come up to feed. I'd circle those three evenings on the calendar before anything else this week.

As for what's actually coming over the rail: it's a mixed bag right now, and I'll be straight with you — it's not been an easy pick. Execution Rocks is still doing what it always does on the outgoing, holding bass tight to the rock pile in that 15 to 25 foot depth range where the current wraps around the ledge. Guys working bucktails — the 1-ounce white with a strip of fresh bunker — down through there on the last two hours of the ebb have been picking up schoolies to the mid-20s, with the occasional better fish mixed in early and late in the tide. Nothing that's going to make the front page, but steady enough that it's worth the trip if you're patient and you fish the whole drop instead of running around.

The bunker schools that stacked up off Matinecock Point back in June haven't fully broken up — they've thinned out and scattered a little with the heat, but there's still enough bait around that the bluefish have found it. Early morning, first light, before the boat traffic picks up, I'm seeing choppers busting on top off Matinecock and around Hart Island. If you can get out there by 5:30, poppers and metal — a Kastmaster or a Hopkins — will get hit almost every cast for a half hour. Once the sun gets up over the trees and the boats start running, that bite shuts off fast, so don't sleep in.

Fluke fishing has been honest work this week, not a giveaway. With the bay-side fish pushed out to the channels, your best drift has been along the Throgs Neck Bridge pilings on the last of the incoming and first hour of the outgoing, working white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails right along bottom in 30 to 40 feet. I've also had good reports off the deeper edge near Stepping Stones, same depth range, same slow bucktail drag with a strip of squid trailing off the hook for scent. Nothing huge — most fish are running 16 to 19 inches — but there's enough keeper-sized fish mixed in that a few solid drifts will put dinner in the cooler.

Porgies remain the most dependable thing going on this stretch of the Sound right now, and honestly, if you want a guaranteed bent rod for the kids, this is it. The humps off Matinecock and around Hart Island are holding good numbers in 20 to 35 feet. Bloodworms or clam on a simple high-low rig, small hooks, and you'll load the cooler on almost any stage of tide, though the bite does turn on hardest through the last two hours of the incoming.

Weakfish, I have to be honest — they're just not here in any numbers worth chasing. The water's warm enough on paper, but warm water alone hasn't been the trigger this species needs the last couple seasons, and this year's no different so far. If you stumble into a few working a bunker school at dusk, consider it a bonus, not a plan.

Looking ahead, my money this week is on that sunset flood window at Kings Point starting Friday and building through Sunday and Monday as the new moon tightens up the tide swing. If the wind stays out of the south and light like it's been, I'd be positioned on the west side of Execution Rocks or working the edge toward Stepping Stones right as the tide turns to high, fishing bucktails and swimming plugs through last light into full dark. Bass have a way of showing up right on that high-water mark when the spring tide is running this hard, and with the bait still scattered around from Matinecock to Hart Island, there's enough forage in the system to hold fish through the weekend. If that window disappoints, the backup plan doesn't change — channel edges for fluke, the humps for porgies. Either way, there's enough happening on this stretch of water to make the trip worthwhile, just don't expect it to be handed to you.

reports.headline: New moon springs load up The Race — sunset flood window back on for eastern Sound bass
reports.subhead: A week of neap-tide sluggishness gives way to building current as the new moon approaches, and the first real evening bass bite since June's full moon is lining up for the weekend.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week was a grind, and I'll say that up front. We were sitting in that dead zone after the June full moon — neap tides, current dying out early in The Race and Plum Gut, and a stretch of southwest wind that let the bay water climb into the upper 70s. That warm, soft water pushed the fluke out of Gardiners Bay and Orient Harbor and stacked them into the channels and inlet mouths where the outgoing tide still moves clean, cooler water off the bottom. Anybody still working the flats got picked apart. Anybody who moved to the drop-offs did fine.

This week the moon changes everything. We're building toward new moon on the 12th-13th, and that means spring tides are loading up fast — bigger exchange, harder current through The Race and Plum Gut, and critically, the PM flood is now lining up with sunset. That's the window I've been waiting on since the last full moon. Friday through Monday, the high stand at Kings Point converges right at dusk, which means the bait gets pushed hard against structure exactly when the light drops and the bass turn predatory. If you've only got one evening this month to fish eastern Sound structure, this is it.

The Race has been the most consistent piece of water for stripers, but you have to work the stage of tide correctly. On the last two hours of the ebb, I'm anchoring up-current of the eddies on the north side — the humps around 80 to 100 feet where the current splits off the reef structure — and drifting big parachute jigs and bunker-imitation umbrella rigs down into the seam. Fish have been holding low, right on the structure, not up in the water column, so weight matters. I've been running 12- to 16-ounce jig heads just to hold bottom in that 4- to 5-knot water. Once the tide starts to slack, that's when the eels come out — 12-inch rigged eels drifted naturally through the slower eddies produce the better fish, mid-20s to low-30s, with a few reports of fish pushing 40 mixed in from boats working the deeper holes off Fishers Island. Nothing guaranteed there, but the size class has been real.

Plum Gut has been more of a bluefish show the last ten days. Diamond jigs — the 4- to 6-ounce Point Jude / Deadly Dick style — worked with a fast retrieve through the rip on the last of the incoming has been drawing blues in the 5- to 10-pound class, sometimes breaking the surface hard enough that you don't even need to jig, just cast into the boil. If you want bass instead of blues in that same water, slow down and go subsurface — bucktails tipped with a strip of squid, bounced along the bottom edge where the Gut narrows down to about 40 to 50 feet, has been the better bet for stripers in that pressure-cooker current.

Fluke are the story worth paying attention to right now because of where they've relocated. With the bay running warm, the better fish have slid out to the mouth of Plum Gut and the deeper flats off Orient Point Reef, where the upwelled Sound water sitting around the low 70s is holding bait. Drifting 4- to 5-inch white or chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾- to 1-ounce bucktails, right on the outgoing tide when that current runs clean out of the harbor mouths, has produced the most consistent keeper-class fish — nothing giant, mostly 18 to 22 inches, but steady enough that a few drifts will fill a limit if you're patient about staying on the edge of the channel rather than working the middle.

Porgies have been reliable filler fish on the structure around Fishers Island and the reef ground off Orient — small green crab or sandworm on a high-low rig, fished tight to the rocks in 20 to 35 feet on the slower parts of the tide, will keep a rod bent between striper drifts. Blackfish are still a ways off from being worth targeting hard this stretch, so I wouldn't burn a trip on tautog just yet — that bite firms up later in the season once water starts to cool.

Looking ahead, the alignment I'm watching hardest is Saturday and Sunday evening. New moon springs plus a PM flood hitting right at last light in The Race and Plum Gut — that's the kind of setup that produces the biggest fish of the summer in this zone, because the current volume moving through those cuts on a spring tide is enormous, and it concentrates bait against structure in a way neap tides simply can't. If the wind stays out of the south and doesn't blow the rips into chop, I'd be anchored on the north side eddies of The Race an hour before sunset with an eel in the water, working through the tide change into full dark. If the wind kicks up and the surface goes ugly, Plum Gut is more protected and will still fish well on bucktails through the same window. Either way, this is the best tide-and-light setup we've had since June, and after a slow stretch, that's worth building a trip around.

reports.headline: New moon springs load up the Stratford Shoal rip as fluke slide into the channels
reports.subhead: Bigger tides and a sunset flood window are setting up the best striper stretch since the June full moon — if the wind cooperates.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the Sound did what it does in early July — it built heat on top and shuffled bait around underneath. Surface temps in the back bays and harbors climbed into the mid-to-upper 70s, and that warm cap pushed a lot of the bait — and the fluke that were eating it — out of the shallow flats and into the channels and inlets where there's still cooler water moving. I saw it in Oyster Bay and again poking around the mouth of the Norwalk Islands: bait balled up tight against structure instead of spread out over the flats like it was in June. Wind was mostly out of the south and southwest for stretches, which didn't help clarity, but it never blew hard enough to really wreck things — just enough to keep the surface stirred and the fishing a notch tougher than it should've been.

This week the moon is the story. We're running up on new moon and the spring tides that come with it, with the peak alignment landing July 11-13. That means bigger tidal swings than we've had since the full moon in June, and — this is the part I care about — the PM flood is going to converge with sunset through that stretch. That's the first evening window like this since last month, and in the Central Sound that combination (big water moving, low light, bait getting squeezed through the narrows) is when the bigger bass show themselves. I'd circle Friday through Monday evening on the calendar. If the wind lays down out of the south for those sunsets, the flood pushing through the Stratford Shoal rip and around the Norwalk Islands should set up about as good as it gets for July.

On the striper front, it's been a real fish but not an easy one. Guys working bunker schools around Middle Ground Light and along the Connecticut shoreline near Charles Island have had good mornings snagging and drifting live bunker on wire leaders, picking off fish in the 20s of pounds mixed with a lot of schoolies. The bite windows are short — usually the last hour of the incoming and the first hour of the outgoing, right when the current starts moving bait off the structure. At Stratford Shoal itself, the rip has been holding fish on the drop, especially on the last two hours of the ebb when the water piles up and pushes bait off the shoal edge into the deeper channel — I've had the best luck there drifting eels or bucktailing 1.5 to 2-ounce white and chartreuse jigs along the break in 20 to 35 feet. Nothing has been stacked up thick, but the fish that are there have some size to them, which tracks with what other boats have been finding scattered from here out to Block Island and the Cape this summer — pockets of bigger bass, not blitzes.

Bluefish have filled in the gaps nicely and are the more reliable bite right now. Wherever the bunker schools have been getting worked over — off Eaton's Neck, around the Norwalk Islands, and in close to the Connecticut beaches near New Haven — the blues have been all over them on top, especially in the first hour of light. Bucktails, poppers, or just cut bunker chunks fished under a float will get bit. It's not subtle fishing and it's a good one to bring kids or a buddy who wants steady action without needing a tide chart memorized.

Fluke is where I'd spend my daylight hours this week, because the pattern is clear: the fish have followed the cooler water out of the warmed-up bays and into the channels, cuts, and inlet mouths. The mouth of the Norwalk Islands channel, the deeper cuts around Charles Island, and the Port Jeff Harbor entrance have all been holding fish on the outgoing tide, when the current sweeps bait — and Gulp — off the flats and funnels it through the deeper water. Five-inch white or chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom in 20 to 40 feet, have been the most consistent producer. It's not a doormat parade — most days you're culling through shorts for a couple of keepers in the 3 to 5-pound range — but it beats fishing the flats right now, where the warm water has the fish either buried deep or just not interested.

Porgies have been the steady, dependable bite all week, and I mean that as a compliment in a summer where a lot of species have been streaky. The reefs around the Norwalk Islands and the rockpiles off Charles Island are loaded, and simple bottom rigs with sandworms or clam pieces in 15 to 30 feet will keep a rod bent most of an afternoon. Good one to fall back on if the tide's wrong for stripers or the fluke aren't cooperating.

Weakfish, I'll be honest, have been a no-show in my part of the Sound, and the broader data backs that up — warm water alone hasn't been enough to trigger a real push this year. I wouldn't plan a trip around them right now.

Looking ahead, the window I'm most interested in is that Friday-through-Monday flood/sunset stretch on the new moon springs. If the wind holds out of the south and stays light in the evenings, I'd be at the Stratford Shoal rip or working the Norwalk Islands current lines right as the sun drops and the flood really gets moving — that's historically when the bigger bass commit. Plan B if the bass don't show is simple: work the fluke through the channel cuts on the strong outgoing that comes with these bigger tides, because more water moving means more bait getting flushed, and that's exactly the kind of current fluke like to sit in and ambush.

reports.headline: New moon springs set up the first real PM flood window at Kings Point since June
reports.subhead: After a week of warm, sloppy bay water pushing fluke out of the back bays, the Sound's tide clock is finally lining up sunset with the flood — and that's when the bass show.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week was one of those stretches where the water looked good but the timing was off. We had warm surface temps building in the back bays — Little Neck, Manhasset, Hempstead Harbor all running warm and a little greasy on calm afternoons — and that warmth did what it always does: it pushed the fluke out of the shallow bay water and down into the channels and toward the inlets, chasing cooler, cleaner water and the bait that goes with it. I saw the same pattern play out on the South Shore with Great South Bay running near 79 degrees, and our Western Sound bays aren't far behind it. The bass, meanwhile, were around — Execution Rocks and the Stepping Stones rockpile never fully shut off — but the good tide stages kept falling in the middle of the day, which on the Sound in July means bright sun, slack current, and fish sitting deep and sour instead of up and hunting.

This week the calendar does us a favor. We're building toward a new moon, which means spring tides are stacking up fast, and more importantly, the timing of the flood at Kings Point is sliding into the sunset hours starting Friday. That's the window I've been waiting on since the June full moon — high stand converging with last light, peaking Saturday through Monday, July 11th through 13th. When that happens on the Western Sound, the bait gets pushed hard up against structure right as the light drops and the bass turn predator instead of just holding station. If you've fished Execution Rocks or the Stepping Stones light long enough, you know this rhythm — the fish don't really turn on until the moon and the tide agree with each other, and for the first time in weeks, they will.

As for what's actually coming over the rail — it's a mixed bag right now, and I'll be straight with you. Striped bass have been present but scattered, mostly schoolie-to-mid-twenties class fish, with the better ones showing on the last two hours of the outgoing off Execution Rocks in 25 to 35 feet, working bucktails — the white 1-ounce with a chunk of pork rind or a 4-inch white Bass Assassin trailer — bounced slow along the rock edges where the current breaks. A few boats working live bunker on a three-way rig off Matinecock Point have connected with better fish, 28 to 34 inches, but you need to find the pods first, and the bunker have been thinner and more scattered than a typical early July push. When you find them stacked, though, that's your green light — snap on a weighted treble, snag one, and free-line it back into the school on 20-pound fluoro leader.

Bluefish have filled in some of the gaps. Choppers in the 3 to 6 pound range are chewing through diamond jigs and Kastmasters off Hart Island and along the Throgs Neck rip on the last of the incoming, especially in that hour around the tide change when the current slows enough for the blues to stack up and feed instead of get pushed through. Wire leader is not optional right now — I lost two bucktails to blues Tuesday because I got lazy and fished straight fluoro.

Fluke inside the Sound have followed the same logic as everywhere else this summer — warm shallow water, cooler deep water, fish moving to find the difference. Your best drifts have been in the deeper channel edges near Throgs Neck Bridge and the drop-off on the Stepping Stones side, 30 to 40 feet, dragging 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, slow and tight to bottom on the outgoing. Nothing spectacular — a fish or two in the 3 to 5 pound range per trip if you put your time in and keep moving — but it's honest fishing, not a pile-up.

Porgies remain the one thing you can count on. Execution Rocks and the rockpiles off Matinecock are stacked with them in 20 to 30 feet, and small hooks with clam or squid strips on a high-low rig will fill a bucket without much drama. If you want a guaranteed bend in the rod for the kids, that's still your play.

I'll be straight about weakfish too — it's been quiet, and I mean quiet. The water's warm enough on paper, but paper doesn't catch fish, and I haven't heard of a single decent weakfish report out of our zone or anywhere close to it. I'm not chasing that one right now, and I wouldn't recommend you do either.

Looking ahead: if the wind lays down Friday and Saturday night like the pattern suggests, I'd be fishing the last two hours of daylight into dark at the Stepping Stones light and off Execution Rocks, right on that flood tide convergence. That's the best setup I've seen in weeks — new moon springs, sunset timing, and bait that's been building all month around Matinecock. It's not a guaranteed pile of stripers, but the ingredients are all there for the first time since June, and that's exactly the kind of alignment that's put fish in my boat for thirty years. Plan B if the bass don't cooperate — work the fluke drift off Throgs Neck on the outgoing and fill in with porgies at the rockpiles. Something's going to eat this weekend. The question is just how big.

reports.headline: New moon springs load up Plum Gut as the sunset bass window reopens
reports.subhead: Bigger tides start pushing bait through the Gut this weekend, and the bass are answering the dinner bell at last light.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week was one of those stretches where you had to work for it. Wind sat out of the southwest most days, laid the Sound down flat by afternoon but stirred just enough chop overnight to keep the bait from settling anywhere predictable. We were coming off the June full moon, so tides were already easing toward neap — slack water lingered longer at Horton Point and Rocky Point, and the current through Plum Gut never really got up on its legs. Fish were around, but scattered, feeding in short windows and shutting off fast. Surface water's been holding warm right through the heat, the kind of warm where the bass want to be down deep during the day and only come up to hunt when the light drops off.

That's changing this week. We're building toward a new moon around the 13th, which means the tides are loading up again — bigger swings, stronger push through the Gut, more water moving past Orient Point on the ebb. The prediction I like most for our stretch is that PM flood window lining up with sunset from Friday through Monday, peaking the 11th through 13th. That's the first evening high-tide bite we've had since before the full moon, and it's worth building your week around. When the flood stacks up against last light out at the Gut approach, bass that have been sulking deep all day get pushed up onto the structure to intercept bait getting squeezed through the current. That's when you want to be standing on the rocks, not sitting in the truck.

Bass fishing off Horton Point has been a game of patience more than volume. Guys working bunker chunks on fish-finder rigs into the deeper water off the point have been picking up fish in the 28 to 34-inch range, mostly on the last two hours of the outgoing when the current slows enough for a bait to sit still. Bucktails haven't been doing much there in daylight — too bright, water's too settled — but at Plum Gut itself, the story's different. Guys drifting white or chartreuse 1 1/2-ounce bucktails with a curly-tail trailer through the rip on the ebb have connected with better fish, some pushing 20 pounds, holding right where the Gut current meets the slower water off Orient. That's classic Plum Gut structure fishing — find the seam, not the middle of the rip, and let the bait swing through it instead of retrieving fast.

Bluefish have been the more reliable show. Bunker schools have been working their way through the Gut on the tide changes, and where you find pods of bunker getting nervous on the surface, there are choppers underneath cutting them up. Topwater poppers and metal — Kastmasters, Deadly Dicks — have been drawing fast strikes off Rocky Point and out toward Orient. Nothing giant, mostly 3 to 5 pounds, but they hit hard and they don't make you wait around.

Fluke have shifted the way you'd expect with the heat we've had. Inshore water's been warm enough that the fluke that were sitting shallow have pushed out toward the deeper channel at Mattituck Inlet and the drop-off just outside it. Guys drifting white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails through that inlet channel on the outgoing have found keeper-class fish, four and five pounds, mixed with a lot of short ones you have to sort through. It's not a bang-bang bite — more like one or two solid fish for every dozen drifts — but the fish are there if you put your time in on the moving current rather than the slack.

Porgies have been steady and unspectacular off the reef structure around Rocky Point, small hooks and sandworms or clam on high-low rigs in 20 to 30 feet. Nothing to write home about size-wise but a good bend-your-rod option when the bigger stuff isn't cooperating, and a fine way to fill an hour waiting on the tide to turn for bass.

Blackfish have been quiet, which isn't unusual for July — tautog don't love the warm water and tend to hold tight to structure in slightly deeper holes this time of year. If you're looking for them, fish green crab on jig heads tucked right against the rock piles off Horton Point in 25 to 35 feet, but don't expect fast action.

Weakfish, I'll be straight with you — still nothing. The water's been plenty warm enough for them by any number I've seen, but warm water alone doesn't bring weakfish back if the fish aren't in the system. I haven't heard a credible weakfish report out of this stretch all season, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise just because the temperature checks a box.

Looking ahead, the new moon springs building into the weekend are the story. If the wind stays reasonable — nothing hard out of the southwest to muddy up the Gut — I'd be at Plum Gut or the Orient Point approach Friday through Monday evening, working that PM flood right into sunset. That's the first real evening window we've had since the last full moon, and the bigger tidal push should wake up fish that have been lying low in the heat. Plan B if the bass don't show: work the Mattituck Inlet channel on the outgoing for fluke, because that bite's been consistent even when the bass have been stubborn.

reports.headline: New moon springs load up Plum Gut as porgies stack thick around Shelter Island
reports.subhead: Bass and blues are riding the building current through the Gut while fluke slide into the channels ahead of the weekend's big tides.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the bay did what it does in early July — it settled into that thick, green, warm-water rhythm that pushes everything toward structure and current. We had a stretch of light southwest wind that let the surface really cook, and with Great South Bay reportedly pushing 78.8 degrees, I'd bet dollars to donuts the shallow flats up here in Noyack and Southold Bay aren't far behind. That kind of heat doesn't ruin the fishing, it just relocates it. Bass, blues and fluke all read water temperature the same way we read a thermostat that's stuck too high — they go find the vent. Around here that means the channels, the Gut, and anywhere current keeps moving cooler water across structure.

This week the moon's swinging toward new, and that matters more in the Peconic system than almost anywhere else on the Island because Plum Gut and the Race live and die by tidal current. Springs build hard Friday through Monday (July 10-13), with peak exchange lining up right around the weekend. Bigger tides mean stronger current through the Gut, Shelter Island Sound, and the cuts around Jessups Neck and Robins Island — and stronger current means bait gets pushed off the flats and concentrated where predators can pin it. If you've been struggling to find fish scattered on the flats, this is the week that current does the work for you and stacks them up in the pinch points.

Porgy fishing has been the one constant, and honestly it's been about as good as it gets. I've been working the rockpiles off Cedar Point, the drop-off outside Fresh Pond, and the rips along the North Ferry side of Shelter Island in 15 to 25 feet, and it's been steady meat right through the tide changes — doesn't seem to matter if it's incoming or outgoing, though the bite does sharpen up in that hour before and after the turn when the current eases and the fish stop fighting to hold position. Standard hi-lo rig, size 6 or 4 hooks, fresh sandworm or a chunk of clam, just enough weight to hold bottom. Nothing fancy needed. These porgies are thick and eager, running 10 to 13 inches with enough 14s mixed in to keep it interesting, and there's no shortage of them right now — this is peak season for a reason.

Fluke have been the trickier read. Bay water warming the way it has pushed a chunk of the population out of the open flats and into the channels — the same pattern we're seeing bayside across the Island, just playing out on our geography. I'm finding better numbers working the Orient Point rip, the North Race, and the deeper cut running along Long Beach Bar in 20 to 35 feet on the outgoing tide, dragging a white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a half-ounce bucktail nice and slow along bottom. It's not been a banzai bite — more a fish here, a fish there, cull through some shorts to find a couple of keepers in the 18 to 20-inch range. If you want a shot at something bigger, work the deeper edge of the channel where it meets the flat, right where the thermocline sets up. That temperature break is holding bait, and bigger fluke sit right on that seam waiting on it.

Stripers have been a mixed bag, which is normal for mid-July in the bay system. The early-morning bite off the Shelter Island rips and around Orient Point has produced schoolies to the mid-20s mixed with the occasional bass pushing 30 inches, mostly on bucktails and swimming plugs worked through the faster water at first light before the sun gets up on it. Bluefish have actually been the more consistent player through Plum Gut itself — anywhere from cocktail-size choppers up to some solid 4 and 5-pounders blitzing bunker pods on the surface, especially on the stronger stages of the tide. Diamond jigs, poppers, anything flashy thrown into the melee gets hit. With the new moon building current through the Gut this weekend, I expect that bluefish action to sharpen up, and there's a real chance some better bass slide in behind the bait as the current rips harder and pins everything against the rocks off Orient.

Weakfish, I'll be honest, are still a no-show. Water's plenty warm enough on paper, but warm water alone isn't the trigger — I haven't heard of a legitimate weakfish catch in the bay in weeks, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. If you're set on weakies, I'd hold off until we see some real reports rather than burning gas on a hunch.

Looking ahead, the building spring tide through the weekend is the headline event for this zone. If the wind stays out of the south and light like it has been, I'd fish the Gut and the North Race on the max ebb Saturday and Sunday morning — that's when the current will be moving the most water and stacking bait against structure. Bring bucktails for bass, diamond jigs for the blues, and don't leave the porgy rig at home, because Shelter Island's rockpiles aren't going anywhere and they'll bail you out if the current fishing goes quiet. Plan B if the Gut gets too ripping to fish comfortably: back off into Shelter Island Sound and work the porgies and fluke on the slower water while you wait for the tide to ease. Either way, there's enough happening in this system right now to make the trip worth it — just go in with a game plan for more than one species.

reports.headline: New moon springs load the Moriches cut as fluke push out and the first bonito show at the bar
reports.subhead: Warm bay water is shoving fluke toward the inlet channels while building tides set up a real outgoing bite through the weekend.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the bay did what warm bay water does in early July — it got soft and slow on the flats and pushed everything with fins toward moving water. Great South Bay readings crossed 78.8°F, and while I don't have a thermometer sitting in the Moriches system itself, the same signature showed up here: fluke that were spread thin over Pattersquash flats and the East Moriches grass beds a week ago are now stacking against hard structure — the inlet's main channel edge, the Cupsogue drop-off, and the deeper cuts along Tuthill Point. Warm, oxygen-poor shallow water pushes bait and predators alike into anything with current and depth, and the inlet is the biggest current-and-depth feature we've got. That's the whole story behind this week's pattern.

We're building toward a new moon, with the tidal springs stacking hard through the weekend — peak alignment looks to land July 11-13. That matters more here than almost anywhere on the South Shore because Moriches Inlet is a narrow, engineered-by-nature cut with a shifting bar, and bigger tidal exchange means more velocity through that throat. More velocity means more bait getting flushed out of the bay on the outgoing, which means predators — bass, blues, fluke — stack on the downcurrent side of the bar and the eastern rock jetty waiting on it. If you've fished this inlet long enough you know the drill: neap tides let fish spread out and sulk in eddies, spring tides concentrate everything into predictable lanes. This is a spring-tide week. Fish the lanes.

Fluke first, because that's where the volume is right now. The drift along the main channel edge off Pattersquash Island, running 18 to 25 feet, has been the most consistent water in the system. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 1- to 1.5-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the last two hours of the outgoing, have been putting keeper fluke in the boat — nothing giant, mostly 17 to 21 inches with the occasional better fish mixed in, which tracks with what's being reported from Shinnecock and the Reynolds Channel side too. The other lane worth working is the deeper hole just inside the inlet proper, on the bay side of the current bar position — that hole has held its depth through this spring's storm cycles and it's collecting fish getting pushed off the flats. Don't waste time on the shallow grass flats behind Cupsogue right now; the water's too warm and the fluke have already voted with their fins.

Striped bass are doing what they do at this inlet in summer — showing best on the edges of light, not the middle of the day. The outgoing tide at dusk, worked with bunker chunks on a fishfinder rig tight to the rocks on the ocean side of the Cupsogue jetty, has produced keeper-class fish mixed with a lot of shorts. If you want numbers over size, work the surf at first light with topwater plugs or bucktail-and-swim-shad combos along the ocean bar east of the inlet mouth — that structure has been holding schoolies stacked tight, and a few 28- to 32-inch fish have come out of that same stretch on outgoing water. The bigger springs building this weekend should sharpen that bite further; more water moving through the cut means a harder edge for bass to sit on.

Bluefish are around in the usual two flavors — snapper blues thick in the bay proper, especially off the Forge River mouth and up into East Moriches creeks, and better cocktail-to-medium blues showing at the inlet itself on diamond jigs and small metal worked on the outgoing tide alongside the fluke and bass. If you're throwing bucktails for fluke and getting your leader bit off, that's not bad luck, that's just Tuesday at this inlet in July.

Honest note on weakfish: water's warm enough on paper, but I'm not hearing anything real out of this system, and that lines up with what the broader region is showing — warm water alone hasn't been translating to weakfish activity anywhere close by this year. I wouldn't plan a trip around them right now. Porgies are a better bet if you want a bend in the rod without overthinking it — sandworms and clam on standard rigs over the deeper holes off Tuthill Point have been steady, if unspectacular.

The one genuinely new development is on the ocean side. This is the tail end of the seasonal window for the first bonito and Spanish mackerel showing at eastern Long Island inlets, and Moriches and Shinnecock have both had early reports on clean incoming water at the ocean bar. If you've got small metal — deadly dicks, epoxy jigs, anything that moves fast and flashes — it's worth a half hour at the bar on a clean incoming tide before you commit to the fluke drift. That window closes fast; by next week the bulk of that bite typically slides east.

Look-ahead: with the new moon springs peaking Friday through Monday, I'd fish the last two hours of the outgoing at the inlet channel edge for fluke, and hit the ocean bar at first light for bass and a shot at bonito before the sun gets up. If the bar's still shifted where it was after the spring storm cycle, expect the strongest current lane to be tighter to the Cupsogue side than the Pattersquash side — that's where I'd start the drift.

reports.headline: Bay Heat Pushes the Doormats Out — Sloop Channel and the Inlet Take Over
reports.subhead: Great South Bay ran hot enough to shove the fluke into the channels while bunker still stack the inlet mouth for blues and the occasional bass.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the bay did what the bay does in a heat spell — it cooked. Great South Bay pushed close to 79 degrees on the flats, and that's too warm for a fluke to sit comfortable on bottom all day. What that does is push fish. The doormats that were scattered around the grass flats off Wantagh and the mouth of the creeks packed up and moved into the channels and the inlet itself, where there's current, cooler bottom water, and bait getting flushed through on the tide. I've said it before and I'll say it again — when the bay gets soupy in July, Sloop Channel and the throat of Jones Inlet become the address. That's exactly what's happening right now, and the ocean side is helping the cause — there's upwelled water sitting around 71 degrees just outside the inlet, which is a nice cool seam for a fluke that just got pushed out of a warm bathtub.

This week the moon's the story. We're building toward a new moon on the 11th, which means bigger tides stacking in through the weekend — the spring tide push peaks right around the 11th through 13th. More water moving on both the flood and the ebb through Jones Inlet means harder current in the throat, which is good news and bad news. Good, because it flushes bait through the cut and gets predators keyed up on a tighter window. Bad, because if you're not there for that window, the fishing can go dead fast once the tide slacks. Wind's been the usual summer variable — when it's held out of the south or southwest, it's kept the ocean side a little riled, but the inlet itself has stayed fishable on the inside of the tide stages. Watch that forecast into the weekend because bigger springs plus any onshore wind can turn Jones Beach ocean side into soup in a hurry.

Fluke is the honest bread and butter right now. Best water has been 15 to 25 feet in Sloop Channel and along the edges of the West End channel where it dumps into the inlet — fishing the last two hours of the outgoing into dead low, then picking back up as it turns. Three-quarter ounce white bucktails with a 5-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullet trailer is what's putting fish in the cooler, dragged slow along bottom, short hops, don't work it too hard. A few guys are doing well with a simple high-low rig and squid strips fished dead-stick style off the channel edges when the current's really ripping on the big tides — sometimes a fluke just wants it sitting still in that kind of flow. Nothing epic size-wise, mostly 16 to 19 inches with a keeper mixed in here and there, but the numbers have picked up noticeably since the bay pushed those fish out.

Bluefish have been the more reliable show at the inlet mouth itself. There's still bunker stacked up around the Jones Beach jetty and out toward Short Beach, and the blues have been slashing through them at first light and again right at dusk — that's your window, don't sleep in. Kastmasters and Hopkins jigs worked fast through the melee, or if you want to match the hatch, a bunker spoon trolled along the edge of the school will get bit hard. Some of these blues are pushing 4 to 6 pounds, real fun on light tackle, and they'll keep you busy while you're waiting to see if anything bigger shows under the bait.

Striped bass, I'll be straight with you — it's a summer lull right now, and anybody telling you different is selling something. The daytime bite on the ocean side is mostly quiet, resident fish holding deep and not real interested until the sun's down. If you want a shot at a bass, it's a night program — live eels or bunker chunks fished tight to the rocks at Short Beach and along the Jones Inlet jetty on the incoming tide has produced some fish in the 20 to 30 pound class for the guys willing to put in dark hours. It's not a blitz fishery this time of year, it's a grind-it-out program, one or two quality bites a trip if you're in the right spot at the right stage of tide.

Weakfish — I know there's been chatter about a comeback, and I want to believe it as much as anybody who grew up fishing these waters when weakfish were a real player in this bay. But I'm not going to blow smoke. Water's been plenty warm enough for weakfish for over two weeks now in the back bay, and I still haven't heard of a single quality fish coming out of Freeport or the South Oyster Bay creeks. Warm water alone doesn't do it — there needs to be the right bait and the right structure lining up too, and right now that alignment hasn't happened. Keep it on your radar for a cooler snap later this summer, but don't build a trip around it yet.

Porgies are around the reef structure off Freeport if you want a bend in the rod and dinner both — clam on a standard porgy rig in 20 to 30 feet has been steady if unspectacular.

Looking ahead, I'd focus hard on that new moon spring push building through the 11th to 13th. Bigger current in the inlet should sharpen up the fluke bite in Sloop Channel on the last of the outgoing, and there's a real chance the harder flow pushes more bunker through the cut and triggers a bass show at dusk that hasn't been there in daylight. If the wind cooperates and lays down out of the south, I'd be at the inlet mouth right at last light with bucktails rigged and a stick bait tied on just in case something bigger comes up under those blues.

reports.headline: Bay water pushes into the 70s and shoves the fluke out to the inlet
reports.subhead: Marine Parkway Bridge sets up for a real outgoing bite as new-moon springs build toward the weekend.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the bay finally got hot — I mean really warmed up, the kind of warm where you can feel it through your waders standing on the flats at Big Egg Marsh at low tide. Surface temps in the back bay pushed into the high 70s, and that's enough to shove fluke off the flats and out toward the channels and the inlet, where there's still some exchange and cooler water moving underneath. That's exactly what I saw fishing the Cross Bay Bridge drift on Sunday — marked bait and marked fish on the meter, but they weren't biting until the current picked up and pulled cooler water through the pilings. The bay's basically told us where it wants us to fish this month: the channels, not the flats.

This week the moon's sliding toward new on the 11th, and that means building spring tides right through the weekend — bigger swings, stronger current at Rockaway Inlet and under Marine Parkway Bridge, and more water moving through the whole system on the outgoing. Bigger tides usually mean a better bite window because bait gets pushed hard and predators know it. I'd circle Friday through Monday, the 10th through the 13th, as the best stretch to be out there right at the top of the tide into the first two hours of the drop. Offshore there's a nice cool upwelled pocket sitting around 71 degrees that's been keeping the ocean side more comfortable than the bay, which is part of why the inlet mouth by Breezy Point has been holding better than the inside water lately.

Fluke are the story right now, but it's not the easy pick-'em-up bite from a few weeks back — you have to find the current seams. The best fish have come from the deeper edge of the main channel off Cross Bay Bridge, 15 to 22 feet, dragging 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails right on the outgoing, slow enough that you feel the bottom bump every few seconds. A few boats working the inlet itself, right off the Breezy Point side in 20 to 25 feet, have been doing better with chartreuse bucktails tipped with squid strips — something about that extra scent has made the difference on the slower bite days. Nobody's filling coolers, but a mixed bag of keepers and shorts with a shot at something better mixed in has been realistic if you put in a few drifts and move when you're not marking bait.

Stripers have been the more consistent story after dark. Marine Parkway Bridge is doing what it always does this time of year — staging bass in the shadow lines and current breaks on the outgoing, especially the first couple hours after the tide turns. Bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig right up against the pilings have been drawing bites from fish in the 24 to 30-inch class, with the occasional better fish mixed in for guys willing to sit through the slow stretches. If you'd rather work artificials, eels swum slow along the current seams at night have out-produced everything else I've heard about — nothing flashy, just a slow swim right along the edge where the light meets the shadow. Dawn has been decent too, casting topwater — a Doc or a needlefish — off the rocks at Breezy Point when there's bait flipping on the surface, though that bite's been short-lived, maybe 30 to 40 minutes right around first light before the sun pushes them down.

Bluefish have started showing inside the bay again, which tracks with what I'd expect this time of year once the bunker schools push in behind the warming water. Snapper blues are all over the shallows off Canarsie Pier and the flats near JFK, small but aggressive, great action if you've got kids who want bent rods on light spinning gear with tiny Kastmasters or Gotcha plugs. The bigger blues, 3 to 5 pounds, have been mixing in with the striper bite at the inlet and hitting diamond jigs worked with a fast retrieve through the same current seams where the bass are holding. It's not a blitz yet, but the bait's building, and that's usually the setup before things get more aggressive later in the month.

Porgies are steady but nothing to write home about — Cross Bay Bridge pilings and the drop-offs near Canarsie Pier have given up decent numbers on high-low rigs with bloodworms or clam, mostly hand-sized fish with the occasional bigger one to reward patience. Weakfish I have to be honest about — they're basically a non-event again this year. Water's been warm enough for a while now, but the reports just aren't there, a fish here or there at dusk on a soft plastic worked slow along the bulkheads, nothing like the run we used to see. I've stopped counting on them and I'd suggest you do the same for now.

For the week ahead, I'm circling that new-moon spring tide stretch, Friday into Monday, as the best window we've had in a while. Bigger current means bait gets moved harder through the inlet and under the bridge, and that usually translates into a better bass and blue bite on the outgoing, especially right around sunset when the light drops and the fish get bold. If the bass don't cooperate at the bridge, my backup plan is working the fluke drift along the channel edges on the same tide — the current that pushes bait past the pilings is the same current that's been holding fluke tight to the deeper structure. Either way, fish the moving water this week, not the slack. The bay's making that pretty clear.

reports.headline: New moon springs load up The Race and Plum Gut for the best current window of July
reports.subhead: Fluke are abandoning the warm bay for the inlets, bonito are creeping toward Fishers Island, and the rips are about to run harder than they have all month.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the Sound was still shaking off the blow that came through around the Fourth. Wind sat in the southwest for three straight days, kicked up a chop through the Gut that made boat control a chore, and pushed a layer of green water against the north shore that took the edge off the bass bite for 48 hours. It cleared by the weekend. Current through The Race stayed strong on the bigger tides — nothing new there — but the water column held together enough that eel guys working the north side eddies near Valiant Rock still connected after dark. Bay water on the western end of my beat has been running warm, pushing fluke out of the back bays and into the channels and inlets, which is exactly the pattern I'm leaning on this week.

Here's what matters: we're building toward a new moon on the 12th, and that means spring tides stacking through the weekend, peaking Friday into Monday. Checked the New London tide station — 8510560 — and the swings are getting bigger by the day, high stands lining up tighter to that afternoon window as the moon goes dark. Bigger tide range means more water moving through the pinch points. The Race and Plum Gut, already two of the meanest current funnels on the whole Sound, are going to be running harder than they have all month — we're talking 4 to 5 knots at max flow through the Race on the bigger swings. That's not a inconvenience, that's an opportunity. When current gets that strong, bass stack in the eddies and current shadows instead of fighting the main flow, and they feed hard right before and right after max current when bait gets disoriented and swept through the seams. That's your window. Fish the transition, not the peak.

Bass fishing right now is real but it's not blanket easy — you have to find the current break. I've been working the north side rip off Valiant Rock at first light and again at the top of the outgoing, drifting live eels on a fish-finder rig with just enough weight to hold bottom in 80 to 110 feet. Fish are there, mostly mid-20s to low-30s, with the occasional better one mixed in — heard of a few genuinely big fish scattered through the Sound corridor this past couple weeks, the kind of fish that make you fish an extra hour past when you should've quit. Plum Gut has been more consistent for numbers than size — daytime bucktail drift, white or chartreuse 1.5-ounce with a Gulp swimming mullet trailer, working the edges where the current slackens against the Orient side. That's also turning into a legit fluke spot right now. With the bay water pushing 78 degrees and fluke bailing out for cooler water, the outgoing tide through the Gut is stacking them against structure in 30 to 45 feet — I had a stretch last outing where three drifts in a row produced keeper-class fish on the same white bucktail-and-Gulp combo. Orient Point ocean side has been the better bet over the bay side for that reason alone.

Bluefish have been reliable but not spectacular — schoolie to mid-size blues chopping bunker pods off Orient and around the Fishers Island side of the Race, best worked with bunker spoons or a wire leader and a Hopkins on the troll during the morning outgoing. Nothing gorging yet, no true blitz, but enough consistent action that if bass go quiet you're not getting skunked.

The piece I'm watching closest is what's happening east of me. The cold wall that usually pins bonito and albies down around Block Island has broken down — Rhode Island Sound water jumped something like 10 degrees warmer than it's been, and that's widening the corridor west. Fishers Island sits right on that edge. I haven't had a confirmed bonito yet off North Dumpling or Race Rock, but the water's right and the bait's right, and if this holds through the week I expect the first fish to show there before they show anywhere else on my beat. Worth running out there with a bag of small Deadly Dicks and epoxy jigs just in case, especially on a calm morning with birds working.

For the coming week: I'd fish the transition tides at the Race and the Gut, not the max current — an hour either side of peak flow, working the eddies with eels at night and bucktails by day. If the wind stays out of the north and lets the water lay down, Friday through Sunday around that new moon spring should be the best current-driven bass window we've had since the June full moon faded. Plan B if the bass don't cooperate is easy — the fluke bite through the inlets is real right now and doesn't need perfect conditions, just clean outgoing water and a bucktail dragged slow along the bottom. Keep an eye east toward Fishers Island too. If that bonito corridor keeps widening the way it has, this could be the week eastern Sound guys get their first shot at them instead of driving to Block Island for it.

reports.headline: New moon springs load the narrows as bass and bunker collide at Stratford Shoal
reports.subhead: Fluke slide out of the warming bays into the inlets while the Sound's middle stretch braces for its biggest tides since June.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the Sound did what it does in early July — it sat there and cooked. Light southwest wind most days, tides running on the smaller side coming off the last quarter, and the harbors and back bays climbing into the mid-to-upper 70s. That warmth is exactly why guys fishing Oyster Bay, Northport, and Port Jeff Harbor started seeing their fluke bite go soft on the inside — the same pattern that's been documented in the Great South Bay all week, where surface temps pushing near 79 degrees are shoving doormats out of the shallow bay water and into anything with current and a cooler bottom. In our zone that means the channels, the inlets, and the mouths of the harbors, not the flats where you found them in June.

This week changes the math. We're building toward a new moon on the 11th, and that means spring tides stacking up through the weekend — bigger swings, harder current, and a lot more water moving through the pinch points that make Central Sound what it is. Stratford Shoal and the Middle Ground Light rip are going to come alive with current the way they do every new and full moon, and that's when this stretch of water earns its name — the Sound narrows here, the tide has to squeeze through, and everything living in it gets funneled and stacked. The reopened PM flood-into-sunset window on the western end (right around the Kings Point high stand) is the first evening bite of real quality since the June full moon, and it's going to bleed east into our water as the tide timing shifts through the week. Peak alignment lands July 11-13 — that's your window.

On the water, the bass bite has been honest but not easy. Boats working the Stratford Shoal rip on the last of the outgoing have been picking at fish in the mid-20s to high-20s, mostly on bucktails — 1 to 1.5-ounce white or chartreuse, tipped with a strip of squid or a 4-inch white Gulp — bounced right through the rip structure in 25 to 40 feet where the current breaks over the shoal. It's not a wide-open bite. You need to hit the tide change right, and you need to be patient through a lot of nothing before the rod loads up. Middle Ground Light has been similar — better at first light and again in that last hour of daylight, live bunker on a fish-finder rig with 3 feet of 40-pound fluorocarbon leader has out-produced anything artificial when there's bait stacked, and there has been bait stacked. Bunker schools have been thick off Port Jeff and pushing west past Mount Sinai, and where you find the bunker balled up and nervous, the blues have been all over them — sometimes so aggressively you can see the surface boil from a quarter mile off. Bring wire or heavy mono leader if you're throwing metal into that — Deadly Dicks and Kastmasters have been getting bit fast and often once you find the school.

Fluke has been the more frustrating story. The inside-the-harbor bite has genuinely slowed as that warm water pushes fish toward the mouths, and the better fish have shown up right at the inlet drains — Port Jeff Inlet, the Mount Sinai channel edge, Northport Bay's outflow — on the last two hours of the outgoing when the current is still moving water but not screaming. Five-inch white or pearl Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom in 20 to 35 feet, have taken keepers to about 5 pounds, but it's been a grind. I'd call it a two-or-three-fish trip if you put in the drift time, not a limit trip. If the water keeps warming the way it has, expect this pattern to hold or get more pronounced through the month — fluke abandoning the shallow bay water for anything with moving current and depth.

Porgies have been the reliable part of the week, which is about what you'd expect in early July. Charles Island and the reef structure around the Norwalk Islands have been giving up steady numbers on simple hi-lo rigs with clam or squid strips, bottom in 20 to 30 feet on the calmer tide stages. Nothing exciting to write home about, but a fun, dependable box-filler while you wait for the bigger tide to turn on the bass. Weakfish, on the other hand, I have nothing to report. Water's warm enough by every measure we track, and the reports just aren't there — same story as the bay systems to our south. I'm not writing that fish off for the year, but the warm-water theory alone clearly isn't the trigger people hoped it would be.

Looking ahead, the new moon spring tide peaking July 11-13 is the thing to build your week around. If the current at Stratford Shoal and Middle Ground runs as hard as I expect, I'd be there on the last two hours of the outgoing both mornings, working the rip edges with bucktails and live bunker where you can get it. The PM flood-sunset window sliding east from the Kings Point area should reach our stretch of water by the weekend — worth a sunset sit at the Norwalk Islands or off Charles Island if the bass follow the bait the way they usually do on a building spring tide. And keep an eye on the bait — if bunker and sand eels keep stacking in the narrows the way they have, and the bonito corridor to our east keeps widening the way it's been reported doing off Rhode Island, there's a real chance we see the first bonito push into the eastern Sound edge before this month is out. Too early to bank on it, but that's exactly the kind of signal worth watching for.

reports.headline: New moon springs load up Stratford Shoal as fluke push out of the warm bays
reports.subhead: Central Sound stripers and blues are keying on the building tide while fluke abandon the overheated flats for cooler inlet water.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the Sound did what it usually does in early July — it split into two different fisheries depending on which side of the rip you were standing on. A few days of northeast wind kept upwelling going along the eastern approaches, holding Stratford Shoal and the water off Middle Ground Light noticeably cooler than the bays tucked in behind Oyster Bay and the Norwalk Islands. Those inner bays have been creeping into the upper 70s, and that temperature split is doing more to organize the bite right now than any single tide or moon phase. Bait doesn't like 78-degree water any more than gamefish do, and both have been sliding toward the cooler edges — the channels, the inlets, the rips where current keeps things mixed.

This week the moon goes new around the 11th-13th, and that means building spring tides through the weekend — bigger swings, more current, more water moved on every stage. For Central Sound that's a big deal because our structure — Stratford Shoal, the Norwalk Islands rock piles, Charles Island — all depends on current to stack bait against something solid. The best alignment I'm watching is the PM flood pushing into sunset Friday through Monday. That's the first evening high-tide window we've had line up with dusk since the June full moon, and historically that's when the bigger fish in this zone decide to feed instead of just cruise. If the wind stays out of the south-southwest and doesn't blow the surface into chop, I'd have my rod in the water for that window over anything else this week.

Striper fishing has been real but it's work, not a gimme. The Stratford Shoal rip on the last two hours of the ebb has been the most consistent — bass in the 24 to 34-inch range on bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig in 25 to 40 feet, and a few better fish, high 30s, coming off live-lined bunker snagged right off the surface schools near the Shoal buoy. Bucktails — 1.5 to 2-ounce white or chartreuse, tipped with a strip of pork rind or a white Gulp swimming mullet — have worked the drift along the rock edges off the Norwalk Islands on the last of the incoming, especially around Sheffield Island and the Cockenoe Reef complex. Nothing has been stacked thick. You're picking off two or three quality fish a trip if you put in the time and hit the tide right, not backing into a blitz.

Bluefish have been the more reliable action for guys who just want bent rods. Peanut bunker showed up thick around Charles Island and the outer Norwalk Islands over the last week, and the blues have been all over them on the tide change — surface blitzes early and late in the day, poppers and metal getting hit almost as soon as they land. Nothing giant, mostly 2 to 4 pounds, but if you want a guaranteed bend in the rod that's your play right now, especially the first hour of light off Charles Island before the boat traffic picks up.

Fluke are the interesting story this week because the pattern has genuinely shifted. The warm bay water — I've heard numbers close to 79 degrees in the shallow flats off Oyster Bay and Huntington — has pushed the better fluke out of the bay and into the channels and inlet mouths where the water stays cooler and better oxygenated. Port Jefferson Harbor's outer channel and the mouth of the Eatons Neck cut have both been holding fish in 30 to 40 feet on the outgoing tide. Standard drift with 3/4-ounce bucktails tipped with white Gulp Swimming Mullets, or plain bait rigs with squid strips, has been the ticket. Fish to 5 pounds have come out of that deeper water, though the average fish is closer to 18 to 20 inches — solid eating fish, not doormats. If you've been fishing the shallow flats all June and getting nothing, this is the week to run out to the deeper structure instead.

Porgies remain the honest bread-and-butter fish of the zone. Middle Ground Light and the rock piles around Stratford Shoal are holding good numbers, and a simple high-low rig with sandworms or clam strips in 20 to 35 feet on either tide will keep a cooler full. Nothing flashy, but it's the most reliable thing going in Central Sound right now.

Weakfish, I'll be honest, are still a no-show. Water temps have been above the old 70-degree threshold for over two weeks now and I haven't heard of a single fish. That old rule of thumb about weakfish showing once the water warms just isn't holding up anymore — necessary, apparently, but not enough on its own. I'd stop planning trips around it.

As for bonito — it's too early for Central Sound. That corridor is spreading out east right now, Newport down through Point Judith and the Block Island edges, and the real push into our waters typically doesn't happen until August when the bait funnels through the narrows. Worth watching, not worth a special trip yet.

Looking ahead, I'm circling Friday through Monday for the evening flood at Stratford Shoal and the Norwalk Islands. Big spring tide, sunset alignment, cooler water still holding bait against structure — that's the recipe. If the wind cooperates I expect a better grade of striper to show up on that tide than what we've seen through the neap stretch. Plan B if the bass don't cooperate is the fluke drift off Eatons Neck — that pattern's been steady enough to fall back on.

reports.headline: Post-blow shelf break opens up east of the Hudson — yellowfin on the warm seam
reports.subhead: A widened thermal edge and a darkening moon set up the best canyon window of the season, while bluefin stack the 20-fathom breaks closer to home.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week beat us up before it paid us back. We had a blow roll through that put a chop on Veatch and Hydrographer that nobody with sense wanted to run into, and for three days the fleet sat at the dock watching the forecast instead of the water. But blows do something out here that flat calm never does — they mix the shelf water and sharpen the edges. When it finally laid down Tuesday night, the boats that got out found a shelf-slope thermal break pushing 10.3 degrees Fahrenheit, the widest differential we've seen all season. That's not a subtle seam. That's a wall you can practically see on the plotter before you see it in the water color.

This week the moon is sliding toward new, which means darker nights and building current — good for the squid-light program on bluefin, tougher on slack-tide structure bites closer to the beach. Tides are building toward the new-moon springs that peak around the 11th through 13th, and that's going to matter more for the guys working the 20-fathom breaks than it will out at the canyons, where the tuna don't care much what the tide is doing at Montauk Point. Water temps on the shelf have been climbing with the second warming surge off Georges Bank, and that's re-energized the Veatch/Hydrographer differential after a stretch where the two canyons were running nearly identical and giving us no reason to pick one over the other. Now there's a reason again.

Wednesday and Thursday were the first real post-blow window and the fleet made the most of it. Yellowfin on the 100-fathom line, working the warm seam between Wilmington and Poor Man's and pushing up the Hudson east wall. Sizes have been mixed — some quality 60-to-80-pound fish mixed with smaller schoolies that show up in pockets and then vanish. The pattern that's worked is trolling a spread of ballyhoo with green machines and small Joe Baggs-style minnows on the shortest lines to mimic the sand eel and squid bait that's been thick on the meter, then switching to spinning gear with stickbaits and poppers the moment you see birds working or fish showing on top. Don't troll through a surface push — stop short, cast into it, and let the fish come to you. That's cost me fish in years past when I plowed straight into a school with four rods in the water instead of pulling back and picking up a popper rod.

Bigeye have been mixed in with the yellowfin on the same warm seam, mostly on the night bite — drift a rigged squid or a big Illex-style jig down under the boat once the sun's down and the current's moving, and don't be shocked if it's a bigeye instead of the yellowfin you were expecting. The squid have been the story all season out here — thick on the sounder, and that's exactly why the tuna have been willing to sit on structure instead of just roaming open water like they did earlier in the season.

Closer to the beach, the bluefin story is the one I'd chase if I only had a day boat and not the fuel budget for a full canyon run. The northeast upwelling this week has sharpened the 20-to-30 fathom breaks, and the corridor out toward Coimbra has bluefin sitting right on the structure at around 20 fathoms. With the moon going dark, the overnight squid-light program is going to be the right call — get out there before dusk, get your lights down, and let the squid stack up under the hull. Once they're thick, switch to jigging or a lightly weighted live squid under a balloon. It's not a fast bite, but it's a real one, and it beats burning four hours each way to the canyon for a coin-flip day.

White marlin haven't shown yet on our side of the ledger. The warm plume that's supposed to trigger the first flags is still pushing toward the bank, and historically that shows up on the mid-Atlantic canyons before it ever reaches us. I wouldn't rig for marlin out of Montauk or Block Island yet — I'd keep the spread tuna-focused and treat any marlin shot as a bonus, not a plan.

Wahoo and mahi have been incidental so far — a few mahi picked up around lobster gear and weedlines on the way out, nothing organized enough to call a pattern. If you're running out anyway, keep a light spinning rod rigged with a small stickbait for anything holding under floating debris. Costs you nothing and it's paid off more than once for me on the ride out.

Looking ahead, the fuel math still rules this beat. From Montauk, Veatch is the shorter run and it's carrying the better thermal setup right now with that Georges Bank surge feeding it — that's where I'd point the bow if I only had one shot this week. If the seas build again with the new moon current, I'd rather work the closer bluefin corridor at night than fight a long slog to Hydrographer in building swell. Best case, that shelf edge holds through the weekend and the yellowfin stay stacked on the warm seam — I've seen that happen before when a strong post-blow break sets up this clean. If it slides or the water mixes back down, I'd shift effort to the bluefin breaks and wait for the next window. Either way, check the swell forecast before you commit fuel — the canyon bite is real right now, but it's only worth the run if the ocean lets you fish it comfortably once you get there.

zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

reports.headline: Widest Thermal Edge of the Season Lights Up Poor Man's–Wilmington Seam for Yellowfin
reports.subhead: A post-blow window with a 10-degree break on the shelf has tuna stacked on the 100-fathom line — and the white marlin clock just started ticking.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week beat us up a little. We had that stretch of onshore breeze push through and stir the shelf water, which is never what you want heading into a canyon run — it mixes the layers, softens the edges, and scatters bait that had been holding tight along the 100-fathom curve. I had two boats scrub trips out of Cape May because the seas weren't worth the fuel bill, and the guys who did get out found the color gone green and confused instead of that clean blue break we chase. But blows like that have a way of setting the table for what comes after, and this one did exactly that.

As of Wednesday-Thursday we're sitting on the best structural setup I've seen all year — a 10.3-degree shelf-slope edge, the widest thermal break of the season, running right through the Wilmington-to-Poor Man's seam and continuing over toward the Hudson east wall. That's not a subtle temperature line, that's a wall of water the bait can't cross, and it's stacking yellowfin right on top of it. The moon's also working in our favor for the overnight game — we're on the darkening side heading toward the new moon around July 11-13, which is exactly when squid stack up under the lights and bluefin come up to feed on them without a lot of moonlight to spook them off. Put those two things together — a hard thermal edge for the daytime yellowfin bite and a dark moon for the overnight squid game — and you've got a genuine one-two punch this week.

On the yellowfin, I'm running numbers along the 100-fathom curve off Poor Man's and working the warm seam east toward Wilmington. Rough marks I'm using: Poor Man's drop at 38°47'N, 73°08'W, and the Wilmington seam edge around 38°58'N, 73°00'W where that Lindenkohl warm water is bleeding into the wall. Spreader bars — green machines and Ilanders in dark colors — pulled tight to the edge where the green water meets the blue, ballyhoo behind, and we've been getting bit on the up-current side of the break where the bait gets pinned. Fish have run 30 to 60 pounds, nothing giant, but a consistent grade, and multiple hookups on the troll when we hit the right push of current against that thermal wall. The bite's not lights-out — some boats worked six, seven hours before finding the right stretch of edge — but when you find it, it's been worth the ride.

The bluefin game has shifted midshore, and that's where the NE upwelling has really sharpened things up. The 20-to-30 fathom break is holding fish tight, and the Coimbra corridor at roughly 20 fathoms has been the address to know — squid jigs and diamond jigs working, but the real producer has been the overnight squid-light setup: run the lights after dark, let the squid ball up under the hull, and jig or livebait them straight down. With the moon going dark this week that program should only get better through the weekend. Schoolie-to-mid-50-pound class bluefin, nothing giant yet, but steady enough that it's worth an overnight trip if you've got the fuel range and the patience to sit on the spot.

Mahi have been a bonus, not a target — picking up gaffer-class fish and a few schoolies under weed lines and debris scattered along the edge, mostly as a chunk bite while we're soaking baits for tuna. Wahoo have shown on the high-speed troll gear when boats have run planers deep along the drop-off, but that's been hit or miss — one for three trips is about where that stands right now, so I wouldn't build a whole day around it.

Here's the one I've got my eye on for the next week and a half: white marlin. The warm plume that's been building is starting to push up onto the bank, and that's the trigger we watch for every year — first flags at the mid-Atlantic canyons usually show within seven to ten days of that push showing up on the charts. I'd be watching Norfolk and the Poor Man's edge closest to the bank contour for the first sightings. If you're rigging for it, naked and lightly-skirted ballyhoo on light drags, worked right along that same temperature break that's holding the yellowfin, is the way I'd start. It hasn't happened yet — I want to be straight with you on that — but the signals are lining up the way they have in years when the bite showed up fast once it started.

My read for the week: Wednesday-Thursday is the best window to run the Poor Man's-Wilmington seam while that 10-degree break holds — if seas cooperate, that's where I'd put my boat. If the wind builds again this weekend like it's shown signs of doing, I'd shift plans to the overnight bluefin program at Coimbra where the dark moon favors the squid lights regardless of surface chop. Either way, run your temperature gauge harder than your fuel gauge this week — the edge is the story, and it's sitting right where the charts say it should be.

reports.headline: Widest edge of the season lights up yellowfin at the Washington wall
reports.subhead: A post-blow shelf break pushed the temperature differential to 10.3°F this week — the sharpest structural setup we've seen all year, and the fish know it.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week's blow did what blows always do out here — it stirred the pot and then walked away, leaving something better behind. We had two days of sloppy swell and a hard NE push that shut the door on running offshore, but that same wind did the real work underneath the surface. It sharpened the shelf-slope break to 10.3 degrees Fahrenheit — the widest thermal edge I've measured all season — and it stacked cold upwelled water against the warm Gulf Stream filament sitting on the 100-fathom line. That's the kind of contrast that concentrates bait, and bait concentrates everything else. The same NE flow tightened up the 20 to 30 fathom breaks midshore, which is why the Coimbra corridor at 20 fathoms has bluefin stacked on it right now — smaller class fish, but plenty of them, and they're there because the upwelling pinned sand eels and squid against that break like a wall.

This week the moon's sliding toward new — dark by the 13th or 14th — which means less light on the surface at night and better squid marks under the boat. That's not a small thing out here. A darkening moon is when the overnight squid-light game gets serious: run the generator, hang the greenstick lights over the transom, and let the squid climb the water column into your Sabiki. If you can put fresh squid in the well before sunrise, you're fishing with better bait than ninety percent of the fleet, and on a bite this edge-dependent, bait quality is the difference between a two-fish day and a six-fish day. Tides aren't the driver out here the way they are inshore — it's the thermal structure and the moon-driven light levels that matter most this week.

The bite itself has been good, not great, and I want to be straight about that. Wednesday and Thursday were the best window we've had all season — the warm seam running from Wilmington down through Poor Man's, and the same signature showing up on our own west wall in 280 to 320 fathoms, produced yellowfin in the 35 to 55 pound class trolling a small spread of Green Machines and naked ballyhoo at 6 to 7 knots, working the temp break itself rather than blasting straight across it. The fish were sitting right on the color change — you could see it, dirty green water butting up against a cleaner blue edge — and every strike came within fifty yards of that line. Chunking behind the troll once we found the school put a few more in the box on butterflied bunker, but it wasn't a stack-and-load bite. More like find the edge, get two or three, watch it go quiet, move a half mile down the wall, find it again.

Bluefin have been the more consistent fish this week, and they're shallower than you'd think. The Coimbra corridor at 20 fathoms has had schools of 40 to 60 pound bluefin working bait balls on the surface mid-morning — small, fast-moving spreads with cedar plugs and green-and-yellow Ilanders in daylight, then the light game overnight once you anchor up or drift on the squid. That midshore bite is worth the shorter run if the canyon proper isn't cooperating, and this week it's been the more reliable of the two.

Wahoo have been a bycatch story so far — a couple came off high-speed spreads run wide off the wake in 400-plus fathoms south toward the Baltimore fingers, but nobody's targeting them yet with real intent. Mahi have shown around any floating structure or weed line we crossed running out — a few schoolies in the 5 to 12 pound range around a lobster pot ball southeast of the canyon mouth, worth a stop if you see anything floating, but not a fishery you'd plan a whole trip around right now.

White marlin is the one I'm watching hardest. The warm plume that's been building on the bank is the trigger everyone's waiting for, and the oceanography says we're 7 to 10 days out from the first real flags at the mid-Atlantic canyons. I'd have the dredge rigged and ready on any trip from here forward — better to be a week early with ballyhoo dredges soaking than a week late scrambling to re-rig on the ride out.

If I had one trip to make this week, I'd run Wednesday or Thursday if the wind allows, straight to the warm seam on the west wall, work the color change with a small troll spread, and keep squid gear rigged for an overnight anchor-up on the dark moon if the yellowfin bite is slow. Best case, that 10.3-degree break holds through the weekend and the yellowfin stack tighter on it. If it slides or collapses like these things sometimes do, I'd pivot inshore to the Coimbra bluefin — twenty fathoms of water and a reliable morning bite beats a long run to a wall that's gone quiet.

reports.headline: Post-Blow Edge Turns On Yellowfin at Wilmington — Widest Break of the Season
